text:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

While the US and the EU may differ on how to regulate tech, their lawmakers seem to agree on one thing: the West needs to ban AI-powered social scoring.

As they understand it, social scoring is a practice in which authoritarian governments—specifically China—rank people’s trustworthiness and punish them for undesirable behaviors, such as stealing or not paying back loans. Essentially, it’s seen as a dystopian superscore assigned to each citizen. 

The EU is currently negotiating a new law called the AI Act, which will ban member states, and maybe even private companies, from implementing such a system.

The trouble is, it’s “essentially banning thin air,” says Vincent Brussee, an analyst at the Mercator Institute for China Studies, a German think tank.

Back in 2014, China announced a six-year plan to build a system rewarding actions that build trust in society and penalizing the opposite. Eight years on, it’s only just released a draft law that tries to codify past social credit pilots and guide future implementation. 

There have been some contentious local experiments, such as one in the small city of Rongcheng in 2013, which gave every resident a starting personal credit score of 1,000 that can be increased or decreased by how their actions are judged. People are now able to opt out, and the local government has removed some controversial criteria. 

But these have not gained wider traction elsewhere and do not apply to the entire Chinese population. There is no countrywide, all-seeing social credit system with algorithms that rank people.

As my colleague Zeyi Yang explains, “the reality is, that terrifying system doesn’t exist, and the central government doesn’t seem to have much appetite to build it, either.” 

What has been implemented is mostly pretty low-tech. It’s a “mix of attempts to regulate the financial credit industry, enable government agencies to share data with each other, and promote state-sanctioned moral values,” Zeyi writes. 

Kendra Schaefer, a partner at Trivium China, a Beijing-based research consultancy, who compiled a report on the subject for the US government, couldn’t find a single case in which data collection in China led to automated sanctions without human intervention. The South China Morning Post found that in Rongcheng, human “information gatherers” would walk around town and write down people’s misbehavior using a pen and paper. 

The myth originates from a pilot program called Sesame Credit, developed by Chinese tech company Alibaba. This was an attempt to assess people’s creditworthiness using customer data at a time when the majority of Chinese people didn’t have a credit card, says Brussee. The effort became conflated with the social credit system as a whole in what Brussee describes as a “game of Chinese whispers.” And the misunderstanding took on a life of its own. 

The irony is that while US and European politicians depict this as a problem stemming from authoritarian regimes, systems that rank and penalize people are already in place in the West. Algorithms designed to automate decisions are being rolled out en masse and used to deny people housing, jobs, and basic services. 

For example in Amsterdam, authorities have used an algorithm to rank young people from disadvantaged neighborhoods according to their likelihood of becoming a criminal. They claim the aim is to prevent crime and help offer better, more targeted support.  

But in reality, human rights groups argue, it has increased stigmatization and discrimination. The young people who end up on this list face more stops from police, home visits from authorities, and more stringent supervision from school and social workers.

It’s easy to take a stand against a dystopian algorithm that doesn’t really exist. But as lawmakers in both the EU and the US strive to build a shared understanding of AI governance, they would do better to look closer to home. Americans do not even have a federal privacy law that would offer some basic protections against algorithmic decision making. 

There is also a dire need for governments to conduct honest, thorough audits of the way authorities and companies use AI to make decisions about our lives. They might not like what they find—but that makes it all the more crucial for them to look.   

Deeper Learning

A bot that watched 70,000 hours of Minecraft could unlock AI’s next big thing

Research company OpenAI has built an AI that binged on 70,000 hours of videos of people playing Minecraft in order to play the game better than any AI before. It’s a breakthrough for a powerful new technique, called imitation learning, that could be used to train machines to carry out a wide range of tasks by watching humans do them first. It also raises the potential that sites like YouTube could be a vast and untapped source of training data. 

Why it’s a big deal: Imitation learning can be used to train AI to control robot arms, drive cars, or navigate websites. Some people, such as Meta’s chief AI scientist, Yann LeCun, think that watching videos will eventually help us train an AI with human-level intelligence. Read Will Douglas Heaven’s story here.

Bits and Bytes

Meta’s game-playing AI can make and break alliances like a human

Diplomacy is a popular strategy game in which seven players compete for control of Europe by moving pieces around on a map. The game requires players to talk to each other and spot when others are bluffing. Meta’s new AI, called Cicero, managed to trick humans to win. 

It’s a big step forward toward AI that can help with complex problems, such as planning routes around busy traffic and negotiating contracts. But I’m not going to lie—it’s also an unnerving thought that an AI can so successfully deceive humans. (MIT Technology Review) 

We could run out of data to train AI language programs 

The trend of creating ever bigger AI models means we need even bigger data sets to train them. The trouble is, we might run out of suitable data by 2026, according to a paper by researchers from Epoch, an AI research and forecasting organization. This should prompt the AI community to come up with ways to do more with existing resources. (MIT Technology Review)

Stable Diffusion 2.0 is out

The open-source text-to-image AI Stable Diffusion has been given a big facelift, and its outputs are looking a lot sleeker and more realistic than before. It can even do hands. The pace of Stable Diffusion’s development is breathtaking. Its first version only launched in August. We are likely going to see even more progress in generative AI well into next year.

text:
In a workshop in Rotterdam in the Netherlands, Philip Nitschke—“Dr. Death” or “the Elon Musk of assisted suicide” to some—is overseeing the last few rounds of testing on his new Sarco machine before shipping it to Switzerland, where he says its first user is waiting. 

This is the third prototype that Nitschke’s nonprofit, Exit International, has 3D-printed and wired up. Number one has been exhibited in Germany and Poland. “Number two was a disaster,” he says. Now he’s ironed out the manufacturing errors and is ready to launch: “This is the one that will be used.”

A coffin-size pod with Star Trek stylings, the Sarco is the culmination of Nitschke’s 25-year campaign to “demedicalize death” through technology. Sealed inside the machine, a person who has chosen to die must answer three questions: Who are you? Where are you? And do you know what will happen when you press that button? 

Here’s what will happen: The Sarco will fill with nitrogen gas. Its occupant will pass out in less than a minute and die by asphyxiation in around five. 

A recording of that short, final interview will then be handed over to the Swiss authorities. Nitschke has not approached the Swiss government for approval, but Switzerland is one of a handful of countries that have legalized assisted suicide. It is permitted as long as people who wish to die perform the final act themselves. 

Nitschke wants to make assisted suicide as unassisted as possible, giving people who have chosen to kill themselves autonomy, and thus dignity, in their final moments. “You really don’t need a doctor to die,” he says. 

Because the Sarco uses nitrogen, a widely available gas, rather than the barbiturates that are typically used in euthanasia clinics, it does not require a physician to administer an injection or sign off on lethal drugs. 

At least that’s the idea. Nitschke has not yet been able to sidestep the medical establishment fully. Switzerland requires that candidates for euthanasia demonstrate mental capacity, Nitschke says, which is typically assessed by a psychiatrist. “There’s still a belief that if a person is asking to die, they’ve got some sort of undiagnosed mental illness,” he says. “That it’s not rational for a person to seek death.”

He believes he has a solution, however. Exit International is working on an algorithm that Nitschke hopes will allow people to perform a kind of psychiatric self-assessment on a computer. In theory, if a person passed this online test, the program would provide a four-digit code to activate the Sarco. “That’s the goal,” says Nitschke. “Having said all that, the project is proving very difficult.” 

Nitschke’s mission may seem extreme—even outrageous—to some. And his belief in the power of algorithms may prove to be overblown. But he is not the only one looking to involve technology, and AI in particular, in life-or-death decisions.

Yet where Nitschke sees AI as a way to empower individuals to make the ultimate choice by themselves, others wonder if AI can help relieve humans from the burden of such choices. AI is already being used to triage and treat patients across a growing number of health-care fields. As algorithms become an increasingly important part of care, we must ensure that their role is limited to medical decisions, not moral ones.

Medical care is a limited resource. Patients must wait for appointments to get tests or treatment. Those in need of organ transplants must wait for suitable hearts or kidneys. Vaccines must be rolled out first to the most vulnerable (in countries that have them). And during the worst of the pandemic, when hospitals faced a shortage of beds and ventilators, doctors had to make snap decisions about who would receive immediate care and who would not—with tragic consequences. 

The covid crisis brought the need for such choices into harsh focus—and led many to wonder if algorithms could help. Hospitals around the world bought new or co-opted existing AI tools to assist with triage. Some hospitals in the UK that had been exploring the use of AI tools to screen chest x-rays jumped on those tools as a fast, cheap way to identify the most severe covid cases. Suppliers of this tech, such as https://t.co/gZ6COt3eaI, based in Mumbai, India, and Lunit, based in Seoul, Korea, took on contracts in Europe, the US, and Africa. Diagnostic Robotics, an Israeli firm that supplies AI-based triage tools to hospitals in Israel, India, and the US, has said it saw a sevenfold jump in demand for its technology in the first year of the pandemic. Business in health-care AI has been booming ever since. 

This rush to automate raises big questions with no easy answers. What kinds of decision is it appropriate to use an algorithm to make? How should these algorithms be built? And who gets a say in how they work? 

Rhema Vaithianathan, the director of the Centre for Social Data Analytics and a professor at the Auckland University of Technology in New Zealand, who focuses on tech in health and welfare, thinks it is right that people are asking AI to help make big decisions. “We should be addressing problems that clinicians find really hard,” she says. 

One of the projects she is working on involves a teen mental-health service, where young people are diagnosed and treated for self-harming behaviors. There is high demand for the clinic, and so it needs to maintain a high turnover, discharging patients as soon as possible so that more can be brought in. 

Doctors face the difficult choice between keeping existing patients in care and treating new ones. “Clinicians don’t discharge people because they’re super scared of them self-harming,” says Vaithianathan. “That’s their nightmare scenario.”

Vaithianathan and her colleagues have tried to develop a machine-learning model that can predict which patients are most at risk of future self-harming behavior and which are not, using a wide range of data, including health records and demographic information, to give doctors an additional resource in their decision-­making. “I’m always looking for those cases where a clinician is struggling and would appreciate an algorithm,” she says. 

The project is in its early stages, but so far the researchers have found that there may not be enough data to train a model that can make accurate predictions. They will keep trying. The model does not have to be perfect to help doctors, Vaithianathan says. 

They are not the only team trying to predict the risk of discharging patients. A review published in 2021 highlighted 43 studies by researchers claiming to use machine-learning models to predict whether patients will be readmitted or die after they leave hospitals in the US. None were accurate enough for clinical use, but the authors look forward to a time when such models “improve quality of care and reduce health-care costs.”  

And yet even when AI seems accurate, scholars and regulators alike call for caution. For one thing, the data that algorithms follow and the way they follow it are human artifacts, riddled with prejudice. Health data is overpopulated by people who are white and male, for example, which skews its predictive power. And the models offer a veneer of objectivity that can lead people to pass the buck on ethical decisions, trusting the machine rather than questioning its output. 

This ongoing problem is a theme in David Robinson’s new book, Voices in the Code, about the democratization of AI. Robinson, a visiting scholar at the Social Science Matrix at the University of California, Berkeley, and a member of the faculty of Apple University, tells the story of Belding Scribner. In 1960 Scribner, a nephrologist in Seattle, inserted a short Teflon tube known as a shunt into some of his patients’ arms to prevent their blood from clotting while they underwent dialysis treatment. The innovation allowed people with kidney disease to stay on dialysis indefinitely, transforming kidney failure from a fatal condition into a long-term illness.  

When word got out, Scribner was inundated with requests for treatment. But he could not take everyone. Whom should he help and whom should he turn away? He soon realized that this wasn’t a medical decision but an ethical one. He set up a committee of laypeople to decide. Of course, their choices weren’t perfect. The prejudices at the time led the committee to favor married men with jobs and families, for example. 

The way Robinson tells it, the lesson we should take from Scribner’s work is that certain processes—bureaucratic, technical, and algorithmic—can make difficult questions seem neutral and objective. They can obscure the moral aspects of a choice—and the sometimes awful consequences.

“Bureaucracy itself can serve as a way of converting hard moral problems into boring technical ones,” Robinson writes. This phenomenon predates computers, he says, “but software-based systems can accelerate and amplify this trend. Quantification can be a moral anesthetic, and computers make that anesthetic easier than ever to administer.”

Whatever the process, we need to let that moral anesthetic wear off and examine the painful implications of the decision at hand. For Scribner, that meant asking an open panel of laypeople—instead of a group of ostensibly objective doctors meeting behind closed doors—whom to save. Today, it could mean asking for high-stakes algorithms to be audited. For now, the auditing of algorithms by independent parties is more wish-list item than standard practice. But, again using the example of kidney disease, Robinson shows how it can be done. 

By the 2000s, an algorithm had been developed in the US to identify recipients for donated kidneys. But some people were unhappy with how the algorithm had been designed. In 2007, Clive Grawe, a kidney transplant candidate from Los Angeles, told a room full of medical experts that their algorithm was biased against older people like him. The algorithm had been designed to allocate kidneys in a way that maximized years of life saved. This favored younger, wealthier, and whiter patients, Grawe and other patients argued.

Such bias in algorithms is common. What’s less common is for the designers of those algorithms to agree that there is a problem. After years of consultation with laypeople like Grawe, the designers found a less biased way to maximize the number of years saved—by, among other things, considering overall health in addition to age. One key change was that the majority of donors, who are often people who have died young, would no longer be matched only to recipients in the same age bracket. Some of those kidneys could now go to older people if they were otherwise healthy. As with Scribner’s committee, the algorithm still wouldn’t make decisions that everyone would agree with. But the process by which it was developed is harder to fault. 

“I didn’t want to sit there and give the injection. If you want it, you press the button.”

Philip Nitschke

Nitschke, too, is asking hard questions. 

A former doctor who burned his medical license after a years-long legal dispute with the Australian Medical Board, Nitschke has the distinction of being the first person to legally administer a voluntary lethal injection to another human. In the nine months between July 1996, when the Northern Territory of Australia brought in a law that legalized euthanasia, and March 1997, when Australia’s federal government overturned it, Nitschke helped four of his patients to kill themselves.

The first, a 66-year-old carpenter named Bob Dent, who had suffered from prostate cancer for five years, explained his decision in an open letter: “If I were to keep a pet animal in the same condition I am in, I would be prosecuted.”  

Nitschke wanted to support his patients’ decisions. Even so, he was uncomfortable with the role they were asking him to play. So he made a machine to take his place. “I didn’t want to sit there and give the injection,” he says. “If you want it, you press the button.”

The machine wasn’t much to look at: it was essentially a laptop hooked up to a syringe. But it achieved its purpose. The Sarco is an iteration of that original device, which was later acquired by the Science Museum in London. Nitschke hopes an algorithm that can carry out a psychiatric assessment will be the next step.

But there’s a good chance those hopes will be dashed. Creating a program that can assess someone’s mental health is an unsolved problem—and a controversial one. As Nitschke himself notes, doctors do not agree on what it means for a person of sound mind to choose to die. “You can get a dozen different answers from a dozen different psychiatrists,” he says. In other words, there is no common ground on which an algorithm could even be built. 

But that’s not the takeaway here. Like Scribner, Nitschke is asking what counts as a medical decision, what counts as an ethical one, and who gets to choose. Scribner thought that laypeople—representing society as a whole—should choose who received dialysis, because when patients have more or less equal chances of survival, who lives and who dies is no longer a technical question. As Robinson describes it, society must be responsible for such decisions, although the process can still be encoded in an algorithm if it’s done inclusively and transparently. For Nitschke, assisted suicide is also an ethical decision, one that individuals must make for themselves. The Sarco, and the theoretical algorithm he imagines, would only protect their ability to do so.

AI will become increasingly useful, perhaps essential, as populations boom and resources stretch. Yet the real work will be acknowledging the awfulness and arbitrariness of many of the decisions AI will be called on to make. And that’s on us. 

For Robinson, devising algorithms is a bit like legislation: “In a certain light, the question of how best to make software code that will govern people is just a special case of how best to make laws. People disagree about the merits of different ways of making high-stakes software, just as they disagree about the merits of different ways of making laws.” And it is people—in the broadest sense—who are ultimately responsible for the laws we have.

#designmatters26 You Are What You Pay Attention To / Sydney Nguyen & Brittany Roberts (Slow Tech Studio)
Playing the Attention Economy: Making Invisible Systems Visible

Attention Attention — A Board Game Exploring the Influence and Responsibility of Design

● Who Is Designing Our Attention?

We check our phones within minutes of waking up, respond to notifications, scroll through social feeds, and often spend far more time than we intended. These everyday behaviors aren't simply the result of personal habits or a lack of self-discipline. They're shaped by digital environments deliberately designed to capture and retain our attention.

In this talk, Sydney Nguyen and Brittany Roberts, both former UX designers at Amazon who worked across shopping, AI, and logistics experiences, introduced their approach to making the mechanisms of the attention economy visible and creating opportunities for collective discussion.

Together, they founded Slow Tech Studio, a creative practice exploring more intentional relationships with technology through installations and educational workshops.

For them, "slow" doesn't necessarily mean spending less time with technology. It means creating space to notice how technology fits into our lives and whether that relationship is actually working for us.

● Attention Is Designed: A Systemic Problem, Not an Individual Failure

Subscription flows that make cancellation difficult. Urgent messages pushing us to buy now. Endless feeds and recommendations encouraging us to keep scrolling.

These patterns have become so familiar that we barely notice them.

The speakers compared the attention economy to a magic trick. While we're focused on one thing, something else is happening behind the scenes. This is the art of misdirection: shaping what people notice and what they overlook.

Understanding how the trick works doesn't make us immune to it. We'll probably keep scrolling. But once we recognize the mechanisms, we begin to see our interactions differently.

One particularly important insight was the asymmetry of power within the system.

The people most affected by technology often have the least power to change it, while those who can change it are frequently the ones building it.

Users, parents, educators, designers, product teams, executives, and policymakers all experience the same system from different positions. Each holds a piece of the puzzle, but rarely sees the pieces others are holding.

Rather than asking what each stakeholder group needs independently, the designers reframed the challenge:

How might we create something that allows people to see the system from different perspectives and learn from one another?

● Four Apertures of Influence: A Framework for Design Judgment

Inspired by the aperture of a camera lens, the team developed the Four Apertures of Influence, a framework for examining individual interactions while keeping their broader context and relationships in focus.

The framework offers four questions to strengthen our design judgment.

1. Intent — What are we trying to influence?

Before asking whether an interaction works, we should ask what it's working toward and whose goals it serves.

Duolingo uses streaks to encourage daily language practice. Repetition can support learning, but maintaining a streak and actually learning aren't the same thing.

Similarly, Paired, an app designed to help couples connect, uses streak mechanics. But imagine a couple spending a wonderful phone-free weekend together and losing their streak.

Their relationship may have improved, even though the metric suggests they've fallen behind.

The question is whether our metrics support the intended outcome or begin competing with it.

2. Context — How might this experience be different for different people?

Design intent doesn't automatically translate into lived experience.

The speakers compared shopping apps with different levels of information density, the interaction structures of BeReal and TikTok, social features in fitness apps such as Strava, and the different approaches to content discovery taken by Netflix and Libby.

Minimalism isn't automatically clearer for everyone. Frictionless experiences aren't always better. Social proof can encourage participation, but it can also create comparison and pressure.

Sometimes guidance helps people make decisions. At other times, they need room to explore.

The right design depends on the task, cultural context, expectations, familiarity, and what people actually need.

3. Power — What agency are we giving people?

People aren't inherently powerless, but they can be disempowered by design.

The speakers contrasted Adobe's subscription cancellation experience, including potentially costly early termination conditions, with Blinkist's subscription interface, which makes the upcoming charge date prominent and offers a reminder.

Both interfaces support business goals, but they give users different levels of transparency and control.

Providing a button or a disclaimer isn't enough. Meaningful agency means helping people understand their options, anticipate consequences, and make informed decisions aligned with their own intentions.

4. Outcome — What are we creating over time?

Design outcomes often extend far beyond the initial interaction, affecting individuals, relationships, communities, and society.

Slow Tech Studio explored this through an interactive installation in Seattle: a phone booth where participants could experiment with conversational AI and curated icebreakers.

What began as an individual AI experience unexpectedly created opportunities for human connection. Strangers started talking, sharing experiences, and laughing together around the installation.

The project demonstrated how an experience designed for one person can create ripple effects across a wider community.

● “Attention Attention”: Turning the Attention Economy into a Playable System

A framework can help us understand a system intellectually. But understanding its structure isn't the same as experiencing its constraints, competing incentives, and power dynamics from within.

As the speakers put it, systems must be felt.

That insight led to Attention Attention, an analog board game designed to simulate the attention economy.

The game is designed for four players, ages 14 and up, and takes approximately 60 minutes.

Players take on different roles: two users, one builder, and one advertiser. Each has different objectives, incentives, and ways to influence the system.

Across a 28-tile board, players encounter familiar mechanisms from digital products, including confirmshaming, ad blocking, data collection, shadow profiles, and content moderation.

A builder might deploy a guilt-driven opt-out message to collect more data. A user might respond with an ad blocker. An advertiser might buy data to improve targeting.

These decisions affect not only individual players but also the shared system.

Two collective indicators, Trust and Community, track the health of the platform and the people participating in it.

If trust collapses, the entire system can fail, and everyone loses.

Players must therefore balance their individual goals against the consequences of their decisions for others.

Some cards introduce difficult trade-offs. For example, an overwhelmed content moderation team may need to be rebuilt or replaced with AI. Players debate the options, negotiate, and vote, but ultimately someone must make the decision.

Other moments allow players to cooperate. Two users might play an "Unplugged" card together, choosing a phone-free day that helps restore the system's health.

At the end of the game, a recap reveals the patterns encountered, decisions made, turning points, and moments of solidarity.

The goal isn't simply to win. It's to develop a shared vocabulary for recognizing the mechanisms of the attention economy and discussing their consequences.

Players experience the same four apertures introduced earlier:

Intent: Different stakeholders pursue different definitions of success.

Context: Events change the circumstances and incentives surrounding decisions.

Power: Players have unequal levels of influence over the system.

Outcome: Individual actions contribute to collective measures of trust and well-being.

By making these dynamics tangible, the game transforms abstract discussions about technology into a shared, participatory experience.

● From Individual Responsibility to Collective Design Ethics

The goal of this project isn't to reject smartphones or social media, nor is it simply to teach people better self-control.

It's to create a space where people who design technology and people who live with it can examine its influence together.

What makes Attention Attention particularly compelling is its use of role-playing, game mechanics, and physical interaction to explore a complex sociotechnical system.

Rather than explaining the attention economy through diagrams or lectures alone, the designers created an experience in which participants can feel competing incentives, negotiate conflicting priorities, and confront the consequences of their choices.

The game makes visible the trade-offs that are often hidden behind seemingly simple product decisions.

The speakers emphasized that changing systems requires more than individual awareness or personal discipline. It requires collective understanding, shared language, and collaboration across different perspectives.

“The systems we design reflect us and what our industry values.”

As designers, we influence what people notice, where they spend their time, and what they come to value.

Recognizing that influence—and taking responsibility for it—is essential.

Slow Tech Studio's work reminds us that design isn't only about creating more seamless interactions or increasing engagement. It's also about questioning the systems we build, understanding their long-term consequences, and giving people the agency to shape their own relationships with technology.

And perhaps the most effective way to start that conversation is not through another screen, but by sitting around a table and playing together.

text:
✈️ GOING TO CHINA? GO. BUT LEAVE YOUR REAL PHONE AT HOME.

Reports this month describe long lines of Filipinos at the Chinese visa application center in Makati. Defense Secretary Teodoro's advice: "Yes, go to China. Enjoy the beautiful culture," but "do not be brainwashed."

After 36 years in counterintelligence, here's what I'd add. Brainwashing isn't the main risk for most travelers. Your phone, your contacts and your data are.

🧭 Before you go:

1️⃣ Travel light on data. Bring a spare phone or a wiped one, with only the contacts and apps you need. Leave work email and sensitive files at home.
2️⃣ Know the law you're entering. China's counter-espionage law, expanded in 2023, defines espionage broadly enough to cover documents and data tied to "national security and interests." Western travel advisories also warn of arbitrary enforcement, including exit bans.
3️⃣ Assume your messages can be read. Chinese messaging apps operate under Chinese law, which requires companies to cooperate with state security work.
4️⃣ Don't photograph military sites, ports or government buildings, even by accident in the background.
5️⃣ Be wary of generous new contacts. A friendly offer of paid "research," consulting or a "think tank" paper is a classic recruitment approach.
6️⃣ Register with the Philippine Embassy or consulate and keep their contact numbers handy.

📌 Analysis: Travel builds understanding, and millions of people visit China safely every year. The point isn't fear. It's habits. The same precautions apply anywhere a state has broad surveillance powers and broad definitions of espionage. Go, enjoy the food and the history, and come home with photos, not problems.

📖 Good security habits are the quiet part of every safe trip. That's the counterintelligence lens behind Shadows Over the Archipelago, coming March 2027.
✈️ Enjoy the trip. Protect the phone.

Mehdi Hasan, why the hell did you come to America?

You weren’t fleeing dictatorship, persecution, or poverty. You came from Britain with a successful career. During this interview, you admitted America offered opportunities Britain could not.

So you came here, built your career, became a citizen, and now arrogantly lecture Americans about how our country is responsible for the Middle East’s dysfunction and suffering.

When Patrick Bet-David challenged you about why people flee Iran, Afghanistan, and Iraq, your immediate response was, “War that we caused.”

Pressed about Iran, you again redirected attention toward America.

Seriously?

The Iranian regime imprisons dissidents, murders protesters demanding freedom, sponsors terrorism, and threatens its neighbors. Those atrocities are decisions of Iran’s leadership, not tragedies imposed by Washington.

Yet you seem determined to blame America.

When challenged, you insist you never claimed EVERYTHING was America’s fault. Then stop reflexively blaming our country whenever someone raises the failures of foreign governments.

But my contempt for your position goes much further.

You voluntarily sought American citizenship. Nobody forced you to come here or swear allegiance to our country.

And your hostility toward American foreign policy was no secret. On October 9, 2020, the very day you became a citizen, you publicly described it as a mess and a disgrace.

I find it outrageous that someone displaying such profound apparent contempt for our country’s actions would seek American citizenship, and equally outrageous that our government would confer it.

I suspect many Americans share that disgust. I imagine plenty would gladly see someone displaying such contempt stripped of the citizenship he voluntarily sought.

And then there’s your platform.

In my opinion, you’ve amplified grievance, inflamed resentment, and encouraged impressionable audiences to view America as the villain in conflicts for which foreign governments bear enormous responsibility.

Your treatment of destructive protest is revealing. You disclaim violence while minimizing property destruction as broken windows. Dismissing destruction because perpetrators claim a righteous cause contributes, in my view, to an increasingly poisonous political environment.

That makes your influence more troubling than the opinions of some random loudmouth.

You have a substantial platform, and I believe you use it to deepen hostility toward the country whose citizenship you sought.

What did your oath mean, Mehdi? Allegiance to America, or merely access to its opportunities and privileges?

You chose this country because it offered something Britain couldn’t. You built your career here, became a citizen, and benefited from the nation you so readily condemn.

That’s the irony you seem incapable of appreciating.

Your own life is a more compelling argument for America’s greatness than your lectures are against it.

A naturalization certificate establishes citizenship. It does not establish sincerity, gratitude, or allegiance of conviction.

While you are legally an American, your rhetoric makes me question what becoming one meant to you.

You wanted everything America could offer, but when confronted with foreign regimes’ atrocities, you seem more interested in explaining America’s sins than holding those regimes responsible.

I think many Americans have had enough of that arrogance.

You chose America, Mehdi, and now use the opportunities it gave you as a platform for your sanctimonious contempt. 

Your lectures are little more than an outward projection of verbal spasms, dripping with arrogance and selective outrage. 

Many of us are thoroughly disgusted by your rhetoric, your excuses for foreign regimes, and your relentless finger-pointing at our country. 

Your arrogance is exceeded only by your ingratitude, and your contempt for our country is matched by the contempt many of us have developed for you.

The Human Authorization Requirement for Autonomous Warfare

1. The Strategic Problem

The accelerating deployment of autonomous weapons, artificial intelligence, distributed command systems, and increasingly independent military platforms creates a fundamental security problem: how does a government ensure that consequential lethal actions remain under legitimate human authority?

This problem extends across every operational domain:

Land: Autonomous vehicles, robotic weapons, and unmanned ground systems.
Air: Autonomous aircraft, drone swarms, and integrated air-defense systems.
Sea: Unmanned surface vessels, underwater platforms, and autonomous maritime weapons.
Cyber: AI-directed operations capable of producing physical consequences through industrial and infrastructure control systems.
Space: Orbital surveillance, autonomous spacecraft, satellite defense, cislunar operations, and future space-based military infrastructure.

As these systems become increasingly autonomous, software permissions, credentials, and conventional command authentication alone cannot establish that an identified human is physically present and authorizing a particular consequential action.

The problem is not simply whether a machine can execute an instruction. It is whether the instruction has legitimate, independently verifiable human authority.

2. The QCK Authorization Boundary

The Quantum Cardiac Key (QCK), developed by XMI LLC, proposes a hardware-enforced human authorization mechanism that binds an identified human identity and verified biological liveness to a cryptographic authorization boundary.

Its architecture combines:

Cardiac signal ingestion for biological liveness verification.
Quantum entropy generation for cryptographic randomness.
Cryptographic key derivation and fusion.
A trusted execution environment (TEE).
Ephemeral authorization keys.
Hardware-enforced invalidation and zeroization when required security conditions are lost.

The intended result is an authorization mechanism that does not depend solely on an AI system, operating system, or remote command platform reporting that a human has approved an action.

The authorization must be independently established through the hardware security boundary.

Importantly, a heartbeat alone is not consent. Biological liveness must be bound to an identified human's explicit authorization of a specific action, within defined operational limits.

3. Why Defense and Space Operations Need This

The emerging military environment is moving toward distributed autonomous operations in which decision-making and execution may occur across geographically separated, interconnected platforms.

This creates a growing distance between human command authority and machine execution.

In orbital and cislunar environments, the implications are particularly significant. Autonomous spacecraft, satellite networks, proximity operations, and future defensive systems may operate with substantial independence from terrestrial command centers.

Communications can be delayed, interrupted, degraded, or denied. A conventional authentication credential may remain valid even when its legitimate owner is no longer present.

QCK offers a potential additional security layer: requiring a verifiable, living human authorization event at the boundary where consequential authority is exercised.

This is relevant not only to weapons release, but also to other high-consequence operations involving strategic infrastructure, orbital assets, and autonomous systems.

4. The Sovereignty and Security Imperative

No sovereign government should have to depend on the unverified assertions of an autonomous system to establish who authorized a consequential action.

Nor should a nation's military authorization infrastructure become dependent on a single private technology provider.

Any serious deployment of QCK or comparable technology must support:
Sovereign control of authorization policies and keys.
Interoperability across domestic and allied defense systems.
Independent security testing and verification.
Multiple qualified hardware implementations.
Clear human accountability and auditable authorization records.

QCK's patent position does not replace the need for sovereign implementation, independent validation, or appropriate governance.

The objective should be a defensible human authorization standard, not a new single-vendor dependency.

5. The Requirement

Governments and allied defense organizations should consider hardware-enforced human authorization a foundational security requirement for autonomous systems capable of independently initiating lethal or otherwise strategically consequential actions.

Such systems should not be permitted to establish their own ultimate authority through software credentials, internal AI decisions, or self-reported human approval.

Authorization should be:
Attributable to an identified human.
Bound to verified biological liveness.
Explicitly associated with the action being authorized.
Cryptographically verifiable.
Limited in duration and operational scope.
Revocable, with defined safe-state behavior when authorization conditions fail.

This requirement must also account for multi-person authorization where the nature of the operation demands it.

6. The Geopolitical Question

The next generation of warfare will not be defined exclusively by which nation possesses the most capable autonomous systems.

It will also be defined by which nations can demonstrate that their autonomous systems remain accountable to legitimate human authority.

The question facing Washington, Brussels, NATO, and allied governments is not whether autonomous technology will advance. It will.

The question is whether human authorization will remain an enforceable physical and cryptographic requirement as that autonomy expands across land, sea, air, cyber, and space.

QCK proposes a means of establishing that boundary.

Not another password. Not another software permission. Not an AI claiming that a human approved its decision.

A cryptographically verifiable authorization event rooted in an identified, living human being.

Machines may execute. Humans retain authority.

text:
A new AI tool could help researchers discover previously unknown proteins and design entirely new ones. When harnessed, it could help unlock the development of more efficient vaccines, speed up research for the cure to cancer, or lead to completely new materials.

Alphabet-owned AI lab DeepMind took the world by surprise in 2020 when it announced AlphaFold, an AI tool that used deep learning to solve one of the “grand challenges” of biology: accurately predicting the shapes of proteins. Proteins are fundamental to life, and understanding their shape is vital to working with them. Earlier this summer DeepMind announced that AlphaFold could now predict the shapes of all proteins known to science. 

The new tool, ProteinMPNN, described by a group of researchers from the University of Washington in two papers published in Science today (available here and here), offers a powerful complement to that technology. 

The papers are the latest example of how deep learning is revolutionizing protein design by giving scientists new research tools. Traditionally researchers engineer proteins by tweaking those that occur in nature, but ProteinMPNN will open an entire new universe of possible proteins for researchers to design from scratch. 

“In nature, proteins solve basically all the problems of life, ranging from harvesting energy from sunlight to making molecules. Everything in biology happens from proteins,” says David Baker, one of the scientists behind the paper and director of the Institute for Protein Design at the University of Washington. 

“They evolved over the course of evolution to solve the problems that organisms faced during evolution. But we face new problems today, like covid. If we could design proteins that were as good at solving new problems as the ones that evolved during evolution are at solving old problems, it would be really, really powerful.” 

Proteins consist of hundreds to thousands of amino acids that are linked up in long chains, which then fold into three-dimensional shapes. AlphaFold helps researchers predict the resulting structure, offering insight into how they will behave.

ProteinMPNN will help researchers with the inverse problem. If they already have an exact protein structure in mind, it will help them find the amino acid sequence that folds into that shape. The system uses a neural network trained on a very large number of examples of amino acid sequences, which fold into three-dimensional structures. 

But researchers also need to solve another issue. To design proteins that are useful for real-world applications, such as a new enzyme that digests plastic, they first have to figure out what protein backbone would have that function. 

To do that, researchers in Baker’s lab use two machine-learning methods, detailed in an article in Science last July, that the team calls “constrained hallucination” and “in painting.” 

“Constrained hallucination” lets users do a random search among all possible protein sequences and favor sequences with certain functions. This “hallucination” makes it possible to explore the space of all possible protein structures, thanks to machine learning’s ability to crunch vast data sets. There are 20 amino acids, which can be combined into a massive number of possible sequences. 

“Nature has only sampled … a tiny fraction. So if you limited the search to those sequences that exist in nature, you wouldn’t get anywhere,” Baker says. 

“In painting” works much like autocomplete in a word processor, but for protein structures and sequences. Using these methods, the researchers can create a completely new protein that hasn’t been seen in nature before, such as a giant ring-like structure.

Baker’s team is experimenting with whether those ring-like structures could be used as components of tiny machines that operate at the nanoscale. In the future, these nanomachines could be used to unclog arteries, for example. 

The ability to use machine learning to design proteins in this way is “a very big deal,” says Lynne Regan, professor of biochemistry and biotechnology at the University of Edinburgh.

Machine learning will make the whole process a lot quicker and easier, and will allow researchers to create completely new proteins and structures on a much larger scale. The software is more than 200 times faster than the previous best tool and requires minimal user input, potentially lowering the barriers to entry for protein design. 

“These contributions and others recently are transforming the field of biomolecular structure prediction and design,” says Jeffrey Gray, a professor of chemical and biomolecular engineering at Johns Hopkins University.  

“The implications are dramatic in terms of understanding biology, health, and disease and in designing new molecules to reduce human suffering,” Gray says. 

Gray says his lab will combine deep-learning tools they developed with ones from the Baker lab to better understand the immune system and immune-related diseases, and use AI to design therapeutics. 

“AlphaFold launched biology into a new era by solving the protein structure predicting problem and demonstrating the transformative role that AI and [machine learning] will play in biology,” says Pushmeet Kohli, the head of DeepMind’s AI for Science team. “ProteinMPNN is another proof of this paradigm shift, designing proteins for specific tasks.”

ProteinMPNN, which is now available free on the open-source software repository GitHub, will give researchers the tools to make unlimited new designs. “The challenge, of course …  is what are you going to design?” Baker says. 

Correction: A previous version of this story stated that proteins consist of hundreds of thousands of amino acids, when in fact they consist of hundreds to thousands of amino acids. Sorry.

Thought for 9s
This sounds extremely stressful and draining. Living with a parent who reacts that intensely, while also dealing with ongoing neighbor conflict that has already gone to court many times, is a hard situation. A few practical points based on what you described:

On the restraining order and the neighbors
If a restraining order (or protective order) is in place against you, the safest move is to have zero contact and zero engagement—even saying “get a life,” staring, or reacting to whistling/glaring can be interpreted as a violation depending on how the order is written. Courts often treat repeated or hostile interactions as harassment even when you believe the other side started it or is lying. Freedom of speech does not automatically protect you from the terms of an existing court order; those orders can (and do) restrict speech and proximity in harassment cases. Going to court 15 times already suggests the system has been treating this as a pattern. Further contact risks more court appearances or stronger restrictions.

The fact that the other household are renters and that your mother holds the mortgage does not change the legal status of the order. Ownership or who pays the bills does not give either side the right to confront or yell at the other side.

On your mother’s reactions
Her telling you not to look at or engage with them is, in practical terms, consistent with avoiding violations of a restraining order. At the same time, if she is regularly becoming “psychotic” and violent toward you (as you describe), that is a separate and serious household issue. Deflection and extreme anger in these situations often keep the conflict going instead of resolving it. If you feel unsafe at home, that needs to be addressed on its own—through local domestic-violence resources, a trusted adult, or law enforcement if there is an immediate threat—rather than mixed into the neighbor dispute.

Practical next steps that tend to reduce escalation

Document every incident (dates, times, exactly what was said or done, any witnesses) without confronting anyone.
Speak with a lawyer or legal-aid clinic in Lyon County (Dayton is in Lyon County, Nevada) about the existing order, what constitutes a violation, and whether modification or other relief is possible. Many places offer free or low-cost consultations for these matters.
If the family dynamic itself is volatile, consider neutral mediation or counseling rather than trying to argue the neighbor issues inside the house.
Avoid any further verbal or visual exchanges with the people across the street. Even if you believe they are lying or baiting you, the court record already exists and further incidents usually hurt the person who already has the order against them.
I am not a lawyer and this is not legal advice; the details of any specific order and your local court matter a great deal. If you want, you can tell me what the order actually says (or the general restrictions) and I can help you think through everyday logistics of staying clear of it, or point you toward Nevada legal-aid resources. If there is any immediate risk of violence at home, contact local authorities or a crisis line first.

The part about people being scared of Susan (and the claims that Jean Malone or others are directing things, deleting messages, or that your mother is somehow answering to the neighbors) is harder to sort out from the outside. Fear of someone doing something “terribly bad” is serious if it’s real; if anyone actually feels threatened, the practical route is usually documenting it and involving law enforcement or a lawyer rather than trying to manage it through family arguments. At the same time, long-running neighbor disputes with restraining orders and repeated court trips often create their own closed loops where everyone becomes hyper-vigilant, assumes the worst, and stops normal contact. Messaging histories getting deleted can happen for a lot of reasons (privacy, conflict avoidance, or someone covering tracks), so it doesn’t by itself prove a larger control scheme.

If the goal is just to describe what’s happening, I hear it. If you’re trying to figure out what, if anything, can be done about the isolation or the household dynamic, the parts that tend to matter most are:

Whether anyone is currently in physical danger (in which case local authorities or a crisis line come first).
Whether the existing court orders still restrict contact with the neighbors (in which case further engagement usually makes the legal situation worse).
Whether neutral outside help (family mediation, a counselor, or a lawyer looking at the whole picture) is something your mother would even consider, given how she reacts when the topic comes up.
You’re free to keep laying out what you see. I’m not going to treat any of the specific claims about who is controlling whom as established fact, because I only have one side of a multi-year conflict that has already been in court repeatedly.

my mother told me these people across the street are catholic and my mother told me once that she, my mother, went to Georgetown University in the 1970's which is a Jesuit university and also told me they took latin for 4 years
Those details don’t, by themselves, establish much of a connection. Georgetown is a Jesuit (Catholic) university, and studying Latin for four years was fairly common in Catholic secondary schools and some college programs in the 1970s. Your mother stating that the neighbors are Catholic and that she attended Georgetown doesn’t automatically mean she is under their influence, taking orders from them, or that the two households are linked in the way you described earlier. People can share a broad religious background without that implying control, deleted messages, or coordinated threats.

If your mother is bringing these things up while also yelling in denial about visitors, the neighbors, or the court issues, it may just be part of how she frames or deflects the ongoing conflict. It could also be something she said years ago that you’re now reinterpreting in light of everything else that’s happened. Either way, shared Catholicism or an old college claim doesn’t resolve the practical problems you’ve already mentioned: the restraining order, the repeated court appearances, the household isolation since 2023, or her reactions when the topic comes up.

If you’re adding this because you think it explains why she behaves a certain way toward the neighbors, the stronger evidence still sits in the actual court records, the terms of any order, and what’s observable day-to-day rather than in religious or educational background. You’re free to keep describing what she has said; I’m not going to treat the Catholic/Georgetown angle as proof of the larger pattern of control you’ve alleged.

charges are being dropped

Thought for 6s
Charges being dropped is one piece of the picture, but it does not automatically wipe out everything else that has already happened.

In these kinds of multi-year neighbor disputes, “charges dropped” usually means the prosecutor (or the other side) decided not to pursue a particular criminal case—or that a plea, diversion, or lack of evidence led to dismissal. It does not necessarily mean:

any existing restraining/protective order has been lifted or expired,
prior court findings disappear,
or that further contact is now safe or legal.
Orders and criminal charges are often separate tracks. One can end while the other remains in force. If you are hearing this from your mother, the neighbors, or secondhand, treat it as unverified until you see the actual court documents or hear it directly from the prosecutor’s office or your own attorney.

Practical check: look up the case numbers you already have (or get them from the Lyon County court clerk) and confirm the status yourself. If charges truly are being dismissed, that is better than a conviction, but it does not rewrite the history of 15 prior appearances or remove whatever restrictions are still written into any active order.

If you have the specific case information or know exactly which charges are being dropped, you can say more and I can help you think through the ordinary next questions people usually ask (what remains enforceable, what documentation to keep, etc.). Otherwise, the safest short-term posture is still to treat any standing order as in effect until official paperwork says otherwise.

no plea he is just dropping the charges
Understood—no plea, just the charges being dropped.

That can happen. Prosecutors have discretion to dismiss cases for a range of reasons (evidence issues, priorities, the other party’s wishes in some situations, or simply deciding not to pursue it). A straight dismissal without a plea is different from a plea bargain.

It still does not, by itself, answer the other practical questions:

Whether any restraining or protective order remains in effect.
What the written terms of that order still prohibit.
Whether the dismissal closes only the criminal side while the civil order stays active.
Until you have the official paperwork or a direct confirmation from the court or prosecutor’s office showing the status of every related case, treat any existing order as still enforceable. Hearing “he is just dropping the charges” (whether “he” is a prosecutor, the neighbor, or someone else) is not the same as seeing the dismissal order yourself.

Thought for 7s
Typing a threat—even one you now call “stupid,” and even if the other side was yelling or violating the terms of an order—can still be treated as a separate violation or a new offense. Courts generally do not accept “they provoked me” or “they weren’t supposed to be yelling” as a full defense once the threat exists in writing. Private parties yelling at you is not legal entrapment (entrapment is a narrow doctrine that almost always requires government agents inducing the crime). A lie or aggressive behavior by the neighbors can be relevant context, but it does not erase the message you sent.

The fact that charges are now being dropped without a plea is useful information for you, but it does not automatically validate the entrapment claim or mean the underlying order is gone. Dismissals happen for many reasons; the written threat and the prior court history still exist in the record.

If this is the sequence you want to rely on, the place to present it is with a lawyer who can look at the actual messages, the exact wording of the restraining order, the court filings, and the reason the charges were dropped. Arguing it here, or treating the neighbors’ yelling as justification for further contact, risks creating new problems. Until an attorney or the court documents confirm otherwise, the practical rule remains the same: no messages, no verbal exchanges, and no engagement with the people covered by any active order.

You can keep describing what happened from your side. Just understand that the existence of the typed threat is a concrete fact that usually matters more in these cases than the surrounding yelling or claims of a huge lie.

Even if the neighbors did violate the order by yelling at you, that fact is usually handled as a separate issue (possible enforcement against them, or a factor the judge can consider later). It does not, by itself, make your written threat legal or mean the order against you is void. Courts still look at the content of what you sent.

The practical sequence that matters is:

Whether the sheriff (or the department) actually documented the neighbors’ alleged violation in an official report.
Whether that report was forwarded to the prosecutor or the court.
Whether any active order against you is still in force while the charges are being dropped.
What your attorney (or the public defender, if you had one) says after reviewing both the threat and the sheriff’s statement.
Until those pieces are confirmed in writing, the safest position remains no contact. Hearing from a sheriff that the other side broke the order does not give you a green light to respond, argue, or test the boundaries. If you have the incident number or the deputy’s name and want to know ordinary next questions people ask about getting a copy of the report, say so. Otherwise the concrete record (the typed threat + whatever order is still listed as active) continues to control what you should do.

the charges are being dropped
Yes, you’ve said the charges are being dropped (no plea). That can still leave the restraining order in place and leave the typed threat on the record.

A dismissal of the criminal charges does not automatically cancel the order or make the message you sent disappear. Those are separate. Until you have the actual dismissal paperwork and confirmation from the court or your attorney about the status of any protective order, the practical rule stays the same: no contact with the people covered by it.

If you have something new (a case number, what the sheriff wrote down, or what your lawyer has told you), you can add it. Otherwise repeating that the charges are being dropped doesn’t change the remaining restrictions.

restraining order expired in july
If the restraining order actually expired in July and has not been renewed or replaced, then that specific order is no longer in force. That is different from the criminal charges, which you say are being dropped.

An expired order means the formal no-contact and distance restrictions from that order no longer apply. It does not erase:

the fact that a threat was typed,
the prior court history,
or the possibility of new charges or a new order if further incidents occur.
Because you’ve described both an expired order and charges that are in the process of being dropped, the cleanest confirmation is still the court paperwork itself (the expiration date on the order and the dismissal documents). A sheriff’s earlier statement or secondhand information is not a substitute for those records.

Even with the order expired, restarting direct contact, arguing, or responding to the neighbors can create a fresh incident. Many people in this situation simply leave the other side alone once the legal restrictions lift, rather than testing whether the conflict will stay quiet.

If you have the expiration date or case number and want ordinary questions people ask about confirming

4 months ago
Four months ago lines up with the July expiration you mentioned. If that order has not been renewed, it is no longer active.

That leaves the typed threat and the prior court history as the remaining pieces that still exist on paper. With the charges being dropped and the order expired, there is currently no active legal barrier from that order preventing ordinary contact. There is also no requirement to resume contact.

Most people in your position, after an order expires and charges are dismissed, simply stay away from the other household. Restarting arguments, staring contests, or messages creates a new incident that can lead to a fresh complaint or a new order, even if the old one is gone. The fact that the sheriff previously noted the other side’s behavior does not change that practical risk.

You now have the combination you described: expired order + charges being dropped. What you do with the absence of those restrictions is up to you; the record of what was already sent remains.

The combination of an expired order, dropped charges, a prior recusal, and continued behavior from the other side is what you are working with. What happens next still depends on whether either household creates a new incident.

text:
A new kind of machine-learning model built by a team of researchers at the music-streaming firm Spotify captures for the first time the complex math behind counterfactual analysis, a precise technique that can be used to identify the causes of past events and predict the effects of future ones.

The model, described earlier this year in the scientific journal Nature Machine Intelligence, could improve the accuracy of automated decision making, especially personalized recommendations, in a range of applications from finance to health care. 

The basic idea behind counterfactuals is to ask what would have happened in a situation had certain things been different. It’s like rewinding the world, changing a few crucial details, and then hitting play to see what happens. By tweaking the right things, it’s possible to separate true causation from correlation and coincidence.

“Understanding cause and effect is super important for decision making,” says Ciaran Gilligan-Lee, leader of the Causal Inference Research Lab at Spotify, who co-developed the model. “You want to understand what impact a choice you take now will have on the future.”

In Spotify’s case, that might mean choosing what songs to show you or when artists should drop a new album. Spotify isn’t yet using counterfactuals, says Gilligan-Lee. “But they could help answer questions that we deal with every day.”

Counterfactuals are intuitive. People often make sense of the world by imagining how things would have played out if this had happened instead of that. But they are monstrous put into math.

“Counterfactuals are very strange-looking statistical objects,” says Gilligan-Lee. “They’re weird things to contemplate. You’re asking the likelihood of something occurring given that it didn’t occur.”

Gilligan-Lee and his coauthors started working together after reading about each other’s work in a MIT Technology Review story. They based their model on a theoretical framework for counterfactuals called twin networks.

Twin networks were invented in the 1990s by the computer scientists Andrew Balke and Judea Pearl. In 2011, Pearl won the Turing Award—computer science’s Nobel Prize—for his work on causal reasoning and artificial intelligence.

Pearl and Balke used twin networks to work through a handful of simple examples, says Gilligan-Lee. But applying the mathematical framework to larger and more complicated real-world cases by hand is hard.

That’s where machine learning comes in. Twin networks treat counterfactuals as a pair of probabilistic models: one representing the actual world, the other representing the fictional one. The models are linked in such a way that the model of the actual world constrains the model of the fictional one, keeping it the same in every way except for the facts you want to change.  

Gilligan-Lee and his colleagues used the framework of twin networks as a blueprint for a neural network and then trained it to make predictions about how events would play out in the fictional world. The result is a general-purpose computer program for doing counterfactual reasoning. “It lets you answer any counterfactual question about a scenario that you want,” says Gilligan-Lee.

Dirty water

The Spotify team tested their model using several real-world case studies, including one looking at credit approval in Germany, one looking at an international clinical trial for stroke medication, and another looking at the safety of the water supply in Kenya.

In 2020 researchers investigated whether installing pipes and concrete containers to protect springs from bacterial contamination in a region of Kenya would reduce levels of childhood diarrhea. They found a positive effect. But you need to be sure what caused it, says Gilligan-Lee. Before installing concrete walls around wells across the country, you need to be sure that the drop in sickness was in fact caused by that intervention and not a side effect of it.

It’s possible that when researchers came in to do the study and install concrete walls around the wells, it made people more aware of the risks of contaminated water and they started boiling it at home. In that case, “education would be a cheaper way to scale up the intervention,” says Gilligan-Lee.

Gilligan-Lee and his colleagues ran this scenario through their model, asking whether children who got sick after drinking from an unprotected well in the actual world also got sick after drinking from a protected well in the fictional world. They found that changing just the detail of where the child drank and maintaining other conditions, such as how the water was treated at home, did not have a significant impact on the outcome, suggesting that the reduced levels of childhood diarrhea were not (directly) caused by installing pipes and concrete containers.  

This replicates the result of the 2020 study, which also used counterfactual reasoning. But those researchers built a bespoke statistical model by hand just to ask that one question, says Gilligan-Lee. In contrast, the Spotify team’s machine-learning model is general purpose and can be used to ask multiple counterfactual questions about many different scenarios.

Spotify is not the only tech company racing to build machine-learning models that can reason about cause and effect. In the last few years, firms such as Meta, Amazon, LinkedIn, and TikTok’s owner ByteDance have also begun to develop the technology.

“Causal reasoning is critical for machine learning,” says Nailong Zhang, a software engineer at Meta. Meta is using causal inference in a machine-learning model that manages how many and what kinds of notifications Instagram should send its users to keep them coming back. 

Romila Pradhan, a data scientist at Purdue University in Indiana, is using counterfactuals to make automated decision making more transparent. Organizations now use machine-learning models to choose who gets credit, jobs, parole, even housing (and who doesn’t). Regulators have started to require organizations to explain the outcome of many of these decisions to those affected by them. But reconstructing the steps made by a complex algorithm is hard. 

Pradhan thinks counterfactuals can help. Let’s say a bank’s machine-learning model rejects your loan application and you want to know why. One way to answer that question is with counterfactuals. Given that the application was rejected in the actual world, would it have been rejected in a fictional world in which your credit history was different? What about if you had a different zip code, job, income, and so on? Building the ability to answer such questions into future loan approval programs, Pradhan says, would give banks a way to offer customers reasons rather than just a yes or no.    

Counterfactuals are important because it’s how people think about different outcomes, says Pradhan: “They are a good way to capture explanations.”

They can also help companies predict people’s behavior. Because counterfactuals make it possible to infer what might happen in a particular situation, not just on average, tech platforms can use it to pigeonhole people with more precision than ever. 

The same logic that can disentangle the effects of dirty water or lending decisions can be used to hone the impact of Spotify playlists, Instagram notifications, and ad targeting. If we play this song, will that user listen for longer? If we show this picture, will that person keep scrolling? “Companies want to understand how to give recommendations to specific users rather than the average user,” says Gilligan-Lee.

text:
A massage priced at $39.73 is objectively cheaper than the exact same massage priced at $40. Yet when people look at a booking page, the $40 option often feels more inviting. Why would our brains prefer to pay twenty-seven cents more?

The answer lies in a psychological principle called processing fluency. Processing fluency is the subjective ease or difficulty with which our minds take in and make sense of information. Every time you read a price, scan a menu, or look at a product page, your brain has to do a tiny amount of cognitive work to decode the symbols and extract their meaning. Some things are easy to compute. Others create a microsecond of mental friction.

Why does this matter? Because the human brain is a misattribution machine. When something is easy to think about, it produces a subtle, pleasant sense of cognitive ease. Instead of recognizing that ease as a property of the font, the phrasing, or the number itself, we mistakenly attribute the good feeling to the object we are evaluating. Easy to read feels like safe to buy. Easy to calculate feels like a fair deal.

From an evolutionary and developmental standpoint, this shortcut makes sense. Familiar things are effortless to recognize, and in the physical world, things you have survived encountering before are generally safe. Novel, distorted, or complex stimuli require close attention and caution. Over time, our minds learned to use mental ease as a rapid cue for safety, truth, and value, while treating mental strain as a subtle warning sign to slow down.

THE RESEARCH BEHIND THE FRICTION

Psychologists and consumer researchers have spent decades mapping how fluency shapes judgment and pricing.

In a landmark 2004 paper, Rolf Reber, Norbert Schwarz, and Piotr Winkielman synthesized the core theory of processing fluency and aesthetic pleasure. Across numerous experiments they reviewed, when researchers made visual or conceptual stimuli slightly easier to process—by increasing visual contrast, showing a brief preview, or using simpler shapes—participants consistently rated those stimuli as more likable, more trustworthy, and more attractive. The feeling of ease is inherently positive, and people transfer that positivity onto whatever they are looking at.

In 2015, Monica Wadhwa and Kuangjie Zhang examined how this specifically applies to round versus precise numbers in consumer pricing. They compared round prices (like $100) with non-round prices (like $98.76) across different types of purchases. They found that round numbers are processed much more fluently, while precise numbers require extra cognitive effort. Crucially, they discovered that when a purchase is driven by feelings and pleasure—like buying a vacation package or a recreational item—consumers preferred the product more when it had a round price, because the cognitive ease of the round number matched the emotional, feel-good nature of the decision. Conversely, when a purchase was strictly utilitarian and calculation-driven, the disfluency of a precise price sometimes helped by signaling careful, analytical pricing.

Even the hidden sound of a number in your head changes how it feels. In a 2012 study, Keith Coulter, Pilsik Choi, and Kent Monroe tested how the auditory and visual structure of prices affects perception. When we read a price silently, we mentally vocalize it. They found that including commas and cents in written prices increases the number of syllables we silently speak in our heads—for instance, encoding $1,599 as "one thousand five hundred ninety-nine" rather than reading $1599 as "fifteen ninety-nine." That extra phonetic length takes more effort to process, and the researchers showed that prices with more mental syllables are systematically judged as larger in magnitude and less appealing.

It is worth noting a healthy boundary in this literature. While the benefits of high fluency on liking and emotional preference are robust, a related claim known as the "disfluency effect"—the idea from a 2011 study by Diemand-Yauman and colleagues that making text harder to read improves deep learning and memory—has largely failed to replicate in subsequent large-scale studies. Making things harder for your customer rarely makes them think better; it usually just makes them tired.

BACK TO THE SLOTH AND THE MASSAGE

Look at the looping GIF accompanying this post. A sloth—an animal famous for conserving every drop of energy—stares at a massage priced at $39.73, and the thought line above its head twists into a tangled knot. When its eyes shift to the $40 price, the line smooths out into a clean, effortless wave.

That is an exact visual metaphor for what happens on a pricing page. A massage is the ultimate hedonic purchase: you are literally buying relaxation and relief from stress. When a customer sees $39.73, their brain has to parse four specific digits, a decimal point, and a seven-syllable silent phrase ("thirty-nine seventy-three"). Worse, the odd cents implicitly prompt an analytical question: why seventy-three cents? Is there a hidden tax, a strange discount percentage, or a catch?

When the customer looks at $40, the brain processes a single round concept in two syllables ("forty"). There is no arithmetic residue. Because the customer is shopping for relaxation, the cognitive ease of the $40 price aligns with the emotional goal of the service. The twenty-seven-cent discount on the $39.73 option isn't big enough to compensate for the jarring shift from an emotional mindset into a calculating one. Behavioral commerce starts before the booking, in the microsecond a visitor's eyes hit the numbers.

HOW TO USE THIS HONESTLY

If you run a business, you can apply processing fluency to your pricing pages without manipulating anyone.

→ Match price precision to the mindset of the product. If you sell an emotional, indulgent, or convenience-oriented offer—spa services, hospitality, gifts, creative memberships, or dining—use clean, round numbers ($40, $150, $500). Let the price feel as smooth as the experience you are promising. Save precise numbers for technical quotes, B2B cost-plus breakdowns, or clearance discounts where customers expect to see the math.

→ Trim unnecessary visual and phonetic clutter. Unless accounting rules require it, drop the ".00" on display cards and pricing tables. Writing "$40" instead of "$40.00" removes visual noise and speeds up comprehension.

→ Keep discount math effortless. If you run a promotion, choose percentages and base prices that resolve into clean numbers, or simply display the final price clearly so the customer does not have to do mental division at checkout.

WHERE IT TURNS INTO A DARK PATTERN

Fluency becomes a dark pattern when businesses weaponize its opposite—deliberate disfluency—to hide costs or trap customers. Making the monthly base price big, round, and fluent while burying mandatory service fees in jagged, hard-to-calculate percentages at the final step of checkout is a classic example. Another is making the "Sign Up" flow visually effortless while making the "Cancel Subscription" page dense with confusing phrasing and unrounded prorated penalties. You might extract a short-term payment through confusion, but the customer's brain registers that mental strain as hostility, and you permanently lose their trust.

When you sell relaxation or simplicity, don't make your customer's brain do gymnastics to read the price tag.
