text:
NIGHT DISPATCH UPDATE
Saturday, November 14, 2026 

Police, fire, medical and traffic activity across Jefferson County, Denver, Boulder County, Adams County, Arapahoe County and Douglas County.

Reports are organized geographically, beginning with Red Rocks and Jefferson County.

JEFFERSON COUNTY

RED ROCKS AND MORRISON

Red Rocks Amphitheatre | Intoxicated Person
8:36 PM | 18300 W. Alameda Parkway, Morrison

Emergency medical personnel were dispatched to the stage right door at Red Rocks Amphitheatre for a reported intoxicated person experiencing a possible alcohol-related medical emergency. Medic 1 was requested.

Red Rocks Amphitheatre | Smoking Shuttle
7:16 PM | 18300 W. Alameda Parkway, Morrison

A park ranger requested towing assistance for a shuttle reportedly smoking in a parking area near the training post.

LAKEWOOD

Assault Victim Reported
7:25 PM | Oak Street

Fire and medical units were dispatched for a reported assault victim. Responders were instructed to stage near Holland Street and Horsebit Street pending further information.

Structure Fire
7:55 PM | South Field Street

Fire crews responded to a reported structure fire near a Green Creek location. Initial radio traffic described the situation as quiet and apparently under control. Another dispatch at approximately the same time referenced a structure fire on South Field Street in the Littleton area. The exact relationship between the reports remains unclear.

Outside Fire
6:36 PM | West 10th Avenue and Ames Street

Engine 1 was dispatched for a possible outside fire near Ames Street. Dispatch information contained an inconsistent reference to West Track Avenue.

Two-Vehicle Collision
5:08 PM | Union Boulevard near West 4th and West 5th Avenues

Emergency crews were dispatched after reports of a two-vehicle collision in the Union Boulevard corridor. Separate dispatch entries identified West 4th and West 5th avenues at approximately the same time. Whether these were separate collisions or conflicting location descriptions has not been confirmed.

Vehicle Collision
6:06 PM | West Mexico Avenue and South Garrison Street

Emergency crews responded to a reported motor vehicle collision. One radio transmission contained an inconsistent street direction, but the repeated location was South Garrison Street.

GOLDEN

Possible Overdose
5:00 PM | South Elm Street

Engine 12 and Medic 12 were dispatched to a possible overdose. No patient condition was available in the dispatch summary.

Motor Vehicle Collision
6:06 PM | 21st Street near Dairy Street

Engine 3 was assigned to a reported two-vehicle collision west of 21st Street near Dairy Street.

Vehicle Crash Near Youngfield
7:35 PM | Youngfield Street

Emergency crews responded to a reported collision near Youngfield Street. An ambulance was requested. Dispatch descriptions referenced a parking lot and an additional location near the I-70 eastbound ramp and West Sixth Avenue in Wheat Ridge. The reports may describe separate incidents.

Hotel Fire Alarm
8:10 PM | West Colfax Avenue

Firefighters responded to a commercial fire alarm at a hotel after alarm zones and a guest laundry smoke detector activated.

Hotel staff were evacuating. Responders initially reported no visible fire, and the issue may have involved the laundry dryers.

Erratic Driver Near I-70
5:58 PM | C-470 westbound toward I-70 eastbound

Dispatch received a complaint involving a red Chevrolet SUV reportedly weaving and changing speeds. The vehicle was described as operating with its hazard lights activated and possibly displaying a fleet registration.

An officer advised they were responding.

Traffic Stop
8:26 PM | Westbound I-70 near C-470

Officers conducted a traffic stop involving a black Toyota. Dispatch traffic referenced a records check and a possible identity discrepancy.

EVERGREEN

Reported Structure Fire
8:15 PM | Burro Drive area

Firefighters and medical personnel were dispatched to a reported structure fire near Burro Drive in Evergreen.

Multiple engines, truck companies, medical units and command personnel were assigned.

WHEAT RIDGE

Emergency Medical Response
7:18 PM | West 44th Avenue

Emergency medical crews were dispatched for a reported hemorrhage at an apartment complex. The dispatch headline referenced West 64th Avenue, but the location details identified West 44th Avenue.

Motor Vehicle Collision
7:35 PM | Youngfield Street near I-70 and West Sixth Avenue

A separate dispatch entry placed a vehicle collision near the eastbound I-70 ramp and West Sixth Avenue. Crews were assigned to investigate.

COLUMBINE AND SOUTH JEFFERSON COUNTY

Reckless Driver
7:49 PM | West Ken Caryl Avenue and South Pierce Street

A white Nissan Rogue was reported weaving between lanes and braking unexpectedly while traveling eastbound near South Pierce Street.

Two Vehicles on Shoulder
6:25 PM | West Bowles Avenue near C-470

Dispatch received reports of two vehicles stopped along the right shoulder near the C-470 corridor. Related radio traffic described a possible two-vehicle crash.

Disabled Vehicle
8:21 PM | Southbound C-470 near Columbine Trail

A disabled vehicle was reported blocking the left lane. A later transmission indicated the vehicle was moving away from the roadway.

Reckless Driver
6:33 PM | C-470 and West Chatfield Avenue

A black four-door sedan was reported weaving across lanes and continuing northbound on Chatfield Avenue.

DENVER COUNTY

ASSAULTS, WEAPONS AND DISTURBANCES

Injured Dog

BOULDER COUNTY

BOULDER

Bus Strikes Pedestrian
6:30 PM | Walnut Street and Broadway

Fire and medical crews responded to a reported collision involving a bus and pedestrian near the southeast corner of the intersection.

The pedestrian was reportedly conscious and breathing when the incident was dispatched.

Assault Suspect Search

Road Hazard

Raccoon Trapped Behind Wall

Vehicle Strikes Deer

The caller could not identify the apartment involved.

LAFAYETTE AND SUPERIOR

Two-Vehicle Rear-End Collision
6:22 PM | Arapahoe Road and North 95th Street, Lafayette

A black pickup truck and black Honda Civic were involved in a reported property-damage collision. Both vehicles were reportedly moving into a nearby parking lot.

6:54 PM | Highway 36 near South Cherryvale Road

A pickup truck driver was reported swerving along Highway 36. The reporting party was following the vehicle and offered to assist officers.

Traffic Complaint at Costco

LOUISVILLE

Suspicious Noise
4:39 PM | West Alder Street

Officers investigated a report of an unusual screeching noise. The caller was uncertain whether the sound came from an animal.

Suspicious Activity
5:53 PM | Pheasant Run

Officers checked a residence following a report of someone possibly outside the home. A second unit was requested when available.

SOUTH BOULDER COUNTY

Unusual Roadside Report
7:57 PM | South Boulder Road and Barcelona Drive

Police were asked to investigate a large trash bag in the westbound lanes after a caller expressed concern that it might contain a body.

ADAMS COUNTY

FEDERAL HEIGHTS

Suspicious Door-to-Door Activity

WESTMINSTER

Motorcycle and SUV Collision

5:51 PM | South Broadway

8:14 to 8:17 PM | West Dorado Drive, Governors Ranch/Littleton area

8:15 PM | Arapahoe Drive area

The precise incident location and relationship between these responses require confirmation.

⸻

DISPATCH INFORMATION NOTICE

These reports are compiled from publicly available emergency radio traffic and automated dispatch summaries. Locations, incident descriptions and initial conditions may change as responders investigate.

A dispatch does not establish that a crime occurred, that a suspect was responsible, or that an initially reported emergency was confirmed.

Some entries contain conflicting location information, which has been identified where relevant.

text:
🏈 TEXANS vs. BROWNS — NFL WEEK 10 PREVIEW

Houston has a massive advantage at quarterback, but its defensive injuries could make this a much closer game than expected. Can Cleveland keep it within one possession?

📊 FAIR MARKET
• Fair Spread: Texans -3.0 | Market: Texans -4.5
• Fair Total: 41.0 | Market: 40.5
• Fair ML: HOU -143 / CLE +143
• Confidence: 62/100

🎯 SCORE PREDICTION
Texans 22 — Browns 19

🧠 HOW THIS GAME PLAYS OUT
• The QB gap is enormous. C.J. Stroud carries an 85.8 PFF grade compared with Deshaun Watson’s 54.3. Stroud has a 6.55% big-time throw rate and just a 1.19% turnover-worthy play rate. Watson sits at 2.44% and 3.96%, respectively.
• Houston should move the football. The Texans rank 9th offensively and average +0.19 EPA per pass compared with Cleveland’s 26th-ranked offense and +0.01 EPA per pass.
• Cleveland’s defense keeps this interesting. The Browns rank 11th defensively, ahead of Houston at 15th. Their defensive front should make Houston work for points rather than surrender easy touchdowns.
• Houston’s injuries are significant. Danielle Hunter is out, while Will Anderson Jr. is questionable. Cleveland may have opportunities to establish longer drives against a weakened defensive front.

🔑 X-FACTOR: Can Watson protect the football? His 3.96% turnover-worthy play rate against Houston’s defense is the biggest threat to Cleveland keeping this close.

⚠️ MARKET CHECK
PFF projects Houston -4.5, matching the sportsbook. Our matchup-adjusted number is Houston -3.0, largely reflecting defensive availability and Cleveland’s home-field advantage.
MIDP: PASS on the spread at current prices. The disagreement is meaningful but doesn’t establish sufficient value by itself.

💰 BETTING CARD
🔥 BEST BET: PASS — No reliable edge at current prices.
🟡 Browns +4.5 (-110): Estimated +3.9% EV, below our 5% betting threshold.
🟡 Texans ML (-223): Houston is our projected winner, but that price is too expensive relative to our fair -143.
🟡 Total 40.5: Our fair number of 41.0 offers no meaningful advantage.

🚨 WHAT COULD GO WRONG?
If Watson gives Houston short fields through sacks and turnovers, Stroud could turn a close game into a double-digit win. Conversely, further defensive absences could allow Cleveland to control possession and produce an upset.

👀 LIVE BETTING WATCHLIST
• Houston trailing by 3–7 at halftime, Stroud protecting the ball: reassess Texans live ML at +100 or better.
• Cleveland producing fewer than 4.0 yards per play through two quarters: reassess Browns team total Under 17.5 at -110 or better.
Both require updated live fair-value checks before wagering.

🏁 FINAL VERDICT
🎯 Texans 22–19
📊 Fair Spread: Houston -3.0
📈 Market: Houston -4.5
🔢 Fair Total: 41.0
🔥 Best Bet: PASS
💵 Total Exposure: 0.00u

Houston is the better football team. Cleveland has the defense to make it uncomfortable. But there’s no reason to force a wager simply because the projected margin differs from the market.

Does Cleveland’s defensive front keep Watson in this game, or does Stroud’s efficiency prove too much to overcome?

text:
🏈 CHIEFS vs. FALCONS — NFL WEEK 10 PREVIEW

Kansas City ranks 8th offensively and defensively. Atlanta ranks 25th offensively. Yet the Chiefs are only laying a field goal against a 3–6 team. Is Vegas seeing something the public isn’t?

📊 FAIR MARKET
* Fair Spread: Chiefs -4.8 | Market: KC -3
* Fair Total: 47.0 | Market: 47.5
* Fair ML: KC -177 / ATL +177
* Confidence: 68/100

🎯 SCORE PREDICTION
Chiefs 26 — Falcons 21

🧠 HOW THIS GAME PLAYS OUT
🏈 QB mismatch: Mahomes owns an 83.6 passer rating under pressure versus Penix’s 30.5. Penix’s 7.26% turnover-worthy play rate is particularly concerning against Kansas City’s defense.
🔥 Passing efficiency: KC generates +0.16 EPA/pass compared with Atlanta’s -0.11. Mahomes should have opportunities to exploit Atlanta’s secondary, especially if its injured pass rushers are limited.
💪 Bijan factor: Atlanta’s clearest path is establishing Robinson early, controlling possession and preventing Mahomes from dictating the tempo.
📉 Schedule adjustment: Atlanta has faced the NFL’s 7th-hardest schedule versus Kansas City’s 29th. The Falcons’ record understates their competitiveness.

🔑 X-Factor: Can Atlanta protect Penix and avoid the negative plays that consistently derail its passing offense?

⚠️ MARKET CHECK
Kansas City has attracted overwhelming public support, yet some tracked markets moved from KC -4.5 toward -3. Our independent projection remains -4.8. MIDP: SMALL BET, with reduced exposure for adverse movement and injury uncertainty.

💰 BETTING CARD
🔥 BEST BET: Chiefs -3 (-110)
* Fair win probability: ~51–52%, plus ~8% push probability
* Fair odds: Approximately -125, excluding pushes
* Estimated EV: ~+5–6%
* Stake: 0.50u
The quarterback and passing-efficiency advantages justify modest exposure at the key number.

🟡 PASSES: Chiefs ML -173 offers insufficient value. Under 47.5 has no meaningful edge.

🚨 WHAT COULD GO WRONG?
Walker remains questionable, while Delane’s availability matters defensively.  More importantly, Bijan could sustain drives and keep Kansas City’s offense on the sidelines.

👀 LIVE WATCHLIST
If the first quarter ends tied, with both QBs healthy and no major efficiency change, reassess KC -1.5 (-110 or better). No automatic bet without an updated fair line.

🏁 FINAL VERDICT
🎯 Chiefs 26–21
📊 Fair Spread: KC -4.8
📈 Market: KC -3
🔢 Fair Total: 47.0
🔥 Best Bet: Chiefs -3 (-110)
💵 Total Exposure: 0.50u

Can Bijan Robinson control this game, or will Penix’s struggles under pressure ultimately decide it?

Colts 22 — Dolphins 16

text:
Reverend Father Jenkins,

I am a 46-year-old Polish man, married to my Polish wife, with two sons. We have been living in Ireland since 2004. Although we were baptised, confirmed, and married in the Novus Ordo in Poland, and our children were baptised in Ireland, we lived in Ireland for the first 10 years almost like atheists.

I have been watching the episodes from 2014—the archived ones still featuring you, Father, Bishop (at the time still a priest) Kelly, and Father Sanborn—when I was still in the Novus Ordo and did not fully understand what had happened to the Church since Pope Roncalli occupied the throne and modernists took control of the Holy See.

I was often critical of your discussions, but they intrigued me so much that I had to study and find out what had happened regarding the treason carried out by modernists and lukewarm Catholics against Our Mother the Church.

From 2017 we began attending the Latin Mass provided by Ecclesia Dei communities. Since 2020 we have stopped attending the Novus Ordo Mass completely.

Unfortunately, we do not have as many options as Catholics in the United States, or France, Italy and Poland. Most so-called sedevacantist priests there are under Bishop Sanborn or the SSPX Resistance. To us the only available traditional Masses are those of the FSSP, ICKSP, while FSSPX requires us a drive of 1.5 to 2 hours each way (with Mass offered every day), or a chapel about 45 minutes away that has Mass on two Sundays a month, Resistance is 4 hours drive.

The priest from the FSSP neither promotes nor criticizes Vatican II or the teachings and decisions of the current modernist popes. He focuses mainly on the traditional teaching of the Church, the writings of past popes and saints, and some current political and social issues. Privately he called Bergoglio the enemy of the Church; another FSSP priest, when Prevost was elected, said he would be even worse than Bergoglio.

I am afraid that if we left the Sunday and occasional weekday Masses within the FSSP we could lose the rest of our Faith. We are not as strong as the Japanese faithful of the pre-20th century yet, I fear. We go to hear Holy Mass with the SSPX occasionally. All the SSPX priests in Ireland are validly ordained as far as I know, unless some are visiting, in which case I am not sure.

I have three questions:

1. Are there any plans for the Society of St. Pius V to expand beyond the United States and Canada? Are there many vocations? Can we count on your prayers, and, if God wills and circumstances allow, that you might send a priest (or more) to Europe for a temporary missions or permanent ? What conditions would need to be met to accommodate priests so far from home? Are there any talks with priests from the SSPX or Ecclesia Dei communities, or even with Novus Ordo priests or laity who may have received a vocation and are willing to convert to the true Catholic Faith, receive the Holy Sacraments sub conditione, and serve as chaplains on European soil?

2. Are there any other options for people living so far from SSPV parishes on other continents to become true Roman Catholics? I have heard that one may contact the Society for online Catechism classes. Is this still available? Would it be possible, if there is the will to travel two or three times a year (for Christmas or Epiphany, Easter, and once more on the Feast of Christ the King or All Saints), to receive the Sacraments (likely Baptism, Confession, Holy Communion, Confirmation, and Marriage) sub conditione?

3.* (Please skip this question if it has already been addressed in an earlier episode, dear Thomas Nagle.) Do children and embryos conceived via IVF possess souls?

Thank you for your prayers, time, sharing online with your knowledge and experience and for any guidance you can offer.

Respectfully in Christ,
Emil Wilkowski

School Assignment Bearing Ja'Niyah’s Name Found in Gary Abandoned House — Never Turned Over to FBI or Police

Missing Lost And Trafficked 
Lured Lost And Unsolved 

GARY, Ind. — A school assignment bearing the handwritten name “Ja’Niyah” was recovered from an abandoned house in the 2500 block of Connecticut Street and never submitted to the FBI or Gary Police Department, according to recent updates from the social media news platform, Missing Lost And Trafficked.

The document was reportedly retrieved by Lorenzo Longoria, founder of Team NWI Independent Search Team, a volunteer search-and-rescue organization based in Northwest Indiana, during efforts related to another missing person case.

 An eye witness source, who requested anonymity told Missing Lost And Trafficked that Longoria did not turn the assignment over to federal or local investigators. 

 Amanda Agr discussed the retrieval on the Nov. 12, 2026, episode of the podcast “The Missing Struggle,” hosted on Team Canine of NWI’s YouTube channel.

The abandoned property, located near East 25th Avenue, was described as a house frequented by squatters. 

Emma Baum was reportedly dropped off at
 the same location on Oct. 10, 2024. The assignment’s presence there has drawn attention because of its potential to place physical material connected to Ja’Niyah McMichael at a site tied to other activity under scrutiny in the broader search for missing people in Gary.

Ja’Niyah McMichael, then 13, was reported missing by her mother, Jasmine McMichael, on Aug. 12, 2024, from the 1900 block of Malcolm X Boulevard (also referred to as Virginia Street). 

She was last seen the evening before she was due to start eighth grade, wearing black pajama pants, a black hoodie and black-and-red shoes. 

The FBI and Gary Police Department have said they believe she may be the victim of foul play. A combined reward of at least $20,000 has been offered for information leading to an arrest and conviction.

Missing Lost And Trafficked has framed the assignment discovery against a series of allegations circulating in the case. In private Facebook Messenger messages, Jeffrey Farmer, a registered sex offender, claimed Ja’Niyah was sold by her mother to Antwon Butler to settle a drug debt, was abused and was killed.

 Farmer alleged she was thrown into the Grand Calumet River in August 2024 near Broadway Street, where the river intersects the northern end of downtown Gary near the main entrance to the U.S. Steel Gary Works facility at 1 North Broadway.

 MLAT  has also pointed to geographic connections. Kevin Kizer resided in the 1900 block of Carolina Street on Aug. 12, 2024 — the day Ja’Niyah was reported missing — a location described as directly behind or a short walk from the 1900 block of Virginia Street/Malcolm X Boulevard where she was last seen. Kizer has a documented criminal history that includes aggravated battery, kidnapping with moderate bodily injury, confinement with moderate bodily injury, domestic battery involving a pregnant woman, strangulation and intimidation.

 Separately, Marietta Banks, also known as “Pebbles,” told the group that Kizer assisted Butler in removing a deceased Emma Baum from her apartment on Oct. 10, 2024.

Additional context cited by Missing Lost And Trafficked includes an incident on Sept. 16, 2024, in which Dalia Guerrero, Ja’Niyah’s maternal grandmother, sought police assistance after being threatened by family members of Ja’Niyah’s mother’s girlfriend while near the Grand Calumet River in the 2800 block of Georgia Street.

MLAT  has repeatedly urged a specialized underwater search of the Grand Calumet River. Ohio Special Response Team offered its resources for that effort. Gary Police Chief Derrick Cannon rejected the offer amid the accusations leveled by Jeffrey Farmer.

The school assignment’s recovery and the decision not to submit it to authorities have intensified questions about how volunteer-found potential evidence is handled in a case that has already stretched more than two years.

 Investigators continue to treat the disappearance as an active investigation involving possible foul play.
Anyone with information about Ja’Niyah McMichael’s disappearance is urged to contact the FBI at 1-800-CALL-FBI (1-800-225-5324) or submit a tip online at https://t.co/o9SNTsfpIN. Tips may also be provided to the Gary Police Department.

Taxpayers should be concerned about the qualifications, professional conduct and performance of attorneys receiving court appointments and public contracts to represent children, incapacitated adults and elderly people who depend on the legal system to protect their rights.

Rick Kilfoy's professional record raises serious questions about why he continues receiving these appointments.

In January 2023, Kilfoy received a formal disciplinary admonition from the Arizona Supreme Court's Presiding Disciplinary Judge after conditionally admitting FIVE violations of the Arizona Rules of Professional Conduct.

The case involved a 16-year-old boy Kilfoy was appointed to represent in a wrongful-death lawsuit. Kilfoy failed to communicate a $5 MILLION settlement offer to the child, failed to adequately advise him about the consequences, filed untimely responses to summary-judgment motions and failed to notify him of the resulting judgment and the deadlines to challenge it.

A $50,060,000 judgment was entered against the minor, followed by $1,142,465.21 in sanctions.

The admitted violations involved lack of diligence, failure to communicate, failure to follow the scope of representation, failure to fulfill obligations when representation ended and conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice.

The case also went before the Arizona Court of Appeals in Gibson v. Theut, 246 Ariz. 297 (2019). The court rejected Kilfoy's claim that court-appointed attorneys are entitled to absolute judicial immunity and ruled that a minor represented by a guardian ad litem could bring a malpractice claim against his own attorney.

𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗔𝗣𝗣𝗘𝗟𝗟𝗔𝗧𝗘 𝗖𝗢𝗨𝗥𝗧 𝗔𝗟𝗦𝗢 𝗣𝗨𝗧 𝗠𝗔𝗥𝗜𝗖𝗢𝗣𝗔 𝗖𝗢𝗨𝗡𝗧𝗬'𝗦 𝗔𝗧𝗧𝗢𝗥𝗡𝗘𝗬-𝗩𝗘𝗧𝗧𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗣𝗥𝗢𝗖𝗘𝗦𝗦 𝗨𝗡𝗗𝗘𝗥 𝗦𝗖𝗥𝗨𝗧𝗜𝗡𝗬.

The lawsuit alleged that Kilfoy & guardian ad litem Paul Theut lacked the skill and experience necessary to handle a complex, multi-million-dollar wrongful-death case, despite having County contracts and appearing on a list of attorneys prequalified or preselected for court appointments.

The Court of Appeals ruled that the allegations were sufficient to allow a negligent-hiring claim against Maricopa County to proceed beyond dismissal based on the County's role in selecting or qualifying the attorneys. The court also allowed the claim against the State to proceed concerning its role in preapproving them for potential appointment.

The court specifically stated that it was unclear whether the County, the State or both were responsible for prequalifying or preselecting the attorneys, and whether a judicial officer played a role in approving the list.

text:
Machine-learning researchers make many decisions when designing new models. They decide how many layers to include in neural networks and what weights to give inputs at each node. The result of all this human decision-making is that complex models end up being “designed by intuition” rather than systematically, says Frank Hutter, head of the machine-learning lab at the University of Freiburg in Germany.

A growing field called automated machine learning, or autoML, aims to eliminate the guesswork. The idea is to have algorithms take over the decisions that researchers currently have to make when designing models. Ultimately, these techniques could make machine learning more accessible. 

Although automated machine learning has been around for almost a decade, researchers are still working to refine it. Last week, a new conference in Baltimore—which organizers described as the first international conference on the subject—showcased efforts to improve autoML’s accuracy and streamline its performance. 

There’s been a swell of interest in autoML’s potential to simplify machine learning. Companies like Amazon and Google already offer low-code machine-learning tools that take advantage of autoML techniques. If these techniques become more efficient, it could accelerate research and allow more people to use machine learning.

The idea is to get to a point where people can choose a question they want to ask, point an autoML tool at it, and receive the result they are looking for.

That vision is the “holy grail of computer science,” says Lars Kotthoff, a conference organizer and assistant professor of computer science at the University of Wyoming. “You specify the problem, and the computer figures out how to solve it—and that’s all you do.”

But first, researchers will have to figure out how to make these techniques more time and energy efficient.

What is autoML?

At first glance, the concept of autoML might seem redundant—after all, machine learning is already about automating the process of gaining insights from data. But because autoML algorithms operate at a level of abstraction above the underlying machine-learning models, relying only on the outputs of those models as guides, they can save time and computation. Researchers can apply autoML techniques to pre-trained models to gain fresh insights without wasting computation power repeating existing research.

For example, research scientist Mehdi Bahrami and his coauthors at Fujitsu Research of America presented recent work on how to use a BERT-sort algorithm with different pre-trained models to adapt them for new purposes. BERT-sort is an algorithm that can figure out what is called “semantic order” when trained on data sets—given data on movie reviews, for example, it knows that “great” movies rank higher than “good” and “bad” movies. 

With autoML techniques, the learned semantic order can also be extrapolated to classifying things like cancer diagnoses or even text in the Korean language, cutting down on time and computation. 

“BERT takes months of computation and is very expensive—like, a million dollars to generate that model and repeat those processes,” Bahrami says. “So if everyone wants to do the same thing, then it’s expensive—it’s not energy efficient, not good for the world.” 

Although the field shows promise, researchers are still searching for ways to make autoML techniques more computationally efficient. For example, methods like neural architecture search currently build and test many different models to find the best fit, and the energy it takes to complete all those iterations can be significant.

AutoML techniques can also be applied to machine-learning algorithms that don’t involve neural networks, like creating random decision forests or support-vector machines to classify data. Research in those areas is further along, with many coding libraries already available for people who want to incorporate autoML techniques into their projects. 

The next step is to use autoML to quantify uncertainty and address questions of trustworthiness and fairness in the algorithms, says Hutter, a conference organizer. In that vision, standards around trustworthiness and fairness would be akin to any other machine-learning constraints, like accuracy. And autoML could capture and automatically correct biases found in those algorithms before they’re released.

The search continues

But for something like deep learning, autoML still has a long way to go. Data used to train deep-learning models, like images, documents, and recorded speech, is usually dense and complicated. It takes immense computational power to handle. The cost and time for training these models can be prohibitive for anyone other than researchers working at deep-pocketed private companies. 

One of the competitions at the conference asked participants to develop energy-efficient alternative algorithms for neural architecture search. It’s a considerable challenge because this technique has infamous computational demands. It automatically cycles through countless deep-learning models to help researchers pick the right one for their application, but the process can take months and cost over a million dollars. 

The goal of these alternative algorithms, called zero-cost neural architecture search proxies, is to make neural architecture search more accessible and environmentally friendly by significantly cutting down on its appetite for computation. The result takes only a few seconds to run, instead of months. These techniques are still in the early stages of development and are often unreliable, but machine-learning researchers predict that they have the potential to make the model selection process much more efficient.

text:
Is Fable 5.2 worth it over Opus 5.5 for everyday work?

Claude Fable 5.2 costs exactly twice as much per token as Claude Opus 5.5, and Anthropic's own launch post calls Opus 5.5 "our strongest daily driver." Yet on Artificial Analysis, Fable 5.2 at Medium effort averaged 55 seconds on single-request workloads while Opus 5.5 at Medium took 93. So which one should be open on your screen from 9 to 6: the cheaper default, or the stronger model that sometimes finishes first?

This piece covers daily use: chat, writing, coding sessions, agents, waiting time, cost and failure modes. Every number comes from a source listed at the end, read November 15, 2026.

What is identical, so you can stop comparing it

Much of the spec sheet is the same, so the choice is never about capacity:
Context window: Fable 5.2 1M tokens, Opus 5.5 1M tokens
Max output per request: Fable 5.2 128K, Opus 5.5 128K
Knowledge cutoff: Fable 5.2 June 2026, Opus 5.5 June 2026
Thinking: Fable 5.2 adaptive and always on, Opus 5.5 adaptive and always on
Effort levels: both offer Low, Medium, High, Xhigh and Max

The defaults you get without touching anything

In Claude Code, both Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5 start at Medium effort. Anthropic's launch post says Medium is also the default in the Claude apps. On the raw API it differs: Fable 5.2 defaults to High and Opus 5.5 to Medium. API users who never set effort are comparing Fable at High with Opus at Medium.

No plan makes Fable the default in Claude Code. You pick it with /model fable, and it needs Claude Code v2.1.321 or later.

Speed: where the waiting actually happens

All figures here are from Artificial Analysis, which ran both models at every effort level.

Time to first answer token, matched effort:
Low: Fable 5.2 8.7 s, Opus 5.5 5.4 s
Medium: Fable 5.2 10.4 s, Opus 5.5 17.1 s
High: Fable 5.2 27.9 s, Opus 5.5 30.4 s

End-to-end time, mean of single-request workloads:
Low: Fable 5.2 49.8 s, Opus 5.5 63.7 s
Medium: Fable 5.2 55.3 s, Opus 5.5 93.1 s
High: Fable 5.2 81.1 s, Opus 5.5 120.8 s

Time per Intelligence Index task:
Low: Fable 5.2 5.6 min, Opus 5.5 3.1 min
Medium: Fable 5.2 7.4 min, Opus 5.5 6.9 min
High: Fable 5.2 15.5 min, Opus 5.5 9.3 min

The two views disagree usefully. On a single request at the same effort, Fable often finishes sooner. On longer multi-step tasks, Fable does more work and Opus finishes first.

In the Slack agent test covered below, Opus had a median response of 23 seconds and a 90th percentile of 48. Fable had 52 seconds and 1 minute 43.

Both models offer fast mode on the API, with up to 2.5x output speed at double the price. Fast Opus costs the same as standard Fable.

What a normal day costs

List prices per million tokens:
Standard: Fable 5.2 $8 in and $40 out, Opus 5.5 $4 in and $20 out
Batch API: Fable 5.2 $4 and $20, Opus 5.5 $2 and $10
5-minute cache write: Fable 5.2 $10, Opus 5.5 $5
Cache read: Fable 5.2 $0.20, Opus 5.5 $0.20

A simple API example, my arithmetic at list price, not a measurement. Take 80 chat turns in a day, each with 3,000 input tokens and 800 output tokens, no caching. Opus 5.5 costs $0.028 per turn, or $2.24 for the day. Fable 5.2 costs $0.056 per turn, or $4.48. That assumes equal token use, which flatters Fable: Anthropic says Fable 5.2 thinks before almost every reply at High and above, and a prompt asking it not to deliberate did not stop it at Medium and above.

Measured cost per task on Artificial Analysis, matched effort:
Low: Fable 5.2 $3.10, Opus 5.5 $0.98
Medium: Fable 5.2 $3.80, Opus 5.5 $2.45
High: Fable 5.2 $9.08, Opus 5.5 $3.46
Xhigh: Fable 5.2 $14.83, Opus 5.5 $6.05
Max: Fable 5.2 $26.54, Opus 5.5 $10.04

At matched effort, Fable costs 1.6x to 3.2x more per task. The more useful comparison is matched score. Fable at Low scored 54 on the index against Opus at High with 52, for $3.10 against $3.46. Fable at High scored 62 against Opus at Max with 59, for $9.08 against $10.04, and in 15.5 minutes against 25.5. From Opus High upward, there is a Fable setting that matches or beats it for less. Below Opus High there is not, because Fable's cheapest setting already costs more than Opus at Medium.

One cache detail for API builders. Anthropic measured Fable 5.2 on a 20-issue triage job. With no pauses, the 5-minute cache cost $2.18 per session. When every turn came after a 6-minute pause, the 5-minute cache expired each time and the session cost $20.36. The 1-hour cache cost $2.61 on the same schedule. If a human takes breaks between turns, use the 1-hour cache.

Where Fable 5.2 actually earns the price

1. Factual recall and admitting uncertainty. On AA-Omniscience, which rewards correct answers and penalizes confident wrong ones, Fable 5.2 at High scored 64 against Opus 5.5 at High with 42. Even Fable at Low scored 63. It is the biggest gap between the two models.
2. Hard reasoning. On HLE-Diamond at Max, Fable scored 80.2% against 67.9%. On CritPt v2 hard subset at Max, it was 76.5% against 68.0%.
3. Judgment calls inside agents. In the Deepnote agent benchmark, Fable 5.2 was the strongest model of all twelve on Decide tasks, which ask for comparing options and recommending a next step, and it was stronger than Opus at Diagnose, which asks for a root cause.
4. Digging until it finds the real evidence. In one Deepnote task, Fable compared report tables itself, found a mismatch and scored 10 out of 10. It took 1 minute 49 seconds, 34 tool calls and $4.67. Opus never opened the linked report, ranked by a health score and scored 7, in 39 seconds with 15 calls for $0.826.
5. Long, checkable work. On Anthropic's internal agentic coding benchmark, Fable 5.2 at High was the only setting above 93%, with 93.5% against 91.1% for Opus at Xhigh. On Remote Labor Index, which is vendor-reported, Fable at High scored 41.3% against 21.3%.
6. Fewer fallbacks and refusals in an independent suite. On the Vals Index, Fable 5.2 had a 1.88% fallback rate and 0.00% refusals. Opus 5.5 had 2.68% and 0.87%. Vals ran Fable at High and Opus at Max, so treat this as indicative.
7. Charts and screenshots of data. On Chartography with no tools, a vendor figure, Fable scored 73.4% against 64.4%.
8. Honesty behaviors. Anthropic's behavioral audit of Mythos 5.2, the same underlying model as Fable 5.2, found lower rates of hallucinating inputs, falsely claiming a task was done, omitting important information and hiding lazy work than Opus 5.5. Vendor finding, sibling model.

Anthropic's Claude Code docs say Fable investigates before acting and verifies its own work more often. They advise describing the outcome, not the steps, and skipping reminders to test.

Where Opus 5.5 is still the better pick

1. Anything where someone is waiting. Opus at Low gets its first answer token out in 5.4 seconds.
2. Office deliverables and briefs. On AA-Briefcase, Opus at Max scored 1801 Elo against 1785 for Fable at Max, and at High it was 1682 against 1677. On GDP.pdf, Opus at High scored 28.8% against 21.8%.
3. Legal and tax work in Vals: Legal Index 72.37% against 69.17%, Tax Agent Bench 44.54% against 32.09%.
4. Screenshots and UI mockups into code. On SWE-bench Multimodal in Vals, Opus scored 70.21% against 62.29%.
5. Ordinary coding with a clear spec. On a 463-problem SWE-bench Pro subset that Anthropic measured, Opus at Medium solved 93.1% for $0.22 per solved task. Opus at Xhigh solved 96.5% for $0.75, level with Fable at High (96.3%, $1.39). In my same-prompt test this week, both passed 162 of 162 hidden tests, and Fable cost 2.15x as much and took 29.8 seconds against 24.1.
6. Knowing when to stay quiet. When a background agent should not have posted at all, Opus held back 8 times out of 10 and Fable 6 times out of 10.
7. Coordination. In the Deepnote benchmark, Opus was stronger at coordinating teams and explaining how things work.
8. Batch jobs. On the Batch API, Opus 5.5 supports up to 300K output tokens per request with a beta header. Fable 5.2 stays at 128K.
9. Data rules. Fable 5.2 requires 30-day data retention and is not available under zero data retention unless Anthropic expressly authorizes it.

Writing: different voices, not a clear winner

Writing has the weakest evidence. Fable 5.2 has no score yet on the LMArena text board. Opus 5.5 at High is fourth there at 1507, with a margin of 6.

An Artificial Analysis personality test compares the two at Max. Judges picked Fable as more natural sounding 75% of the time. They picked Opus as more lexically varied 93% of the time and more metaphorical 80% of the time.

Fable reads plainer, Opus reads richer. For docs and release notes, Fable's voice may suit you. For copy and narrative, Opus has the measured edge. Anthropic also says Fable follows style rules closely, and a hard sentence-length limit can make its prose choppy.

Background agents: what the Deepnote benchmark says

Deepnote's Agent Initiative Benchmark, released November 13, is the closest thing to a daily-use test for an always-on agent. Each model watches a synthetic company's Slack with 11 connected services, decides whether to help, digs for evidence, then posts or stays silent. It covers 50 situations at High effort with a 180-second budget.

Score out of 10: Fable 5.2 8.17, Opus 5.5 7.84
95% interval: Fable 5.2 7.34 to 8.89, Opus 5.5 7.14 to 8.46
Cost per task: Fable 5.2 $1.87, Opus 5.5 $1.28
Median response time: Fable 5.2 52 s, Opus 5.5 23 s
Tool calls per task: Fable 5.2 20.9, Opus 5.5 10.0
Helped when help was needed: Fable 5.2 40 of 40, Opus 5.5 40 of 40
Stayed silent when it should: Fable 5.2 6 of 10, Opus 5.5 8 of 10
Perfect 10 scores: Fable 5.2 18, Opus 5.5 14
Zero scores: Fable 5.2 4, Opus 5.5 2
One month of one company's Slack: Fable 5.2 $4,684, Opus 5.5 $3,196

Deepnote's summary: Fable makes twice the tool calls, takes twice the time and costs 47% more for a score 4% higher. The intervals overlap.

For a live thread bot, Opus is faster, quieter and good enough. For background digests and decisions, Fable's digging bought more perfect scores, with more zeros and unneeded messages.

Failure modes you will hit in a normal week

Fable 5.2 stopping early. On long multi-step tasks, Fable sometimes ends a turn with a list of what remains, an offer to continue, or a stop at an ordinary obstacle. Anthropic says this happens more often at Low and Medium, and Medium is the Claude Code default. For long jobs, run Fable at High or tell it plainly to finish the whole task.

Fable 5.2 not fixing what it finds. In Anthropic's tests on small coding tasks, when the prompt did not say who owned the code, Fable tended to build on the existing structure and report nearby problems instead of fixing them. Say "you own this code, fix what you find" when that is what you want.

Fable 5.2 thinking on easy questions. Lower the effort for quick questions instead of prompting around it.

Fable 5.2 subagent bills. Fable delegates readily, and subagents can be a large share of session cost. CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL keeps them on a cheaper model.

Fable 5.2 output cap trap on the API. In Anthropic's tests with max_tokens at 16,384, 85% of Fable 5.2 attempts were cut off and it solved 20.3% of tasks. At 64,000 it solved 77.4%. Opus at 16,384 solved 57.6%, so the cap hurts Fable far more.

Opus 5.5 stopping at the first plausible answer. In the Deepnote example above, it never opened the linked report. On evidence-heavy questions, raise effort or name the sources to check.

Opus 5.5 at Low on open-ended work. Anthropic measured a big drop at Low on its internal coding set, 74.8% against 86.6% at Medium. Use Low only with a checker such as tests.

Safety fallbacks. Fable requests flagged in cybersecurity and biology fall back to another model, Opus 4.8 or Opus 5 on the API.

Switching models mid-conversation

Fable 5.2 can read thinking blocks from Opus 5.5, so moving a conversation up from Opus to Fable keeps the earlier reasoning on the Claude API. Moving down from Fable to Opus drops Fable's reasoning for the turns that run there, because no model except Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 reads Fable 5.2's thinking blocks.

The practical rule is to start a task on Opus and escalate to Fable if it struggles, rather than starting on Fable and dropping down. Changing models also rewrites the prompt cache, while a per-message effort change keeps it.

If you build your own requests, Fable 5.2 returns a 400 error when anything before a thinking block has changed. Claude Code and the apps handle this for you.

Plans and access, as facts

Free: neither Fable nor Opus.
Pro and Team standard seats: Opus 5.5 is included. Fable runs on pay-as-you-go usage credits. During launch week, Fable is included up to 50% of weekly limits, plus one Fable reset, until November 16 at 11:59 pm PT, which is November 17 at 1:29 PM IST.
Max, Ultra and premium seats: Fable is included up to 50% of the weekly limit, and it uses limits faster than other models. Past that, you continue on usage credits or switch models. Launch resets, one to three depending on how long you have subscribed, expire March 8, 2027.
Enterprise usage-based and API: standard API rates.
Claude Code on Pro shows "Requires usage credits" on the Fable row in the model picker. In non-interactive mode (claude -p), it bills credits without asking, so check scripts before pointing them at Fable.

My day with each

A typical engineering day, with the pick and why. These are recommendations built from the numbers above, not a new test.

1. 9:00, inbox triage and quick questions: Opus 5.5 at Low. First token in 5.4 seconds, and nobody needs deep reasoning to sort email.
2. 9:30, a factual question you will act on, such as a library's behavior or a spec detail: Fable 5.2 at Low or Medium. Omniscience 63 to 64 against Opus at 39 to 42 is the largest gap between the two models, and Fable Medium answered single requests faster than Opus Medium.
3. 10:00, standup notes and a status email: Opus 5.5 at Medium. Short writing, someone is waiting, and Fable's thinking adds nothing you can see.
4. 10:30, a Claude Code feature with a clear spec and tests: Opus 5.5 at Medium. The SWE-bench Pro subset gave 93.1% for $0.22 per solved task, and in my test Fable matched its pass rate at 2.15x the cost.
5. 11:30, the same feature fails tests twice: rerun on Opus at High. Anthropic measured Low or Medium with failures rerun at High at about 97% solved, for about $0.17 and $0.24 per task.
6. 12:30, the bug survives that: switch to Fable 5.2 at High in the same session. Escalating from Opus keeps the reasoning, and Fable High was the only setting above 93% on the internal coding set.
7. 14:00, a long design doc or quarterly brief: Opus 5.5 at High. Briefcase and GDP.pdf both lean Opus.
8. 15:00, reading a 300-page contract or document set for inconsistencies: Fable 5.2 at High if accuracy decides it, Opus 5.5 if it needs a polished deliverable. Fable leads on recall and reasoning, while Opus leads on Vals Legal at 72.37 against 69.17.
9. 16:00, turning a Figma screenshot into a component: Opus 5.5. Vals measured SWE-bench Multimodal at 70.21% against 62.29%.
10. 16:30, a chart or dashboard screenshot to explain: Fable 5.2. Chartography was 73.4% against 64.4%, a vendor figure.
11. 17:00, a Slack bot that answers teammates live: Opus 5.5. A median response of 23 seconds, and 8 of 10 correct silences.
12. 18:00, an overnight migration or refactor agent with a test suite: Fable 5.2 at High with max_tokens at 64,000 or more. This is the long, checkable work it was built for.
13. 18:30, a batch of 5,000 tickets to classify by morning: Opus 5.5 or a cheaper tier on the Batch API. At $2 and $10 per million tokens, Fable's premium buys nothing without evals that prove it.

Count the picks: Opus takes 8 of 13 outright, Fable takes 4, and one depends on the deliverable. Fable's slots are the ones where a wrong answer costs the most.

Side by side

Price per million tokens: Fable 5.2 $8 in and $40 out, Opus 5.5 $4 in and $20 out
Default effort on the API: Fable 5.2 High, Opus 5.5 Medium
Default effort in Claude Code and the apps: Fable 5.2 Medium, Opus 5.5 Medium
AA Intelligence Index at High: Fable 5.2 62, Opus 5.5 52
AA Intelligence Index at Max: Fable 5.2 65, Opus 5.5 59
AA cost per task at Medium: Fable 5.2 $3.80, Opus 5.5 $2.45
AA single-request time at Medium: Fable 5.2 55.3 s, Opus 5.5 93.1 s
AA-Omniscience at High: Fable 5.2 64, Opus 5.5 42
AA-Briefcase at Max: Fable 5.2 1785, Opus 5.5 1801
GDP.pdf at High: Fable 5.2 21.8%, Opus 5.5 28.8%
Vals Index: Fable 5.2 71.31% at High, Opus 5.5 70.14% at Max
Vals SWE-bench Multimodal: Fable 5.2 62.29%, Opus 5.5 70.21%
Deepnote agent score: Fable 5.2 8.17, Opus 5.5 7.84
Deepnote correct silences: Fable 5.2 6 of 10, Opus 5.5 8 of 10
Deepnote median response: Fable 5.2 52 s, Opus 5.5 23 s
LMArena text: Fable 5.2 not ranked, Opus 5.5 4th at 1507
Batch max output: Fable 5.2 128K, Opus 5.5 300K with beta header
Plan inclusion on Pro: Fable 5.2 usage credits after launch week, Opus 5.5 included

Decision checklist

Ask these in order and stop at the first yes:
1. Is it a quick reply where speed matters more than precision? Use Opus 5.5 at Low or Medium.
2. Is it a batch that can wait until tomorrow? Use Opus 5.5, or a cheaper tier, on the Batch API.
3. Is it a polished document, a legal or tax deliverable, or a UI screenshot? Use Opus 5.5 at High.
4. Will you act on a factual answer, and would a confident wrong answer hurt? Use Fable 5.2 at Low or Medium.
5. Is it a long agent run with a test, spec or other check at the end? Use Fable 5.2 at High, with max_tokens of 64,000 or more.
6. Has Opus 5.5 at High already failed a check you can repeat? Escalate to Fable 5.2 at High in the same conversation.
7. Is it a decision or root-cause question that needs digging across sources? Use Fable 5.2.
8. None of the above? Use Opus 5.5 at Medium.

Two more rules apply in every case. Never run either model at Max by default, because Fable's Max costs 2.9x its High for 3 more index points, and Opus's Max costs 2.9x its High for 7. And when you change your mind mid-task, move up from Opus to Fable, not down.

The verdict

For everyday work, Fable 5.2 is not worth it as a default, and it was never meant to be. Anthropic says to start on Opus 5.5. The measured gaps on writing, office deliverables, UI code and quick answers either favor Opus or are too small to pay double for. And Opus has the better instinct for staying quiet in an agent.

Fable 5.2 is worth it as a deliberate second gear. Switch to it when being wrong costs more than the token bill: factual answers you will act on, decisions, root causes, long agent runs with a finish line, and anything Opus has already failed. On the Artificial Analysis index, a Fable setting matches Opus's top settings for less money and time. In a 13-task day, that is 4 or 5 Fable tasks. The rest belong on Opus.

What this comparison does not settle

Artificial Analysis figures were read November 15 and are recomputed every few days, so speed numbers move. Deepnote is 50 tasks at one effort level, and the intervals overlap. Vals ran Fable at High and Opus at Max.

The SWE-bench Pro subset, internal coding set, output-cap and cache studies are Anthropic measurements. Remote Labor Index, Chartography and the audit are vendor-reported. Anthropic publishes no token figures for plan limits, so Fable's drain rate has no official ratio. The cost example and the 13-task day are illustrations, not measurements.

For those who don't think it's me anymore, I wrote this for my members weeks ago. Also, Axe Edge Members have been well aware. 

I hope everyone is doing well. I wanted to take a minute to share my views for the upcoming weeks, and possibly into the end of the year. 

$ETH

Given the latest market developments surrounding the Binance hack, it is becoming increasingly clear to me that ETH may have formed its local top for the coming weeks. I was hoping for one final push above 3k during this initial impulse, but I am starting to see signs on the weekly timeframe that 2.8k may be the local top. 

Currently, the asset is trading near its 20WMA, which is upsloping (a good sign), and the 0.5 Fibonacci level from its June low to its most recent September high. 

That said, the weekly oscillators and indicators have started to roll over from the top of their respective ranges, suggesting ETH may need to correct after printing a significant move from roughly 1.5k to 2.8k in a relatively short period. In my opinion, this is normal market behavior. 

Much like BTC and the TOTALs, I think ETH is forming a macro Inverse Head and Shoulders (IH&S) pattern targeting 4k. That said, the IH&S is still under construction and may take more time/downward price action to complete. 

The areas of demand I'm looking at presently are the .618 near 2k and the .786 at roughly 1.75k. If you look at the chart, you'll notice that the .786 is co-located with the bottom of the log regression band and the left shoulder of the IH&S pattern. I think ETH could trade near the levels mentioned above at some point during Q4. 

I want to be clear: I think the June low of 1.5k will hold, but this corrective period may come close to challenging those lows, forcing many to capitulate, especially if they were late to the party and started buying ETH and Altcoins near their local tops. 

So what does this mean for our on-chain positions?

First and foremost, it means these aren’t levels to capitulate. It also means we may need to exercise a bit more patience before we see higher prices. Lastly, and most importantly, this means the market may be preparing to offer us one of the best opportunities to add to our positions once again, but from much lower levels ahead of 2027.

If Ethereum continues to correct and reaches some of the lower targets mentioned above, rest assured that on-chain tokens will keep bleeding. 

Signs are emerging that a final, massive, multi-week shakeout is about to take place on-chain. If that's the case, I think being positioned to deploy a bit more dry powder will pay off big next year—obviously, not more than you can afford to lose, as these are all high-risk trades. 

Take $STONK, for instance. At this stage, I would consider $STONK an on-chain blue-chip launchpad. However, it's currently flashing warning signs that it may test much lower levels before reversing higher. $STONK is flashing a large bear flag on the 3D timeframe, similar to the flag I preemptively mentioned $PONS was flashing last month. 

The chart below is inverted to more clearly illustrate the flag. The intended target of the bear flag is below its .886 Fib near 30M. What an incredible opportunity it would be to buy $STONK near those levels. And a move down like that would coincide with a sub-2k move for Ethereum. 

The same goes for $PONS right now. $PONS is on the verge of losing its .786 Fibonacci and a key horizontal support level. If this level breaks, there is essentially no support until the .886 below 100M, near the cluster of 4h candle closes in the chart below. Also, the 200MA on the 4h timeframe is declining sharply, suggesting further bearish momentum may be on the way. This viewpoint also aligns with some bearish ETH price action in the interim. 

I think the best way to play this potential drawdown is to be extremely patient and start DCA’ing once ETH begins trading below the 2k zone.

text:
Me: How Not to Be Wrong: The Hidden Maths of Everyday Life

Ai: Written by mathematician and University of Wisconsin professor Jordan Ellenberg, How Not to Be Wrong is an engaging exploration of how mathematics quietly shapes the way we understand the world, make decisions, interpret information, and navigate everyday life.
Ellenberg challenges the conventional perception of mathematics as a collection of abstract formulas and complicated calculations. Instead, he presents it as a powerful way of thinking—a method for recognizing patterns, questioning assumptions, evaluating evidence, and making more intelligent judgments. His central argument is that mathematical thinking is not reserved for scientists or professional mathematicians; it is an essential tool for anyone who wants to understand reality more clearly.
Through entertaining examples, historical anecdotes, scientific discoveries, and everyday situations, Ellenberg reveals the mathematics concealed within seemingly ordinary experiences. He explores subjects such as probability, statistics, risk, economics, politics, elections, gambling, and human behavior. He examines why coincidences occur, how misleading statistics can distort public opinion, why averages can be deceptive, and how mathematical reasoning can expose errors in arguments that initially appear convincing.
One of the book's most interesting themes is the distinction between simply possessing information and knowing how to interpret it. Numbers can appear objective and authoritative, yet they can easily mislead when presented without context. Ellenberg demonstrates how mathematical literacy helps us recognize manipulation, distinguish meaningful patterns from random fluctuations, and make better decisions when faced with uncertainty.
The book also introduces fascinating mathematical concepts, including calculus, regression to the mean, probability theory, and mathematical logic, without requiring an advanced mathematical background. Ellenberg combines intellectual rigor with humor and accessible storytelling, making complex ideas surprisingly approachable.
At its deeper level, the book is about developing a more disciplined relationship with reality. It encourages readers to question their intuitions, recognize the limitations of their own reasoning, and approach complicated problems with greater intellectual humility. Mathematics becomes less about finding the correct answer to an equation and more about learning how to ask the right questions.

Overall, How Not to Be Wrong is an illuminating book about mathematics as a practical philosophy of thought. It is particularly valuable for readers interested in critical thinking, psychology, science, decision-making, philosophy, and the hidden systems that organize everyday existence. It offers a compelling reminder that understanding even a little mathematics can fundamentally change the way we see the world.

Central theme: Mathematics is not merely a subject to study; it is a way of thinking that helps us see through appearances, recognize underlying patterns, and become less susceptible to mistaken conclusions.
Originally published in 2014, the book is also known by its subtitle, which is the phrase you provided.

GroK: what country was the cement ship registered in?
The ship—which is actually an asphalt and bitumen tanker named the Atlantic Asphalt—was registered in the Marshall Islands.

Are there a lot of shell comanpies in the Marshall Islands
Yes, absolutely. The Marshall Islands is one of the world's biggest hubs for offshore shell companies and a major "flag of convenience" for the global shipping industry.

There are a few key reasons why so many corporations and ship owners register there:

High Secrecy: They offer a high degree of corporate anonymity. The names of shareholders and directors are not required to be on public record.

Tax Benefits: Non-resident companies registered in the Marshall Islands are completely exempt from local taxes.

Ease of Setup: Companies can be formed very quickly, often in just a day, with minimal reporting or compliance requirements.

This is exactly why commercial vessels like the Atlantic Asphalt are so frequently registered there, even if the actual owners, operators, and crew have no physical connection to the islands whatsoever. It shields the true owners from liability and taxes in their home countries.

A Delhi Police chargesheet has alleged that an Indian Air Force Wing Commander shared highly sensitive military information, including classified w@r plans, drone capabilities and fighter aircraft deployment details, with a suspected Pakistani intelligence operative. The allegations also include the disclosure of sensitive military installation coordinates and information about a specialised drone unit, potentially exposing operational vulnerabilities and putting national security at risk.
A Wing Commander of the Indian Air Force (IAF), who was arrested five months ago and booked under the Official Secrets Act, allegedly shared classified military information with a suspected Pakistani intelligence operative, according to a Delhi Police chargesheet filed in court. The officer reportedly exchanged information through WhatsApp between January 12 and April 1, 2026. According to the chargesheet, he allegedly shared a page of a secret war plan after receiving an explicit photograph from the suspected operative and offered to provide additional pages in exchange for more photographs. The information allegedly included details about a specialised drone unit's strength, organisational structure, operational capabilities, drone trials, weapon endurance and targeting mechanisms. 
Police further alleged that the officer disclosed fighter aircraft deployment details in Leh, information about a military exercise at the Mahajan Field Firing Range in Suratgarh, and locations of sensitive military installations. The suspected Pakistani operative allegedly sent malware and spyware applications, which the officer was accused of installing on the devices of five subordinates to potentially access sensitive information and official communications. An analysis of WhatsApp records reportedly revealed an exchange of 3,008 text messages, 65 images, 65 reactions, 42 voice calls, four video calls and six URLs between the two. Police told the court that the alleged disclosures could have compromised critical military assets, exposed operational vulnerabilities and threatened national security.

Boston, Massachusetts.

9.
This historical photograph, dating from the late 1870s or early 1880s, shows the rear (east side) of Trinity Church on Copley Square in Boston.
While most well-known views depict the west façade facing Copley Square, this photograph offers a perspective from Clarendon Street:

• The chancel apse and the central (crossing) tower. In the center of the left half of the image, one can see the semicircular apse of the chancel, punctuated by large round-arched windows. Rising above it is the massive central tower, which is modeled after the tower of the Old Cathedral of Salamanca in Spain.

10.
This historical photograph, dating from shortly after 1906, shows The First Church of Christ, Scientist (also known as The Mother Church) in Boston’s Back Bay neighborhood—the global headquarters of the Christian Science religious movement. The original Mother Church (on the right)—a smaller, granite-built structure featuring a pointed bell tower and a large rose window—dates back to 1894. It was designed by architect Franklin I. Welch in the Richardsonian Romanesque style and provides seating for approximately 900 people.

The monumental domed structure (on the left)—as the following of founder Mary Baker Eddy grew rapidly, a massive expansion (The Mother Church Extension) was added directly onto the original building between 1904 and 1906. Architects Charles Brigham and Solon Spencer Beman created a monumental edifice in a neoclassical-Byzantine style, designed to accommodate around 3,000 visitors.

8 Things You Need to Know about Surveillance
8 important truths about surveillance
ai-in-society
Author
Rachel Thomas

Published
August 7, 2019

Over 225 police departments have partnered with Amazon to have access to Amazon’s video footage obtained as part of the “smart” doorbell product Ring, and in many cases these partnerships are heavily subsidized with taxpayer money. Police departments are allowing Amazon to stream 911 call information directly in real-time, and Amazon requires police departments to read pre-approved scripts when talking about the program. If a homeowner doesn’t want to share data from their video camera doorbell with police, an officer for the Fresno County Sheriff’s Office said they can just go directly to Amazon to obtain it. This creation of an extensive surveillance network, the murky private-public partnership surrounding it, and a lack of any sort of regulations or oversight is frightening. And this is just one of many examples related to surveillance technology that have recently come to light.

I frequently talk with people who are not that concerned about surveillance, or who feel that the positives outweigh the risks. Here, I want to share some important truths about surveillance:

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
Data often contains errors
Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
Surveillance changes our behavior
Surveillance disproportionately impacts the marginalized
Data privacy is a public good
We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
While I was writing this post, a number of investigative articles came out with disturbing new developments related to surveillance. I decided that rather than attempt to include everything in one post (which would make it too long and too dense), I would go ahead and share the above facts about surveillance, as they are just a relevant as ever.

Surveillance can facilitate human rights abuses and even genocide
There is a long history of data about sensitive attributes being misused, including the use of the 1940 USA Census to intern Japanese Americans, a system of identity cards introduced by the Belgian colonial government that were later used during the 1994 Rwandan genocide (in which nearly a million people were murdered), and the role of IBM in helping Nazi Germany use punchcard computers to identify and track the mass killing of millions of Jewish people. More recently, the mass internment of over one million people who are part of an ethnic minority in Western China was facilitated through the use of a surveillance network of cameras, biometric data (including images of people’s faces, audio of their voices, and blood samples), and phone monitoring.

Adolf Hitler meeting with IBM CEO Tom Watson Sr. in 1937. Source: Computer History
Pictured above is Adolf Hitler (far left) meeting with IBM CEO Tom Watson Sr. (2nd from left), shortly before Hitler awarded Watson a special “Service to the Reich” medal in 1937 (for a timeline of the Holocaust, see here). Watson returned the medal in 1940, although IBM continued to do business with the Nazis. IBM technology helped the Nazis conduct detailed censuses in countries they occupied, to thoroughly identify anyone of Jewish descent. Nazi concentration camps used IBM’s punchcard machines to tabulate prisoners, recording whether they were Jewish, gay, or Gypsies, and whether they died of “natural causes,” execution, suicide, or via “special treatment” in gas chambers. It is not the case that IBM sold the machines and then was done with it. Rather, IBM and its subsidiaries provided regular training and maintenance on-site at the concentration camps: printing off cards, configuring machines, and repairing them as they broke frequently.

Data is often used for different purposes than why it was collected
In the above examples, the data collection began before genocide was committed. IBM began selling to Nazi Germany well before the Holocaust (although continued for far too long), including helping with Germany’s 1933 census conducted by Adolf Hitler, which was effective at identifying far more Jewish people than had previously been recognized in Germany.

It is important to recognize how data and images gathered through surveillance can be weaponized later. Columbia professor Tim Wu wrote that “One [hard truth] is that data and surveillance networks created for one purpose can and will be used for others. You must assume that any personal data that Facebook or Android keeps are data that governments around the world will try to get or that thieves will try to steal.”

Plenty of data collection is not involved with such extreme abuse as genocide; however, in a time of global resurgence of white supremacist, ethno-nationalist, and authoritarian movements, it would be deeply irresponsible to not consider how data & surveillance can and will be weaponized against already vulnerable groups.

Data often has errors (and no mechanism for correcting them)
A database of suspected gang members maintained by California law enforcement officials was found to be full of errors, including 42 babies who had been added to the database when they were less than 1 year old (28 of whom were marked as “admitting to being gang members”). Even worse, there was no process in place for correcting mistakes or removing people once they’ve been added.

An
@NPR

  reporter recounts his experience of trying to rent an apartment and discovering that TransUnion, one of the 3 major credit bureaus, incorrectly reported him as having two felony firearms convictions. TransUnion only removed the mistakes after a dozen phone calls and notification that the story would be reported on. This is not an unusual story: the FTC’s large-scale study of credit reports in 2012 found 26% of consumers had at least one mistake in their files and 5% had errors that could be devastating. An even more opaque, unregulated “4th bureau” exists: a collection of companies buying and selling personal information about people on the margins of the banking system (such as immigrants, students, and people with low incomes), with no standards on what types of data are included, no way to opt out, and no system for identifying or correcting mistakes.

Surveillance typically operates with no accountability
What makes the examples in the previous section disturbing is not just that errors occurred, but that there was no way to identify or correct them, and no accountability for those profiting off the error-laden data. Often, even the existence of the systems being used is not publicly known (much less details of how these systems work), unless discovered by journalists or revealed by whistleblowers. The Detroit Police Dept used facial recognition technology for nearly two years without public input and in violation of a requirement that a policy be approved by the city’s Board of Police Commissioners, until a study from Georgetown Law’s Center for Privacy & Technology drew attention to the issue. Palantir, the defense startup founded by billionaire Peter Thiel, ran a program with New Orleans Police Department for 6 years which city council members did not even know about, much less have any oversight.

After two studies found that Amazon’s facial recognition software produced inaccurate and racially biased results, Amazon countered that the researchers should have changed the default parameters. However, it turned out that Amazon was not instructing police departments that use its software to do this either. Surveillance programs are operating with few regulations, no oversight, no accountability around accuracy or mistakes, and in many cases, no public knowledge of what is going on.

Surveillance changes our behavior
Hundreds of thousands of people in Hong Kong are protesting an unpopular new bill which would allow extradition to China. Typically, Hong Kong locals use their rechargeable smart cards to ride the subway. However, during the protests, long lines of people waited to use cash to buy paper tickets (usually something that only tourists do) concerned that they would be tracked for having attended the protests. Would fewer people protest if this was not an option?

In the United States, in 2015 the Baltimore Police Department used facial recognition technology to surveil people protesting the death of Freddie Grey, a young Black man who was killed in police custody, and arrested protesters with outstanding warrants. Mass surveillance could have a chilling impact on our rights to move about freely, to express ourselves, and to protest. “We act differently when we know we are ‘on the record.’ Mass privacy is the freedom to act without being watched and thus in a sense, to be who we really are,” Columbia professor Tim Wu wrote in the New York Times.

Flyer from the company Geofeedia Source
Surveillance disproportionately impacts those who are already marginalized
Surveillance is applied unevenly, causing the greatest harm to people who are already marginalized, including immigrants, people of color, and people living in poverty. These groups are more heavily policed and surveilled. The Perpetual Line-Up from the Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology studied the unregulated use of facial recognition by police, with half of all Americans appearing in law enforcement databases, and the risks of errors, racial bias, misuses, and threats to civil liberties. The researchers pointed out that African Americans are more likely to appear in these databases (many of which are drawn from mug shots) since they are disproportionately likely to be stopped, interrogated, or arrested. For another example, consider the contrast between how easily people over 65 can apply for Medicare benefits by filling out an online form, with the invasive personal questions asked of a low-income mother on Medicaid about her lovers, hygiene, parental shortcomings, and personal habits.

In an article titled Trading privacy for survival is another tax on the poor, Ciara Byrne wrote, “Current public benefits programs ask applicants extremely detailed and personal questions and sometimes mandate home visits, drug tests, fingerprinting, and collection of biometric information… Employers of low-income workers listen to phone calls, conduct drug tests, monitor closed-circuit television, and require psychometric tests as conditions of employment. Prisoners in some states have to consent to be voiceprinted in order to make phone calls.”

Data privacy is a public good, like air quality or safe drinking water
Data is more revealing in aggregate. It can be nearly impossible to know what your individual data could reveal when combined with the data of others or with data from other sources, or when machine learning inference is performed on it. For instance, as Zeynep Tufekci wrote in the New York Times, individual Strava users could not have predicted how in aggregate their data could be used to identify the locations of US military bases. “Data privacy is not like a consumer good, where you click ‘I accept’ and all is well. Data privacy is more like air quality or safe drinking water, a public good that cannot be effectively regulated by trusting in the wisdom of millions of individual choices. A more collective response is needed.”

Unfortunately, this also means that you can’t fully safeguard your privacy on your own. You may choose not to purchase Amazon’s ring doorbell, yet you can still show up in the video footage collected by others. You might strengthen your online privacy practices, yet conclusions will still be inferred about you based on the behavior of others. As Professor Tufekci wrote, we need a collective response.

We don’t have to accept invasive surveillance
Many people are uncomfortable with surveillance, but feel like they have no say in the matter. While the threats surveillance poses are large, it is not too late to act. We are seeing success: in response to community organizing and an audit, Los Angeles Police Department scrapped a controversial program to predict who is most likely to commit violent crimes. Citizens, researchers, and activists in Detroit have been effective at drawing attention to the Detroit Police Department’s unregulated use of facial recognition and a bill calling for a 5-year moratorium has been introduced to the state legislature. Local governments in San Francisco, Oakland, and Somerville have banned the use of facial recognition by police.

For further resources, please check out: - Georgetown Law Center on Privacy and Technology - Digital Defense Playbook

8 Things You Need to Know about Surveillance
8 important truths about surveillance
