text:
Then forensic science offered investigators a new opportunity.

In 2023, Massachusetts State Police submitted the victim’s DNA for advanced testing through Othram, a forensic laboratory that specializes in difficult DNA identification cases.

The process was not simply a matter of searching a database.

Scientists developed a genetic profile, while genealogists used family connections to trace possible relatives. Eventually, investigators located a close family member who agreed to provide a DNA sample.

The comparison produced a breakthrough.

On June 3, 2026, authorities announced that Chelsea Jane Doe had finally been identified.

Her name was Tiffany Bradley.

She was only 16 years old when she was killed.

She came from Allentown, Pennsylvania, more than 300 miles from where her remains were discovered.

And the last known communication with her family was heartbreaking.

On November 8, 2000, Tiffany called her cousin from Syracuse, New York. She said she would call back later because she had to go.

That call ended without the family knowing it would become one of their last connections to her.

Her cousin later recalled that Tiffany sounded nervous during the conversation.

For more than 25 years, her relatives had lived without knowing what had happened to her.

When the identification was announced, her family finally had confirmation of the truth.

But the story also raised another disturbing concern.

Investigators believe Tiffany may have been in a vulnerable situation and possibly exploited before her death. Her relatives have questioned whether McCollom acted alone.

Those concerns are not proof of additional offenders, and authorities have not established every detail of what happened to her before the murder.

McCollom remains imprisoned for the killing.

Tiffany’s identification did not change the fact that he had already been convicted. What it changed was the story of the victim.

She was no longer an unidentified young woman in a case file.

She was Tiffany Bradley: a daughter, a cousin, and a 16-year-old girl whose life ended far from home.

For 26 years, the mystery was not simply who had killed her.

It was who had been killed.

Now her family can finally remember her by her real name.

The man responsible was already behind bars. But it took another 21 years after his conviction for the world to discover the name of the girl he had murdered.

Sources: A&E’s detailed reconstruction of the case and the June 2026 identification announcement. Hearst Networks EMEA.

text:
16 Years of Marriage, and Her First Visit to My Roots. ❤️

It’s been 16 years since I married this damsel.

And for the first time in our 16 years of marriage, I had the opportunity to take her to my hometown, Osan Ekiti.

If anyone should ask me why it took so long, I honestly wouldn’t have a reasonable explanation. 😂

I wasn’t born in Ekiti, but my daddy made sure we visited home regularly while growing up. Both my mum and dad are from Osan Ekiti, so I can boldly say that our roots run deep in Ekiti. In fact, I had my secondary school education in Ekiti. 

Even my modest participation in politics is rooted in Ekiti, thanks to our leader, Senator Ojudu Babafemi, whose leadership and influence made that choice a very easy one for us. 

So, when I told my wife we would be visiting Osan-Ekiti, she was excited. We planned the trip and made the necessary arrangements to ensure her stay would be comfortable.

But somewhere in my mind, I had a few reservations.

Would she like my town?

Would she even want to stay beyond a day?

Would she ever want to visit again after her first experience?

Mind you, my wife is not Yoruba, although her mum is. Her mother is from Egba in Ogun State, with a family house in Ibadan. But my wife was born and raised in Northern Nigeria, where I eventually met her.

So, you can understand my curiosity about how she would respond to life in my little hometown.

When we arrived in Osan, I quietly began observing her mood and reactions. To my pleasant surprise, she acclimatised remarkably quickly!

Before I knew it, we were both thoroughly enjoying ourselves.

She participated in cultural dances, thanks largely to my big sister and her co-wives, who surrounded her with so much sisterhood warmth and affection that she felt completely at home.

I also drove her to Ado Ekiti, the state capital, and showed her around.

Now, driving through Ekiti is a form of wellness on its own. The lush greenery, beautiful countryside, winding roads and refreshing scenery offer a kind of therapeutic experience that money doesn’t necessarily buy.

We enjoyed every bit of it.

But there was one problem. Pounded yam! 🤣🤣🤣

My wife doesn’t want to see pounded yam again anytime soon!

Before we were even fully awake in the morning, a basin of freshly pounded yam accompanied by delicious iru soup would already be waiting for us.

I’m talking about 6:30 a.m.!

And that was just breakfast!

Lunch? Pounded yam.

Dinner? Another round!

Haha! We practically wounded her with pounded yam. 🤣🤣

But beyond the food, the cultural experience and the beautiful countryside, something else struck me.

The serenity.

Is it the cool night breeze, seemingly descending with the dew from the night sky? Or the ambience of an environment that isn’t necessarily luxurious, yet possesses an extraordinary beauty of its own?

There is something profoundly calming about the place.

A certain stillness. A certain peace. That’s a luxury for people who sleep and wake up in a chaotic place like Lagos. Life seems to slow down just enough for you to breathe, reflect and appreciate the simple things.

And my wife loved it!

Since we returned, she hasn’t stopped talking about the experience. In fact, she has already started planning her next trip to Osan-Ekiti.

Imagine that!

The same woman I wasn’t sure would want to spend more than a day there is now looking forward to going back. And for the first time in my life, I’m seriously beginning to entertain the idea of building a small hut 🛖 in Osan Ekiti.

Nothing extravagant. Just a modest place to retreat to occasionally, reconnect with my roots, enjoy the countryside and escape the relentless noise of city life.

Sometimes, the most beautiful experiences are not found in luxurious destinations.

#GONZOTRON INVESTIGATES

THE FAA GROUND STOP • PROJECT 2025 • NOVEMBER 13–15, 2026

THE SKY IS FALLING — OR IS SOMEONE SELLING US A NEW SKY?

A #GONZO investigation into the false-flag hypothesis, government accountability, and the restructuring of American aviation.

Aloha! 🤙

October 6, 2026: @POTUS publicly teased forthcoming surprises while addressing Project 2025 architect and @WhiteHouse budget director @russvought. @thedailybeast 

November 13, 2026: The @FAANews imposed an extraordinary nationwide ground stop following air traffic control communications failures.

November 14, 2026: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy described the aviation infrastructure problems and called for major modernization funding. @USDOT 

And then we turn to Project 2025, pages 632–634, which you provided.

Those pages explicitly recommend restructuring the FAA and changing how air traffic control is organized and financed.

The connection is worth investigating. But there is a critical distinction between an event being used to promote a preexisting policy and an event being deliberately engineered to promote that policy.

The former can be examined through public statements, budgets, legislation, and contracts. The latter requires additional evidence that has not emerged from the reporting I've reviewed.

Exhibit A: The Project 2025 blueprint

Source: Mandate for Leadership, Department of Transportation, pp. 632–634

Your excerpt contains these specific recommendations:

Page | Policy proposal

633 | Separate the @FAANews from the @USDOT, or separate the Air Traffic Organization (#ATO) from the @FAANews.

633 | Restructure @FAANews funding to reduce dependence on annual congressional appropriations

633 | Require the @FAANews to operate more like a business

634 | Relocate the #ATO to separate headquarters outside Washington, D.C.

634 | Replace aviation-user taxes with fees paid directly for air traffic services

634 | Permit the #ATO to issue long-term revenue bonds for infrastructure

Notice something important: These proposals involve organizational authority, funding, regulation, and financial independence. They are not simply recommendations to replace obsolete computers.

The document also explicitly says that several of these changes require legislation. A nationwide ground stop cannot itself legally accomplish them.

And page 635 transitions into federal transit policy, rather than adding another FAA restructuring recommendation.

🛩️ - Contractor @L3HarrisTech was upgrading telecommunications equipment from copper connections to fiber optics.
🛩️ - During the work, a router reportedly began overwhelming other network routers with connection attempts.
🛩️ - The resulting instability affected air traffic control communications and radar feeds.
🛩️ - Officials ordered the nationwide ground stop as a safety precaution.
🛩️ - As of the November 14 briefing, investigators had not determined whether the underlying cause was equipment failure or installation error. @USDOT 

This matters because a specific, testable technical explanation exists. It does not settle every question about negligence, cybersecurity, or accountability—but it is evidence that a technical failure occurred, not evidence of a staged event.

Exhibit C: The October surprise

I located Trump's actual remarks from October 6.

Speaking in Baltimore, he addressed Russ Vought, the director of the Office of Management and Budget, and said:

“We have some big surprises coming up in another few weeks, right, Russ?”

He then praised Vought's anticipated accomplishments. 
October 6, 2026

That statement is authentic. But @POTUS did not mention the @FAANews, an aviation shutdown, or a nationwide emergency in those remarks.

The dates raise a legitimate question about what Trump and Vought were planning. They do not establish that the November 13 grounding was one of those plans.

Exhibit D: The money trail

Here is where the #GONZO investigation becomes especially interesting.

During the November 13 emergency briefing, Secretary Duffy publicly requested billions in additional @FAANews funding.

@FAANews modernization funding discussed November 13

@POTUS administration request
$30B

These are requested funding amounts, not money newly appropriated because of the November 13 grounding. 

Duffy described the situation as an emergency and called for congressional funding to replace aging communications hardware, software, and infrastructure.

This creates a documented policy connection: The shutdown was immediately used to reinforce an existing argument for major federal investment.

But here's an important difference: Project 2025 proposes structural changes, user fees, and revenue bonds, while Duffy's immediate request was for congressional appropriations. These approaches are related to infrastructure policy but are not identical.

Exhibit E: The contractor

Another significant development arrived November 14.

@L3HarrisTech acknowledged its role in the communications modernization program and stated that more than 70% of the planned copper-to-fiber conversion had been completed. The company said it was cooperating with the investigation. 
@L3HarrisTech Fast. Forward.

@Reuters also reported that the failure affected 17 of the FAA's 22 en route centers. The underlying cause remains under investigation, with installation error and defective equipment among the possibilities. 

This suggests several concrete accountability questions:

🛩️ - Who approved the November 13 maintenance and its risk assessment?
🛩️ - Was the change tested under realistic network loads?
🛩️ - Why did one malfunction propagate across so many control centers?
🛩️ - What independent investigation will examine contractor responsibility?
🛩️ - Will the incident lead to new contracts, organizational restructuring, or both?

Those questions are investigable without assuming deliberate sabotage.

The false-flag hypothesis: What would establish it?

For the grounding to qualify as a false-flag operation, evidence would need to establish intentional orchestration and a deceptive attribution of responsibility, not merely a failure that advanced someone's political agenda.

Hypothesis | Current evidence

Accidental technical failure | Supported by preliminary @FAANews findings and reported router problems

Contractor negligence | Plausible; investigation incomplete

Cyberattack or deliberate sabotage| No supporting evidence reported by investigators so far

Planned political false flag | No verified evidence currently connects the grounding to intentional orchestration

Crisis used to advance preexisting polices | Supported by Duffy's public funding demands immediately after the event

There is also historical context: @Reuters documents previous @FAANews communications and technology failures, including a nationwide #NOTAM outage in January 2023 and major disruptions in 2025 and September 2026. These prior incidents offer an independently documented explanation for why a major system failure could happen without political orchestration. @Reuters 

The #GONZO conclusion 

Imagine a nation where the airplanes stop flying, travelers sleep on terminal floors, and the secretary of transportation goes before television cameras asking Congress for $50 billion.

Now imagine discovering that an influential policy blueprint had already recommended fundamentally restructuring the very agency responsible for keeping those airplanes moving.

That is a compelling investigative story.

But the distinction matters:

The existence of a blueprint does not prove the existence of a plot.

The existence of a funding beneficiary does not establish who caused a crisis.

And the existence of a mechanical or software failure does not automatically excuse the officials and contractors responsible for preventing it.

For Guild Of Weavers Tailoring Our Universal Web, I would frame the central question this way:

When a national emergency accelerates a political agenda that existed before the emergency, who independently verifies the cause—and who safeguards the public interest while the government responds?

That captures the strongest, supportable part of your concern without presenting an unproven false flag as established fact.

One final distinction: The reported @FAANews outage does not establish a nationwide #GPS failure, a broader interruption of essential services, or a plan to suspend constitutional processes. Those claims would require separate evidence.

The most revealing documents to pursue next are the @FAANews's technical incident report, @L3HarrisTech change-control records, any independent findings, and the legislation or contracts proposed after November 13.

#GONZOTRON's investigative principle: Follow the evidence, follow the authority, follow the money—and keep all three connected.

Donbas for NATO Membership and Peace

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky revealed that American negotiators asked him a new question in the week of the Abu Dhabi talks:  would Ukraine withdraw from the Donbas if it joined NATO?  

It was a question, not a formal offer, and Zelensky repeated that Ukraine will not surrender land.

The Donbas is the industrial east of Ukraine, made of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions.  Russia demands all of it, including the quarter of the Donetsk region that Ukraine still holds, with the fortified cities of Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.

The week brought three results:  an agreement on what would be the largest prisoner exchange of the war, a seat for Europe at the next round, and no ceasefire.  

Moscow is not opposing the European seat, but in our opinion it is not certain that more participants will make an agreement easier.  

Moscow also revived its demand that NATO return to its positions of 1997, before 16 countries joined the alliance.

Is Washington favoring Russia?  The facts say otherwise.  

NATO membership for Ukraine is a "red line" for Vladimir Putin, and American negotiators have now returned NATO membership to the conversation as payment for land.  That is pressure on Moscow, not a favor.  

President Donald Trump wants this war to end, and Putin will not sign a peace that gives him nothing to show the Russian people.

Our reading:  The real question is not whether Ukraine will give up land; it is how much, which regions, and in exchange for what.  That is an opinion, not a preference.

Neither Kyiv nor Moscow can pay for this war much longer.  

Donbas for NATO membership may never become a formal offer, but the question has moved the talks from slogans to concrete terms.  

A hard peace is better than an endless war.

text:
A media circus ensued, with Smith being interviewed by Ted Koppel and Johnny Carson, among others, and with nightly reports by the major American networks. On July 7, 1983, she flew to Moscow with her parents, and spent two weeks as Andropov's guest. During the trip she visited Moscow and Leningrad and spent time in Artek, the main Soviet pioneer camp, in the town of Gurzuf on the Crimean Peninsula. Smith wrote in her book that in Leningrad she and her parents were amazed by the friendliness of the people and by the presents many people made for them. Speaking at a Moscow press conference, she declared that the Russians were "just like us". In Artek, Smith chose to stay with the Soviet children rather than accept the privileged accommodations offered to her. For ease of communication, teachers and children who spoke fluent English were chosen to stay in the building where she was lodged. Smith shared a dormitory with nine other girls, and spent her time there swimming, talking and learning Russian songs and dances. While there, she made many friends, including Natasha Kashirina from Leningrad, a fluent English speaker.

Andropov, however, was unable to meet with her during her visit, although they did speak by telephone. It was later discovered that Andropov had become seriously ill and had withdrawn from the public eye during this time. Smith also received a phone call from Russian cosmonaut Valentina Tereshkova, the first woman to orbit the Earth. However, not realizing with whom she was speaking, Samantha mistakenly hung up after only a brief conversation. Media followed her every step—photographs and articles about her were published by the main Soviet newspapers and magazines throughout her trip and after it. Smith became widely known to Soviet citizens and was well regarded by many of them. In the United States, the event drew suspicion and some regarded it as an "American-style public relations stunt".

Smith's return to the U.S. on July 22, 1983, was celebrated by the people of Maine with roses, a red carpet, and a limousine and her popularity continued to grow in her native country. Some critics at the time remained skeptical, believing Smith was unwittingly serving as an instrument of Soviet propaganda. In December 1983, continuing in her role as "America's Youngest Ambassador", she was invited to Japan, where she met with the Prime Minister Yasuhiro Nakasone and attended the Children's International Symposium in Kobe. In her speech at the symposium, she suggested that Soviet and American leaders exchange granddaughters for two weeks every year, arguing that a president "wouldn't want to send a bomb to a country his granddaughter would be visiting". Her trip inspired other exchanges of child goodwill ambassadors, including a visit by the eleven-year-old Soviet child Katya Lycheva to the United States. Later, Smith wrote a book called Journey to the Soviet Union whose cover shows her at Artek, her favorite part of the Soviet trip.

Smith pursued her role as a media celebrity when in 1984, billed as a "Special Correspondent", she hosted a children's special for The Disney Channel entitled Samantha Smith Goes To Washington...Campaign '84. The show covered politics, where Smith interviewed several candidates for the 1984 presidential election, including George McGovern and Jesse Jackson. That same year she guest starred in Charles in Charge as Kim, alongside another celebrity guest star, Julianne McNamara. Her fame resulted in Smith becoming the subject of stalker Robert John Bardo, the man who would later go on to stalk and ultimately murder My Sister Sam actress Rebecca Schaeffer. Bardo traveled to Maine in an attempt to meet Smith, but was stopped by police and returned home.

In 1985 she co-starred with Robert Wagner in a television series called Lime Street.

TRANSCRIPT
AI flight planning now reaches all twenty-two United States air-traffic centers, expanding its potential influence on routes and delays beyond the initial Washington-area rollout. The SMART system combines two hundred data streams, including weather, flight paths, traffic flow and staffing metrics. Federal Aviation Administration specialists analyze and validate the data before providing scheduling recommendations; facility leaders can accept or reject the advice. The nationwide expansion was announced November tenth. Aviation publication FLYING reported that the agency confirmed the system was active across all centers. This is a broader rollout, rather than a new nationwide evaluation of its benefits.

AI-generated medical explanations could make complex health information easier for children and families to read, but accuracy and reading level need checking. Researchers used ChatGPT to generate thirty-six explanations for each of two hundred pediatric conditions and symptoms. They selected four reading levels, spanning grades five through twelve, and pediatric specialists reviewed all eight hundred selected texts. Prompting alone often missed the requested level. The study, published November twelfth in the journal Preventing Chronic Disease, found that most selected explanations needed no added or deleted words during accuracy editing. It did not measure patient comprehension or health outcomes, and the authors say expert verification remains essential before clinical sharing.

AI tutoring could give Chinese learners tailored feedback while helping teachers prepare lessons. The Yufei specialist language model is described as offering personalized question-and-answer tutoring and assessments with immediate feedback. Its launch description says teachers can use conversational exchanges to generate lesson preparation, classroom and review materials. Education organizations are also offered standard interfaces for applications. Yufei was announced at the World Chinese Conference in Beijing on November thirteenth. These are announced functions: the checked reports do not establish public access, classroom deployment or independently measured learning gains.

AI applications in patient care need evidence about safety, access and cost, alongside any promised benefit. The American Institutes for Research has brought researchers, health organizations and technology developers together for eight projects. Applications include AI-powered school vision referrals, bilingual support for Latina breast-cancer patients, emergency-department wait-risk tools and assistance with clinician messages to patients. The network was announced November twelfth. Its research is intended to assess effectiveness, safety, costs, access and risks in real-world settings. The announcement provides no clinical results or evidence that all eight applications have reached routine deployment.

AI can produce fluent but inaccurate climate information, while fabricated images can compete with official disaster warnings, a United Nations-led initiative warns. Its priorities ask AI companies to assess and publish how their systems affect climate-information reliability. They also call for disclosure of energy use and carbon, water and land footprints, and ask governments to incorporate information integrity into national AI and climate strategies. The guidance launched at the United Nations climate conference on November thirteenth. These are voluntary recommendations, not enforceable rules, and the launch provides no company compliance commitments.

AI infrastructure and adoption bring questions about employment, rights, security and public trust to European policymaking. European Union leaders held their first strategic discussion devoted to AI on November thirteenth. They examined investment, stronger European capabilities, technology dependencies and energy supply, alongside wider AI use by businesses and public administrations. Discussion also covered children's rights, labour markets and safeguards for advanced AI. European Council President Antonio Costa said AI and jobs would be the central theme of the twenty twenty-seven social summit. That creates a future policy forum; the meeting itself adopted no new AI law or funding commitment.

text:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

Microsoft is reportedly eyeing a $10 billion investment in OpenAI, the startup that created the viral chatbot ChatGPT, and is planning to integrate it into Office products and Bing search. The tech giant has already invested at least $1 billion into OpenAI. Some of these features might be rolling out as early as March, according to The Information.  

This is a big deal. If successful, it will bring powerful AI tools to the masses. So what would ChatGPT-powered Microsoft products look like? We asked Microsoft and OpenAI. Neither was willing to answer our questions on how they plan to integrate AI-powered products into Microsoft’s tools, even though work must be well underway to do so. However, we do know enough to make some informed, intelligent guesses. Hint: it’s probably good news if, like me, you find creating PowerPoint presentations and answering emails boring. 

Let’s start with online search, the application that’s received the most coverage and attention. ChatGPT’s popularity has shaken Google, which reportedly considers it a “code red” for the company’s ubiquitous search engine. Microsoft is reportedly hoping to integrate ChatGPT into its (more maligned) search engine Bing. 

It could work as a front end to Bing that answers people’s queries in natural language, according to Melanie Mitchell, a researcher at the Santa Fe Institute, a research nonprofit. AI-powered search could mean that when you ask something, instead of getting a list of links, you get a complete paragraph with the answer. 

However, there’s a good reason why Google hasn’t already gone ahead and incorporated its own powerful language models into Search. Models like ChatGPT have a notorious tendency to spew biased, harmful, and factually incorrect content. They are great at generating slick language that reads as if a human wrote it. But they have no real understanding of what they are generating, and they state both facts and falsehoods with the same high level of confidence.

When people search for information online today, they are presented with an array of options, and they can judge for themselves which results are reliable. A chat AI like ChatGPT removes that “human assessment” layer and forces people to take results at face value, says Chirag Shah, a computer science professor at the University of Washington who specializes in search engines. People might not even notice when these AI systems  generate biased content or misinformation—and then end up spreading it further, he adds.

When asked, OpenAI was cryptic about how it trains its models to be more accurate. A spokesperson said that ChatGPT was a research demo, and that it’s updated on the basis of real-world feedback. But it’s not clear how that will work in practice, and accurate results will be crucial if Microsoft wants people to stop “googling” things. 

In the meantime, it’s more likely that we are going to see apps such as Outlook and Office get an AI injection, says Shah. ChatGPT’s potential to help people write more fluently and more quickly could be Microsoft’s killer application. 

Language models could be integrated into Word to make it easier for people to summarize reports, write proposals, or generate ideas, Shah says. They could also give email programs and Word better autocomplete tools, he adds. And it’s not just all word-based. Microsoft has already said it will use OpenAI’s text-to-image generator DALL-E to create images for PowerPoint presentations too. 

We are also not too far from the day when large language models can respond to voice commands or read out text, such as emails, Shah says. This might be a boon for people with learning disabilities or visual impairments.

Online search is also not the only type of search the app could improve. Microsoft could use it to help users search for emails and documents. 

But here’s the important question people aren’t asking enough: Is this a future we really want? 

Adopting these technologies too blindly and automating our communications and creative ideas could cause humans to lose agency to machines. And there is a risk of “regression to the meh,” where our personality is sucked out of our messages, says Mitchell.

“​The bots will be writing emails to the bots, and the bots will be responding to other bots,” she says. “That doesn’t sound like a great world to me.” 

Language models are also great copycats. Every single prompt entered into ChatGPT helps train it further. In the future, as these technologies are further embedded into our daily tools, they can learn our personal writing style and preferences. They could even manipulate us to buy stuff or act in a certain way, warns Mitchell. 

It’s also unclear if this will actually improve productivity, since people will still have to edit and double-check the accuracy of AI-generated content. Alternatively, there’s a risk that people will blindly trust it, which is a known problem with new technologies. 

“We’ll all be the beta testers for these things,” Mitchell says.

Deeper Learning

Roomba testers feel misled after intimate images ended up on Facebook

Late last year, we published a bombshell story about how sensitive images of people collected by Roomba vacuum cleaners ended up leaking online. These people had volunteered to test the products, but it had never remotely occurred to them that their data could end up leaking in this way. The story offered a fascinating peek behind the curtain at how the AI algorithms that control smart home devices are trained. 

The human cost: In the weeks since the story’s publication, nearly a dozen Roomba testers have come forward. They feel misled and dismayed about how iRobot, Roomba’s creator, handled their data. They say it wasn’t clear to them that the company would share test users’ data in a sprawling, global data supply chain, where everything (and every person) captured by the devices’ front-facing cameras could be seen, and perhaps annotated, by low-paid contractors outside the United States who could screenshot and share images at their will. Read more from my colleague Eileen Guo.

Bits and Bytes

Alarmed by AI chatbots, universities have started revamping how they teach
The college essay is dead, long live ChatGPT. Professors have started redesigning their courses to take into account that AI can write passable essays. In response, educators are shifting towards oral exams, group work, and handwritten assignments.  (The New York Times) 

Artists have filed a class action lawsuit against Stable Diffusion
A group of artists have filed a class action lawsuit against Sta­bil­https://t.co/ksD1jVvOhU, DeviantArt, and Mid­jour­ney for using Stable Diffusion, an open sourced text-to-image AI model. The artists claim these companies stole their work to train the AI model. If successful, this lawsuit could force AI companies to compensate artists for using their work.

The artist’s lawyers argue that the “mis­ap­pro­pri­a­tion” of copyrighted works could be worth roughly $5 bil­lion. By way of comparison, the thieves who carried out the biggest art heist ever made off with works worth a mere $500 million. 

Why are so many AI systems named after Muppets?
Finally, an answer to the biggest minor mystery around language models. ELMo, BERT, ERNIEs, KERMIT — a surprising number of large language models are named after Muppets. Many thanks to James Vincent for answering this question that has been bugging me for years. ​​(The Verge)

⚡ JUST IN 🇺🇸🇨🇳🇷🇺 Trump, Xi and Putin Set for First-Ever Three-Way Summit, With Nuclear Arms on the Table

The leaders of the world's three biggest nuclear powers are set to sit down together for the first time, the White House has confirmed.

President Donald Trump will meet China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of next week's APEC summit in Shenzhen, China, with the talks expected on Thursday.

White House spokesperson Olivia Wales said Trump will wrap up his China visit with the trilateral meeting, and will push for cutting nuclear weapons, which he considers a very dangerous threat.

A senior US official said no agreement is expected, calling the session an "entry point" and the "first conversation" between the three.

The summit comes nine months after New START, the last nuclear arms treaty between Washington and Moscow, expired in February, leaving both arsenals uncapped for the first time in over 50 years.

Trump rejected Russia's offer to extend that deal for a year and has demanded a "new, improved and modernized" agreement that also includes China.

The US and Russia are each estimated to hold more than 5,000 warheads, while the Pentagon estimates China has over 600.

According to the US official, Trump also plans to raise the Iran war, but the war in Ukraine will not be on the three-way agenda.

The official said no Trump-Putin one-on-one is scheduled, though Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov has said the two leaders plan a separate meeting in Shenzhen.

Elon Musk will travel with Trump to China but will not join the meeting, the official added.

Both NVIDIA's Jensen Huang (founded in 1993) and Yahoo's Jerry Yang (founded in 1994) were Taiwanese-American founders who started their businesses in Silicon Valley in the mid-1990s. The trajectories of their two companies serve as an excellent historical comparison for examining "true entrepreneurial ethics" and "the right to define system architecture."

1. The Vast Difference Between Shareholder Interests and Wealth Creation

Yahoo's Prolonged Decline and Shareholder Losses: At the peak of the dot-com bubble in 2000, Yahoo's market capitalization reached a staggering $125 billion. However, in the following decade, due to a lack of underlying technological architecture (its search algorithm lagged behind Google, and its social and mobile architectures were completely outdated), it declined steadily. In 2008, Microsoft offered $44.6 billion to acquire it, but was rejected. Finally, in 2016-2017, its core internet business was sold to Verizon for a paltry $4.48 billion—more than $120 billion of shareholder wealth vanished.

NVIDIA's remarkable comeback and shareholder returns: In contrast, NVIDIA, after several near-bankruptcies and an 80% stock price plunge, relied on Jensen Huang's relentless focus on the underlying computing architecture (GPU + CUDA) to gradually push its market capitalization to trillions of dollars, creating a wealth miracle unprecedented in human business history for its long-term shareholders, employees, and supply chain.

2. Why is one subject to "national security controls," while the other is ignored even by politicians?

Yahoo, lacking an irreplaceable core technology architecture, has fallen from a global hegemon to a second-tier portal website, no longer posing a "technological advantage threat" to any country. Washington politicians naturally don't even bother to look at it, let alone use "national security issues" to restrict it.

NVIDIA, however, because Jensen Huang pushed its hardware and software architecture to the limits of human physics and engineering, making it so powerful that all competitors and state apparatuses cannot bypass it, has instead become a target of "national security concerns," inexplicably labeled with national security tags and shackled by export controls.

The Builders. An opportunity, or a network?

Take a one-dollar bill. Look at it calmly.
You see the pyramid. You see the eye at the top. At the bottom, in Latin: *Novus Ordo Seclorum*.

I won’t tell you what it means. I’ll let you find out for yourself. It’s written on the very money that everyone touches.

Now, here is a piece of real history—verifiable facts:

Fourteen U.S. presidents have worn the ceremonial robes.
Washington, the first among them—the man who laid the cornerstone of the Capitol building, carrying a silver trowel, dressed in the regalia of the brotherhood.
Roosevelt. Truman. And many others.

In Europe, the same thing occurred.
Napoleon. Voltaire. Churchill. They all passed through the same door. They all took the same oaths.

I am not telling you that it is good. I am not telling you that it is bad.
I am simply telling you: it is the truth.

And consider their symbols:
The compass—representing those who survey the circle.
The square—representing those who stand on equal footing.
The eye—representing the observer.

Why do these three symbols keep reappearing? On buildings, on currency, within circles, in various numbers?

Why does Washington D.C., when viewed from the sky, reveal the shapes of a star, a compass, and a clock within its street layout? I offer no answer. I leave it to you to seek the answer for yourself.

I am not here to pass judgment.

But ask yourself—in silence, and without anger:

Can a man truly become president solely through the vote of the people? Or is there perhaps another door—one more discreet—through which an individual is chosen, trained, and subsequently introduced to the world?

You have no answer for me. And I do not wish for you to provide one. For anything you are merely told, you will eventually forget; but that which you discover for yourself, you shall never forget.

Observe. Look at the symbols. Look at those who embody them. Look at those who reside in secluded places, within closed circles, bound by a vow of silence.

And then, form your own conclusions.

I share only what I have witnessed. Self-determination is the foundation. You choose what to believe, what to question, and what to experience.

Yet, if this message unsettles you, it is because something within you has begun to awaken.

It is the truth.

Vulcan Avirius

🇮🇷|Ghalibaf Put a Brake on the President's Fuel Reform From the Speaker's Chair. That Is the Domestic File Nobody Will Report.

Mohammad Baqer Ghalibaf, Speaker of the Parliament, delivered the pre-agenda speech in the public session. The date as circulated is 15 November. The content is from this campaign. Note the labelling error in the source material: the missile city, the eight-month war, and the seven conditions are all current, not from 2023.

The New Formulation on the War

Ghalibaf's previous statement, to Al Jazeera, said Iran would not remain in a state of "neither war nor peace." The new speech adds two sentences that were not in the earlier version.

"It is of no importance to us whether the United States wants to negotiate or wage war."

"If the Americans make a mistake this time, the geography of the conflict will be determined by the capabilities and will of Iran's armed forces, not by their desires and will. And the smoke of a new war will affect many."

Read the second sentence against Major General Ali Abdollahi's doctrine. Abdollahi said the response is immediate, impactful, and without geographical limitations. Sardar Radan said geography will no longer have meaning, citing the order of Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Hosseini Khamenei. Ghalibaf's formulation is the parliamentary version: the geography of the conflict is set by Iran's capability, not by the enemy's preference. The Speaker is stating the same doctrine from the legislature.

"The smoke of a new war will affect many" is the warning to the host states. Not to Washington. To the capitals that rent their runways.

The seven conditions are now described as "logical" and "the result of the efforts of the Iranian people." The path to agreement is open if the Americans accept them. That is the same position Rezaei put as "surrender" and Araghchi put as "media fabrications" when the reports said talks were advancing.

The Befitting Statement on Bessent

Ghalibaf responded to the US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent directly: "The offensive statements and unethical language of the US Treasury Secretary are indicative of their deep desperation in the face of the power of the Islamic Republic. Someone who has fled their home to military shelters out of fear of threats would be better off reflecting on their strategic failures in the Persian Gulf, rather than insulting great nations."

Read what that attributes to Bessent. Ghalibaf is saying the Treasury Secretary fled his home to a military shelter out of fear of threats. That is a specific claim about the personal safety of a serving American cabinet officer, made from the Speaker's chair and recorded in the parliamentary minutes.

Bessent's public remarks, the ones Ghalibaf called offensive  were the lines about China being "terrible," Europe committing "slow-motion economic suicide," and the Global South not doing well.

The Speaker answered a Treasury Secretary's dismissal of three economies with a claim that the Treasury Secretary is hiding in a bunker.

The Domestic Brake: Ghalibaf Just Constrained the President's Fuel Reform

This is the section that matters and that no one will report.

Ghalibaf: "Recently, some repeated statements regarding the gasoline issue have caused concern among the people. Gasoline and energy imbalances are a technical and national issue that is resolved through collective wisdom, expert work, reaching optimal and definitive decisions, and with the cooperation of the people. Of course, any decision in this area should be made with the public's consent and in a way that puts the least pressure on our dear people. It is necessary for those responsible in this area to understand the sensitivity and importance of this issue more than others, and to seriously avoid constant positions and statements."

Read who this is aimed at. President Masoud Pezeshkian announced the gradual reform of gasoline and diesel subsidies, the voucher system to redirect the funds to households, and the redirection of water and electricity savings to public sector salary increases. Pezeshkian has spoken about the reform repeatedly, in public, as the signature economic measure of his presidency.

The Speaker of the Parliament has now said, in the chamber, that the repeated statements are causing public concern, that the decision requires public consent, that it must put the least pressure on the people, and that the officials responsible should seriously avoid constant positions and statements.

That is a parliamentary brake on the President's reform. The Speaker is telling the executive to stop talking about the subsidy reform in public and to slow the sequencing.

The reason is the memory of November 2019. The fuel price increase of that month produced nationwide protests and a security crackdown. Ghalibaf is invoking the lesson without naming the date: a price reform delivered as an announcement produces a shock; a price reform delivered with the voucher already in the household's hand does not.

The Inflation File and the Committees

Ghalibaf: "Inflation, unemployment, and price fluctuations are not issues that can be resolved through speeches or decrees. Protecting the well-being of the people, who have resisted one of the largest wars in history for over 8 months, is the most basic and obvious duty of all of us officials."

He then stated: "If, at times, an increase in the price of a product is unavoidable due to inflation, the existence of multiple prices for a similar product is in no way related to inflation and is a result of a lack of market oversight."

And he assigned a task: "I request the Industry and Mining, Legal and Judicial, and Economic committees to prepare and present a supervisory report to the public, identifying those responsible for the lack of oversight over prices and the market."

Read that as an institutional instruction. The Speaker is ordering three parliamentary committees to produce a public report naming the officials responsible for price failures. That is a domestic accountability mechanism aimed at the executive's own market regulators, not at the enemy.

The over 8 months figure is the war's duration. Ghalibaf is using the war to raise the stakes on the domestic file: the population that absorbed the war is owed market oversight.

The Ministry of Intelligence Reform

Ghalibaf praised "the anonymous soldiers of Imam Mahdi at the Ministry of Intelligence" and stated: "God willing, the structural reforms being pursued in this area will be carried out with careful consideration, so that we can both increase the dynamism of the Ministry of Intelligence and implement the directives of the Supreme Leader and the Supreme Commander in these sensitive times for the country. We are striving to ensure that this process is completed quickly through cooperation between the two branches of government."

Read the chain. The structural reform of the Ministry of Intelligence is being tied to the directives of the Supreme Leader. The Speaker is stating that the reform is not the Parliament's initiative. It is the Leader's directive, and the Parliament and the executive are the implementing branches.

That connects to the Ministry of Intelligence announcement that five separatist terrorists and three arms smugglers were arrested across Kermanshah, Alborz, and Tehran, operating under the General Directorates of Intelligence in three provinces. The reform and the operations are the same file.

The Dehloran NGL Bus Accident

Ghalibaf offered condolences "to the families of the employees of the NGL Dehloran company who tragically lost their lives in the bus accident, and to the honorable and martyred people of Ilam province."

Dehloran sits in Ilam province, at roughly 32.69°N 47.27°E, near the Iraq border. The NGL Dehloran is a natural gas liquids facility. The employees were on a bus. The accident killed an unspecified number of them.

Read that against the war economy. The NGL facility is part of the gas processing chain that the state has been expanding to reduce flaring and to supply the domestic network. The workers who died were the workforce of that chain, travelling to or from the plant.

The Speaker mentioned it in the same speech as the fuel reform and the war. The three items are the same ledger: the energy sector's workforce, the energy sector's pricing, and the energy sector's role in the war economy.

The Bill

Ghalibaf, Speaker of the Parliament, pre-agenda speech and public session.

The doctrine: "It is of no importance to us whether the United States wants to negotiate or wage war." "The geography of the conflict will be determined by the capabilities and will of Iran's armed forces, not by their desires and will." "The smoke of a new war will affect many."

The seven conditions: described as "logical" and "the result of the efforts of the Iranian people." The path to agreement open if the Americans accept them.

The Bessent attack: the Treasury Secretary "fled his home to military shelters out of fear of threats." A claim about the personal safety of a serving American cabinet officer, in the parliamentary record.

The domestic brake: Pezeshkian's gasoline reform is causing public concern. The decision requires public consent and must put the least pressure on the people. The officials responsible must avoid constant positions and statements. The Speaker is constraining the President's signature economic measure, citing the 2019 lesson without naming the date.

The inflation file: Industry and Mining, Legal and Judicial, and Economic committees ordered to produce a public supervisory report naming those responsible for price failures.

The Intelligence reform: tied to the directives of the Supreme Leader and the Supreme Commander. The Parliament and the executive are the implementing branches. The reform accompanies the arrests of five separatist terrorists and three arms smugglers in Kermanshah, Alborz, and Tehran.

The Dehloran NGL bus accident: employees of the NGL Dehloran facility in Ilam province killed. The workforce of the gas processing chain, lost on the road.

The bill is being paid in a parliamentary speech that constrains the President's fuel reform while stating the war doctrine, insults the Treasury Secretary as a man hiding in a bunker, and orders committees to name the officials who failed the market. The receipt is the Speaker's own words, recorded in the minutes, on the same day the missile city anniversary was marked and the Intelligence Ministry's reform was tied to the Leader's directive.

text:
Marco Rubio's case against Iran rests on one premise: that it is run by "radical Shia clerics" who make "geopolitical decisions on the basis of pure theology." It is a convenient premise: if Iran's leaders are beyond reason, Washington need never explain why it keeps abandoning agreements with them. The record says otherwise.

Iranian foreign policy is governed by a declared triad: dignity, wisdom and prudence. The third subordinates ideology to national interest. Pragmatism defines Iran's conduct: accepting Resolution 598 in 1988 to end a war Iraq had started; cooperating with Washington on Afghanistan at the 2001 Bonn Conference; concluding the 2015 nuclear agreement and honouring it, as the IAEA repeatedly verified; restoring ties with Saudi Arabia in 2023. Leaders driven by apocalyptic theology do not negotiate inspection regimes clause by clause.

Contrary to Rubio's claim, Iran's Constitution does not call for interference abroad. Article 152 rejects "all forms of domination, both the exertion of it and submission to it" and commits Iran to peaceful relations with all non-belligerent states. Article 154 supports the struggles of the oppressed "while scrupulously refraining from all forms of interference in the internal affairs of other nations." Solidarity is expressly subordinated to non-interference.

Iran's actions in the region have all been defensive in nature. The Islamic Republic has never initiated a war; in 1991 the UN Secretary-General named Iraq the aggressor of 1980. Its role against ISIS in Iraq and Syria came at their governments' invitation, a lawful basis. Hezbollah arose in answer to Israel's 1982 invasion and eighteen-year occupation of southern Lebanon. Iran's strikes since February answer armed attacks on its territory, as Article 51 permits.

Iran's opposition to Israel likewise rests on law: it opposes occupation and apartheid. In July 2024 the International Court of Justice declared Israel's presence in the occupied Palestinian territory unlawful, found its measures in breach of Article 3 of CERD, which prohibits racial segregation and apartheid, and placed all states under a duty not to recognise or assist it. Iran's proposed remedy is not war but a UN-registered referendum (S/2019/862) among all of Palestine's original inhabitants: Muslim, Christian and Jewish.

Iran has avoided war wherever diplomacy offered an alternative. It is Washington that has betrayed diplomacy, repeatedly at Israel's behest. Eight days after Netanyahu's "Iran lied" presentation in 2018, the US quit the JCPOA. In June 2025, Israel struck two days before a scheduled round of Oman-mediated talks; Washington joined. On 28 February 2026, US-Israeli strikes came two days before the next round, hours after Oman's foreign minister declared a deal "within reach." The June Islamabad Memorandum was followed within weeks by renewed American strikes.

The radicalism @SecRubio attributes to Tehran is written into Washington's record.

The Mozilla Fellowship places legal and tech experts into global civil society to shape AI policy.

The program funds policy researchers, legal scholars, and engineers building public-interest safeguards for open AI models and data privacy. Fellows receive funding, mentorship, and direct access to international policy networks.

Most traditional fellowships focus either purely on code or purely on legal theory. Mozilla bridges that gap by embedding fellows inside non-profit organizations, policy labs, and advocacy groups working on real regulatory debates.

As a fellow, your daily work involves drafting policy recommendations, auditing model transparency, evaluating copyright standards for training data, and consulting on regional AI governance frameworks.

The fellowship targets mid-career professionals, legal specialists, and technical researchers who want to steer AI governance outside corporate labs.

Key application areas where candidates stand out:

1. Technical auditing: Demonstrating how open-source models handle data privacy, bias, and security vulnerabilities.

2. Policy translation: Explaining complex model architectures to regulators, judges, and civil society leaders without losing technical accuracy.

3. Cross-border governance: Analyzing how international copyright and data protection laws impact AI deployment across jurisdictions.

To build a competitive application, show tangible evidence of public-interest work. Publish case studies analyzing AI risk frameworks, contribute to open policy briefs, or document model evaluation benchmarks.

If you want to move from technical analysis or corporate legal practice into public tech policy, this fellowship offers a direct path to national and global influence.

Would you rather shape AI policy inside a civil society fellowship or directly within a regulatory agency?

🔹 Dell $DELL: +173.70%
🔹 Micron $MU: +172.70%
🔹 Marathon Petroleum $MPC: +154.97%
🔹 AMD $AMD: +149.37%
🔹 Valero $VLO: +133.33%
🔹 Bloom Energy $BE: +120.96%
🔹 Okta $OKTA: +111.48%
🔹 Phillips 66 $PSX: +105.29%
🔹 Hewlett Packard Enterprise $HPE: +101.04%
These are price returns, excluding dividends.
The more interesting story is what has driven them.
1. AI INFRASTRUCTURE — THE BUILDOUT IS CREATING WINNERS BEYOND NVIDIA
$MU, $AMD, $DELL and $HPE are exposed to different parts of the AI investment cycle.
Micron benefits from demand for high-bandwidth memory and other memory products.
AMD is competing for a larger share of accelerated computing.
Dell and HPE provide servers, systems and infrastructure needed to deploy computing capacity.
But these businesses don't have identical economics.
For Micron, I'm watching memory pricing, supply expansion and whether elevated profitability can survive the next industry cycle.
For AMD, the challenge is converting AI accelerator opportunities into sustained revenue growth and attractive margins.
For Dell and HPE, the question is whether higher infrastructure volumes translate into stronger profitability and free cash flow.
AI demand can be enormous without every supplier capturing equally attractive returns.
2. BLOOM ENERGY — POWER IS BECOMING A STRATEGIC BOTTLENECK
$BE is particularly interesting to me.
As AI data centres expand, electricity availability and time to power are becoming increasingly important.
Bloom's fuel-cell technology offers an alternative for customers seeking on-site power generation.
That creates a potentially significant opportunity.
But I wouldn't value Bloom simply by extrapolating AI power demand.
I want to see manufacturing scale, project execution, sustainable margins and cash generation.
A large addressable market is valuable only if the company can capture it profitably.
I'm bullish on Bloom's long-term opportunity, but the valuation must be supported by execution.
3. ENERGY — STRONG RETURNS, DIFFERENT ECONOMICS
$MPC, $VLO and $PSX have delivered exceptional gains.
But refining businesses operate under very different economic conditions from AI infrastructure companies.
Their profitability depends heavily on refining margins, crude oil differentials, utilisation rates, operating costs and industry supply.
Strong earnings during favourable conditions can produce substantial shareholder returns.
The risk is assuming those conditions will persist indefinitely.
For these companies, I'd focus on mid-cycle earnings power, free cash flow and capital returns rather than valuing peak profitability as permanent.
4. MODERNA AND OKTA — COMPANY-SPECIFIC EXECUTION MATTERS
$MRNA leads the list by an extraordinary margin.
But a large share-price recovery doesn't automatically establish a durable earnings trajectory.
For Moderna, the important questions concern its product portfolio, commercial execution, development pipeline and path to sustainable profitability.
$OKTA represents a different opportunity.
Identity security remains strategically important as enterprises expand cloud adoption and AI-enabled workflows.
But the investment case depends on customer demand, competitive positioning, operating leverage and free cash flow.
Both companies demonstrate why historical returns alone tell us very little about future investment attractiveness.
5. SANDISK — MEMORY OPPORTUNITY OR CYCLICAL RISK?
$SNDK has been one of the year's standout performers.
Its exposure to NAND flash and storage demand creates opportunities as data-intensive workloads expand.
But storage remains a cyclical business.
Pricing, capacity additions, inventory levels and customer demand can materially change profitability.
The key question isn't whether Sandisk has benefited from a strong market.
It's how much sustainable earnings power investors should assign to the business when conditions normalise.
MY TAKE — WHICH COMPANIES INTEREST ME MOST THROUGH 2027?
Among these 11 names, I'm particularly interested in $MU, $AMD and $BE.
Not because they've already delivered exceptional returns, but because each participates in a potentially important part of the AI infrastructure investment cycle.
🔹 $MU: Memory demand and pricing, balanced against industry cyclicality.
🔹 $AMD: AI accelerator adoption, competitive execution and margin expansion.
🔹 $BE: Power availability, deployment economics and the ability to convert demand into profitable growth.
I also see opportunities in $DELL and $HPE, although their profitability and capital intensity deserve close attention.
That doesn't mean these are necessarily the cheapest stocks today.
A strong business opportunity and an attractive entry valuation are two different things.
WHAT MATTERS NEXT
For me, the framework is straightforward.
Revenue growth must translate into margins.
Margins must translate into operating cash flow.
Operating cash flow must support reinvestment.
And after capital expenditure, shareholders need to see sustainable free cash flow and attractive returns on invested capital.
That is how I'd separate a durable compounder from a stock benefiting temporarily from favourable market conditions.
MY FINAL TAKE
Eleven S&P 500 stocks have more than doubled in less than a year.
That's extraordinary.
But I wouldn't chase any of them simply because they've already performed well.
Some may continue compounding through 2027 and beyond.
Others may struggle if earnings expectations become too optimistic, industry conditions normalise or valuations leave little room for disappointment.
The biggest winners of 2026 won't necessarily be the best investments of 2027.
The companies that interest me most are those capable of turning today's growth opportunity into tomorrow's sustainable free cash flow.
That's where I'll be focusing my research.
— EMMANUELINVEST

text:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

Before we get started I wanted to flag two great talks this week. 

On Tuesday, September 12, at 12 p.m. US Eastern time, we will be hosting a subscriber-only roundtable conversation about how to regulate artificial intelligence. I’ll help you decipher what is going on in AI regulation and what to pay attention to this fall. (You can subscribe to get access here.)

On Thursday, September 14, at 12 p.m. US Eastern time, I am interviewing Gareth Edwards, the director behind Rogue One: A Star Wars Story, about his new film, The Creator. The film is about the current state of AI and the pitfalls and possibilities ahead as this technology marches toward sentience. Join us on LinkedIn Live!

Okay, on with the newsletter!

Lawmakers are back from summer vacation and ready for action. The new school year has started with a flurry of action in AI in what is turning out to be one of the most consequential seasons for the technology. 

A lot has changed since I first started covering AI policy four years ago. I used to have to convince people that the subject was worth their time. Not any more. It has gone  from being a super nerdy, niche topic to front-page news. Notably, politicians in countries such as the US, which have traditionally been reluctant to regulate tech, have now come out swinging with lots of different proposals. 

On Wednesday, tech leaders and researchers are meeting at Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer’s first AI Insight Forum. The forum will help Schumer shape his approach to AI regulation. My colleague Tate Ryan-Mosley breaks down what to expect here. 

Senators Richard Blumenthal and Josh Hawley have also said they will introduce a bipartisan bill for artificial intelligence, which will include rules for licensing and auditing AI, liability rules around privacy and civil rights, as well as standards for data transparency and safety. They would also create an AI office to oversee the tech’s regulation. 

Meanwhile, the EU is in the final stages of negotiations for the AI Act, and some of the toughest questions about the bill, such as whether to ban facial recognition, how to regulate generative AI, and how enforcement should work, will be hashed out between now and Christmas. Even the leaders of the G7 decided to chime in and agreed to create a voluntary code of conduct for AI.

Thanks to the excitement around generative AI, the technology has become a kitchen table topic, and everyone is now aware something needs to be done, says Alex Engler, a fellow at the Brookings Institution. But the devil will be in the details. 

To really tackle the harm AI has already caused in the US, Engler says, the federal agencies controlling health, education, and others need the power and funding to investigate and sue tech companies. He proposes a new regulatory instrument called Critical Algorithmic Systems Classification (CASC), which would grant federal agencies the right to investigate and audit AI companies and enforce existing laws. This is not a totally new idea. It was outlined by the White House last year in its AI Bill of Rights. 

Say you realize you have been discriminated against by an algorithm used in college admissions, hiring, or property valuation. You could bring your case to the relevant federal agency, and the agency would be able to use its investigative powers to demand that tech companies hand over data and code about how these models work and review what they are doing. If the regulator found that the system was causing harm, it could sue. 

In the years I’ve been writing about AI, one critical thing hasn’t changed: Big Tech’s attempts to water down rules that would limit its power. 

“There’s a little bit of a misdirection trick happening,” Engler says. Many of the problems around artificial intelligence—surveillance, privacy, discriminatory algorithms—are affecting us right now, but the conversation has been captured by tech companies pushing a narrative that large AI models pose massive risks in the distant future, Engler adds. 

“In fact, all of these risks are far better demonstrated at a far greater scale on online platforms,” Engler says. And these platforms are the ones benefiting from reframing the risks as a futuristic problem.

Lawmakers on both sides of the Atlantic have a short window to make some extremely consequential decisions about the technology that will determine how it is regulated for years to come. Let’s hope they don’t waste it. 

Deeper Learning

You need to talk to your kid about AI. Here are 6 things you should say.

In the past year, kids, teachers, and parents have had a crash course in artificial intelligence, thanks to the wildly popular AI chatbot ChatGPT. But it’s not just chatbots that kids are encountering in schools and in their daily lives. AI is increasingly everywhere—recommending shows to us on Netflix, helping Alexa answer our questions, powering your favorite interactive Snapchat filters and the way you unlock your smartphone. 

AI 101: While some students will invariably be more interested in AI than others, understanding the fundamentals of how these systems work is becoming a basic form of literacy—something everyone who finishes high school should know. At the start of the new school year, here are MIT Technology Review’s six essential tips for how to get started on giving your kid an AI education. Read more from Rhiannon Williams and me here.

Bits and Bytes

Chinese AI chatbots want to be your emotional support
What is Chinese company Baidu’s new Ernie Bot like, and how does it compare to its Western alternatives? Our China tech reporter Zeyi Yang experimented with it and found that it did a lot more hand-holding. Read more in his weekly newsletter, China Report. (MIT Technology Review)

Inside Meta’s AI drama: Internal feuds over compute power
Meta is losing top talent left, right, and center over internal feuds about which AI projects are given computing resources. Of the 14 researchers who authored Meta’s LLaMA research paper, more than half have left the company. (The Information) 

Google will require election ads to disclose AI content
Google will require advertisers to “prominently disclose” when a campaign ad “inauthentically depicts” people or events. As the US presidential election looms closer, one of the most tangible fears around generative AI is the ease with which people can use the technology to make deepfake images meant to mislead people. The changes will come into effect from mid-November. (The Financial Times) 

Microsoft says it will pay for its clients’ AI copyright legal fees
Generative AI has been accused of stealing authors’ and artists’ intellectual property. Microsoft, which offers a suite of generative AI tools, has said it will pay up if any of its clients are sued for copyright violations. (Microsoft) 

A buzzy AI startup for generating 3D models used cheap human labor
The Mechanical Turk, but make it 3D. Kaedim, a startup that says it uses machine learning to convert 2D illustrations into 3D models, actually uses human artists for “quality control,” and sometimes to create the models from scratch. (404 media)

THE BRAIN DRAIN TIME BOMB: Will Nvidia’s Millionaire Engineers Walk Out After Jensen Huang?
Wall Street is focused on Nvidia’s C-suite, but a bigger threat is brewing inside its labs: a mass exodus of Nvidia’s top chip architects and CUDA engineers.
With $NVDA surging 988% over four years, roughly 78% of Nvidia employees are already multi-millionaires from vested stock grants. These senior engineers reached financial freedom years ago. They did not keep working brutal 80-hour weeks for a paycheck—they stayed out of deep personal loyalty to Jensen Huang.
1. The "Faith in Jensen" Glue Just Snapped
Fierce Internal Loyalty: Jensen held a 98% Glassdoor approval rating, and 88% of surveyed Nvidia staff wanted him to stay as CEO.
An Open Engineering Revolt: Over 6,500 current Nvidia employees, 1,200 former staffers, and 71,000 shareholders—part of 131,000+ signatories backed by Elon Musk, Tim Sweeney, and Garry Tan—signed the "Stand with Jensen" open letter demanding the board bring him back.
Mission Over Money: As the employees’ open letter stated verbatim: “Many of us joined because of him. Many of us stayed because of how he treated the work: as something worth getting right, together, at whatever hour it took.” Inside headquarters, a suggestion-box post calling to "bring back THE boss" drew over 1,600 comments.
2. Why "Golden Handcuffs" Won’t Stop the Exodus
Zero Financial Leverage: When a senior chip architect already sits on $15M to $50M in net worth, extra stock grants from an interim CFO will not keep them grinding through corporate bureaucracy.
The End of Jensen’s Flat Culture: Jensen ran Nvidia with roughly 60 direct reports and zero middle-management politics. Shifting to Interim CEO and CFO Colette Kress and a traditional corporate hierarchy gives wealthy engineers every reason to cash out, retire early, or walk away in protest.
3. Where Nvidia’s Elite Talent Will Go Next
Big Tech & Custom ASIC Rivals: Google, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft—scaling TPU 8, Trainium3, MTIA 500, and Maia 200—alongside custom chip leaders Broadcom and Marvell, will offer blank checks to poach Nvidia’s core architects.
Next-Gen AI Startups: Inference challengers like Groq, Cerebras, Etched, and Tenstorrent are hunting for NVLink and CUDA veterans, while millionaire Nvidia alumni now have the capital to launch their own rival startups.

RT @velitesgear | Full Text Article: https://t.co/vKGi5cTRkT | Author: @militarnyi Fewer People in Bashkortostan Are Willing to Join Russia’s Army for the War Against Ukraine 
Authorities in Russia’s Bashkortostan region have acknowledged that fewer people are willing to sign military contracts with Russia’s Ministry of Defense to fight in the war against Ukraine.

This is stated in an explanatory note to the region’s draft budget for 2027–2028, according to The Moscow Times.

The document notes that funding for one-time payments to new military recruits is being reduced because fewer people are signing contracts to join the Russian army.

As a result, the Bashkortostan authorities have reduced planned spending on these payments from RUB 13.6 billion to 12.6 billion. However, the region has kept the one-time payment for signing a military contract at RUB 1 million.

Bashkortostan has become the first Russian region whose authorities have officially acknowledged a decline in the number of people willing to join the military under contract.

 Russian forces carry a wounded soldier on a stretcher. Photo credits: Maximilian Clarke/SOPA Images/LightRocket

Meanwhile, the republic tops the list of Russian regions by the number of confirmed deaths in the war against Ukraine. As of November 2026, the identities of 11,990 residents of Bashkortostan who were killed in the war had been confirmed.

The region is also facing financial difficulties. In May 2026, local authorities reduced the one-time payment to families of soldiers killed in the war from RUB 2 million to 100,000. Since the start of Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, these payments have been cut twentyfold.

Militarnyi previously reported problems with recruiting contract soldiers into the Russian army. In 2025, the number of people willing to sign military contracts in Moscow fell by approximately 25% compared to the previous year.

In total, 24,469 people were sent to the war through Moscow’s recruitment centers during that period. In December 2025, only 879 people signed contracts – the lowest monthly figure since the Moscow recruitment center began operating.

 Russian reservists called up during the “partial mobilization” arrive at an assembly point in Bataysk, Rostov Region. September 2022. Photo credits: Reuters

In September 2026, Militarnyi also reported problems with military recruitment. An analysis of 61 court rulings found that at least 51 Russian regions had introduced administrative penalties for officials who failed to meet recruitment targets for contract soldiers.

Meanwhile, according to calculations by Janis Kluge, a research fellow at the Institute for International Security Studies,234,000 people signed contracts with Russia’s Ministry of Defense between January and August 2026 – 10% fewer than during the same period the previous year.

In August, recruitment rates fell by 20%, despite a record increase in regional payments offered to those signing military contracts.

text:
Jon Snow’s charge at the Battle of the Bastards is better understood as an instinctual act of heroism rather than tactical foolishness. Witnessing his brother’s execution triggered an immediate moral reflex, illustrating a classic archetype: the reluctant leader who does not covet authority, yet rises to meet the moment when duty demands it.

Crucially, however, that instinct did not emerge in a vacuum. While Jon possesses a natural, innate nobility, even the finest steel requires a proper forge. Ned Stark was vital because he provided the rigid moral code that shaped Jon’s character early on. A man can certainly rebel against his upbringing, yet Jon took to that standard naturally because the base metal was already there. Because he was raised around genuine examples of honor and duty, certain compromises simply never entered his mind as options. 

That foundation is precisely what makes him a superior commander: he genuinely cares for his troops and refuses to ask any man to endure a peril he would not face himself. Equally important, his strength is tempered by a deep kindness, an understanding that while any brute can take a life, only a true king possesses the grace to grant mercy.
Leadership in crisis also relies heavily on symbolic example. 

History offers striking parallels, most notably Lord Lovat landing at Normandy in a cardigan sweater with a hunting rifle and his personal bagpiper, or British officers in the First World War crossing no man’s land armed with little more than a walking stick or an umbrella. To a detached observer, such gestures appear theatrical, if not entirely absurd. Yet within the irrational psychology of total warfare, where mortality is already an accepted reality, projecting serene resolve transforms fatalism into morale. When soldiers witness a commander sharing their peril, that quiet audacity compels them forward.

At the same time, the most important thing is knowing when to step into the fray. At Omaha Beach, when the initial assault waves were slaughtered and survivors lay pinned and paralyzed beneath the seawall in the Dog White sector, 51 year old Brigadier General Norman "Dutch" Cota walked calmly upright through heavy German machine gun and mortar fire, chomping on an unlit cigar and refusing to crouch. 

Finding soldiers huddled against the shingle, he asked what outfit they belonged to. When they answered the 5th Rangers, he issued the famous challenge that became their motto: "Well, God damn it then, Rangers, lead the way!" Even after Bangalore torpedoes blew a gap in the concertina wire, the first soldier to sprint through was cut down instantly, freezing the men behind him in terror. Recognizing that no subordinate could break the psychological deadlock, Cota leaped forward himself, dashing through the gap across open ground under fire to show them it could be done, single handedly sparking the breakout up the bluffs.

That is the exact balance Jon had to master: recognizing when his position was too vital not to delegate, and when his presence in the vanguard was the only thing capable of breaking a stalemate. Yet even in its tactical imperfection, that charge transformed both Jon and Sansa. 

After years of enduring cynical manipulators, Sansa watched Jon draw his sword alone against an army and saw the unmistakable image of her father. Knowing full well that the same uncompromising honor had cost Ned Stark his head, she nonetheless felt a profound pride in recognizing her father’s spirit alive in her brother(cousin) Both realized that the road ahead would be unforgiving and that neither could rule alone. Sansa found her true place as an indispensable strategic partner, while Jon recognized that he needed her sharp political mind to survive.

More importantly, learning to delegate and look beyond his own sword allowed Jon to think on a truly grand strategic scale. While rulers like Cersei Lannister remained consumed by petty dynastic squabbles and short-sighted court intrigue, Jon possessed the clarity to identify the existential war against the White Walkers. Knowing he had Sansa’s counsel to anchor the North, Jon was able to set aside pride and seek out Daenerys Targaryen, recognizing that her armies and dragons were essential to defeating the real enemy. 

Soldiers instinctively know what a true combat leader looks like and what will inspire them to overcome fear. By stepping into the breach when necessary and uniting allies for the greater war, a commander provides that exact formula. When a man demonstrates that level of fearless resolve and strategic vision, his troops will follow him anywhere, convinced he is practically a god.

Ultimately, anyone can seize power through force or cunning, yet taking a throne does not make a man worthy of holding it. When a leader proves himself truly worthy of command, he faces no struggle to claim authority; people cannot wait to place it in his hand.
