text:
Draceana had gone rigid, her fingers tightening around her sleeve. She knew that voice all too well. It was the same one that had haunted the halls of Malfoy Manor, the one she had learned to dread whenever it called her name. Hearing it again, even here, brought back memories she would rather have left behind.
"I ask... for only one thing."
The pause that followed seemed to stretch endlessly.
"Bring me Harry Potter. Do so... and no harm shall come to you. Hogwarts shall remain untouched."
A few students exchanged uneasy glances. Others turned towards Harry, though nobody dared speak.
"And naturally... those who assist me shall be rewarded. Generously."
Harry clenched his jaw. He knew better than to believe a word of it. Voldemort had never been one to honour his promises, least of all when he no longer had any use for those who had served him.
"You have... until midnight."
The voice softened, though somehow that only made the warning more dreadful.
"When midnight comes... I shall consider everyone who remains within those walls my enemy."
One final pause followed.
"Choose wisely."
And just as suddenly as it had come, the voice faded away, leaving the Great Hall in stunned silence.
Harry stared towards the great doors, his mind returning to the army he had seen gathered outside. Now he understood why Voldemort hadn't attacked. With hundreds of Death Eaters at his command, he had no reason to believe Hogwarts could withstand him. He was offering them a chance to surrender, confident that they would eventually hand Harry over rather than face his army.
To Voldemort, the battle was already won before it even began.
Panic erupted throughout the Great Hall. Students began shouting over one another, some turning towards the doors while others looked desperately to their professors for reassurance. Voldemort's voice had vanished, but his ultimatum had thrown the entire hall into chaos.
"So much for an orderly announcement," Professor Flitwick remarked dryly.
McGonagall shot him a look before turning back to the students.
"Silence! Quiet, please!" she called, raising her voice above the commotion. But with Voldemort's threat still fresh in their minds, the students were hardly inclined to listen.
"Harry Potter! He's right there!" someone suddenly shouted from among the Slytherins.
It was Pansy Parkinson.
"Someone grab him! If we hand him over, we'll all be spared!"
Her words drew the attention of the other Slytherins, many of whom turned towards Harry. Some exchanged uncertain glances, while others appeared to be seriously considering her suggestion. Harry stiffened beneath their stares, but before he could respond, another voice rang out.
"Never!"
Someone had spoken up in Harry's defence. Under ordinary circumstances, that would hardly have been surprising. But this voice belonged to the very girl who had spent years openly despising him. Draceana Malfoy had stepped directly in front of Harry, placing herself between him and the Slytherin students. The sight was so unexpected that even the commotion seemed to die away.
"Dracy...?" Pansy stared at her, scarcely believing what she had heard.
For the first time since Draceana's return, their eyes finally met. Pansy had spent months imagining what she would say when they saw each other again. She had pictured asking where Dracy had been, hearing all about what she'd missed, perhaps even sharing a little gossip, just as they used to. Instead, the first words her friend had directed at her were a fierce rejection, spoken in defence of Harry Potter.
Who is this person? Is she really Dracy?
Pansy's lips parted, but nothing came out. Draceana was still standing in front of Potter, looking straight at her, as though Pansy were the one who had done something wrong. The friend she remembered would have been the first to agree with her, not the one shielding their old enemy. It stung more than Pansy cared to admit. Of all the people Dracy could have chosen to stand beside, she had chosen Potter, and against Pansy herself. The betrayal cut deep enough to leave her utterly speechless. She pressed her lips together and turned away, unable to bear meeting her friend's eyes any longer.
Draceana's resolve faltered when she saw Pansy retreated. She hadn't imagined their first exchange in months would happen like this. She had wanted to speak to her friend, to explain herself somehow, yet the first thing she'd done was shout at her for threatening Harry. She didn't regret defending him, not for any moment, but the look on Pansy's face was harder to bear than she'd expected. Draceana lowered her eyes, wondering whether she would ever find the courage to face her friend again once all this was over.
Professor McGonagall seized the opportunity presented by the sudden silence.
"As you have all heard, Hogwarts is currently under siege," she announced. "The Dark Lord intends to march upon this castle at midnight. And let me make one thing perfectly clear: we have decided that Mr Potter will not be handed over under any circumstances, Miss Parkinson."
She fixed Pansy with a stern look before addressing the rest of the hall.
"Now, I understand that many of you are frightened. But I want to assure you that no student will be forced to fight. Those of you who are underage will be evacuated through the passage leading to the Hog's Head. From there, you will be escorted to safety and may Apparate away once you are clear of Hogwarts."
McGonagall allowed the instructions to settle before continuing. "You will follow Professor Slughorn and Mr Filch. Please proceed in an orderly fashion." She turned towards her colleague. "Horace, if you please."
"Of course, Minerva." Slughorn stepped forward, gesturing towards the younger students. "All right, everyone, this way, please. First-years first. No pushing, now. Let's keep things orderly."
As Slughorn began directing the younger students towards the exit, McGonagall turned her attention to those who remained.
"And as for those of you who are of age..." She paused, her gaze moving over the older students standing before her.
They were legally adults, certainly, but many were still children in her eyes. Some had barely turned seventeen. Only a few hours earlier, her greatest responsibility had been keeping them safe within the castle walls. Now she was about to offer them a place in the battle that might destroy it.
McGonagall drew a measured breath before continuing. "You are permitted to remain and fight alongside us, should you choose to do so."
Her expression remained solemn as she looked from one row of students to another.
"But understand this: you are under no obligation to stay. There will be no shame, and certainly no punishment, for choosing to evacuate. I would rather see every one of you leave this castle safely than have you remain out of some misplaced sense of duty. This is not the time to play hero."
Her voice softened slightly.
"So I ask you to consider your decision carefully. Those who wish to volunteer may remain. Everyone else is free to join the evacuation."
Much to McGonagall's surprise, most of the Gryffindors chose to stay. The Hufflepuffs followed in similar numbers, while roughly half of the Ravenclaws remained as the others joined the evacuation. Despite the danger awaiting them, far more students had volunteered than she had expected.
Then came the Slytherins.
Draceana watched her former House with considerably lower expectations. She knew her housemates well enough, having once shared many of their beliefs herself. She wouldn't have been surprised if every last one of them chose to leave.
But to her astonishment, three students remained.
"Blood traitors," someone muttered from among the departing Slytherins.
Draceana recognised one of the three immediately. Tracey Davis stood beside two other Slytherins, refusing to follow the rest of their House towards the exit. For a moment, Draceana could scarcely believe it. Then Tracey looked up, and their eyes met.
Draceana gave her a small nod, which Tracey returned.
A quiet sense of pride stirred in her chest, though it was unlike anything she had felt before. She had spent years taking pride in her family name, her blood, and her House. Yet somehow, seeing those three choose to stay meant more to her than any of those things.
Blood traitors? Draceana knew better. Whatever anyone chose to call them, they were nothing of the sort.
"Good," McGonagall said once the departing students had been directed towards the evacuation. She produced a parchment and quill, placing them at the front. "Those of you who have chosen to remain, please write your name and House on this parchment."
She offered no explanation, though the students were old enough to understand what such a list might be needed for.
One by one, the volunteers stepped forward. Some approached without hesitation, while others lingered before putting quill to parchment. Each wrote their name carefully, followed by their House.
McGonagall watched in silence. She had given them a choice, and they had made it freely. Yet as the list grew, she found herself wondering how many of those names would belong to students who might never leave Hogwarts alive. With each addition came a silent apology she could not bring herself to voice.
Harry stood to one side, watching his friends and fellow students sign their names. He had asked for their help, knowing what Voldemort was capable of, but seeing them willingly put themselves in danger made the coming battle feel all the more real. These were people he had shared classrooms and meals with, people who had families waiting for them beyond Hogwarts.
And now some of them might die fighting alongside him.
Another student stepped forward and added a name to the parchment. Harry watched the quill move, silently wishing for something he knew he couldn't guarantee.
Please... everyone, don't die.
******
Eventually, Harry and Draceana made their way out of the Great Hall together. The corridors beyond were just as chaotic, with younger students hurrying towards the evacuation route while professors and members of the Order rushed about preparing the castle's defences. Hogwarts had become a hive of activity, caught between those trying to escape and those preparing to fight.
"Are you sure?" Harry asked as they walked.
"About what?" Draceana replied.
"Pansy. And the others. The Slytherins. Isn't there something you want to say to them?"
Draceana fell quiet for a moment. "And tell them what, Potter? What am I supposed to say? I wouldn't even know where to begin." She glanced towards a group of students passing them before looking away. "So I'd rather not say anything."
"Won't they get the wrong idea? You still care about them, don't you?"
"They already have the wrong idea. Especially after what I did earlier." Her voice tightened slightly. "But I don't regret it. And... I suppose I'd rather have them somewhere safe, away from all this."
Harry glanced at her. Draceana was trying to sound indifferent, but her eyes were beginning to glisten. He knew how much she had worried about facing her friends again, and now her first encounter with Pansy had ended with her openly defending him. It must have been weighing on her, and Harry knew better than to expect her to sort things out in the middle of preparations for a battle.
Rather than press her further, he moved a little closer, letting her rest her head against his shoulder as they continued walking.
"I'll help you talk to them once all this is over," Harry said. "I promise."
"I don't need your help, idiot Potter," Draceana muttered, though she made no attempt to move away.
"We leave you two alone for a few hours, and look at you. Flirting again. Unbelievable."
Harry recognised the familiar voice immediately. He turned, a smile spreading across his face. "Ron!"
Ron and Hermione were approaching from the opposite direction, walking hand in hand.
"Mate, are you really in a position to say that? Look at you," Harry added, glancing pointedly at their joined hands.
"Touché." Ron looked down and broke into a laugh, though he made no attempt to let go of Hermione's hand.
"We managed to collect a few more fangs, just in case," Hermione said, opening her enchanted bag to show them what they'd brought back from the Chamber of Secrets.
Harry eyed the fangs with a mixture of relief and lingering discomfort. "Brilliant. At least we've got something to destroy those bloody Horcruxes with. Though I still can't believe you stabbed me."
"What?" Hermione asked, looking utterly confused.
"Nothing. Never mind." Harry waved the remark aside. Of course, neither of them knew about the peculiar vision he'd experienced in the Great Hall, and he wasn't particularly keen to explain how he'd somehow found himself on the receiving end of Hermione's basilisk fang.
"So, mate, how are things going here?" Ron asked.
"As you can see, complete chaos." Harry gestured towards the busy corridor around them.
"Yeah, I noticed that already, mate. Including that awful announcement. What I meant was the diadem."
"Oh, right! Draceana!" Harry turned towards her, suddenly remembering that he hadn't asked about her search. "Did you find anything?"
Draceana gave a helpless shrug. "No luck, Potter. That replica had nothing but some worthless motivational words and a terrible carving. I couldn't even tell you what the real diadem looks like from it." She pressed her lips together. She wished she had something more useful to offer, but that was genuinely all she'd managed to discover.
"Back to square one, then," Hermione said with a sigh. She turned towards Harry. "Are you absolutely certain it's here?"
"It has to be. I saw it directly through Voldemort's mind," Harry replied. He was about to say more when he spotted a small figure hurrying past them. "Professor Flitwick!" he called.
The Charms professor stopped and turned towards him. "Yes, Mr Potter?"
"Professor Flitwick is the Head of Ravenclaw," Hermione remarked. "He ought to know something about the diadem. Brilliant, Harry."
"Thank you, Miss Obvious," Draceana muttered.
Hermione shot her a glare, which Draceana returned without hesitation. Harry ignored them both and turned his attention to Flitwick.
"Professor, it's about the lost diadem of Rowena Ravenclaw. Do you know anything about it? Anything at all?"
"Oh, yes. I heard you were looking for it back in the headmaster's office." Flitwick looked genuinely apologetic. "I'm afraid I can't help you, Harry. No living person has seen the diadem for centuries. That's precisely why the replica in Ravenclaw Tower looks so unfinished. Nobody knows exactly what the original looked like. I wish I could tell you more, especially knowing how important your mission is, but I'm afraid that's all I have."
The four exchanged disappointed looks.
"All right. Thank you, Professor," Harry said.
Flitwick gave an apologetic nod before hurrying off to resume his preparations.
"Well, now what, mate?" Ron asked once he'd gone.
Hermione folded her arms thoughtfully. "Could Voldemort have been misleading us? Perhaps he realised someone might recognise his habit of using the founders' belongings and decided to use something else instead. It could be any object hidden somewhere in the castle."
Harry considered her suggestion. He hated to admit it, but she had a point. He had been so certain the Horcrux was Ravenclaw's diadem that he'd barely considered anything else. What if
Voldemort had deliberately left a false trail? What if they'd been searching for the wrong thing all along?
"But if that's true, we'd have to turn the entire castle upside down," Draceana pointed out, glancing towards the stream of people hurrying past them. "Every object in Hogwarts could be a possibility. Perhaps even the castle itself. How are we supposed to search all that before midnight?"
"We know, Miss Obvious," Hermione replied sharply.
Draceana turned towards her with an offended look, but for once, she had no immediate retort.
None of them had an answer. With no reliable description of the diadem, and now the possibility that they were looking for the wrong object altogether, their search had become little more than guesswork. Midnight was still hours away, and Harry could only hope, by Merlin, that Voldemort would keep his word and wait until then. Even so, he didn't want to waste a single minute. They needed to keep searching, but without a proper lead, wandering blindly through Hogwarts would only—
"No! I'm staying! I want to help!"
A familiar shout rose above the commotion farther down the corridor, interrupting Harry's thoughts.
"No, Ginny! You're underage. Please, listen to your mother for once!"
Harry and the others turned towards the voices. A short distance away, Ginny was arguing with Molly Weasley, while Arthur and the rest of the Weasleys stood nearby. Ginny clearly had no intention of joining the evacuation, and Molly seemed equally determined to make her leave.
Ron sighed as he recognised the familiar argument. "All right, mate. Let me handle this."
Yet despite his reluctant tone, a smile was already spreading across his face as he looked towards his family. He gave Harry a reassuring nod before heading over with Hermione, their hands still joined.
Harry watched them go with a smile of his own. He suspected Ron was rather glad to have an excuse to spend some time with his family. After all, Harry knew how much his friend had worried about them during their months on the run, and now he finally had a chance to see them properly. Perhaps a short breather would do them all some good. They had been so caught up in the search that they could scarcely think straight, and a little time away from it might help them notice something they'd overlooked.
Meanwhile, the corridor remained busy with professors and members of the Order hurrying between their assigned positions. Among them, Harry spotted Remus Lupin speaking with Kingsley. Remus caught sight of him, exchanged a few final words with Kingsley, and came over.
"Remus!" Harry greeted him with a smile. He had barely had a chance to speak to his father's old friend since their reunion in the headmaster's office, and with Ron and Hermione occupied for the moment, he welcomed the opportunity to take his mind off the search, if only briefly.
"Harry, there you are! I've been looking for you. Could we have a word?" Remus asked, glancing between him and Draceana.
"Of course. Sorry, everything's been so hectic. What is it?"
Remus's gaze wandered to their joined hands, and a faint, amused smile appeared on his face. "So... girlfriend, is it?"
"I'm not his girlfriend," Draceana protested immediately.
Remus chuckled before turning to Harry. "Really?"
"Well, it's complicated," Harry admitted with an awkward smile. He made no attempt to release Draceana's hand, however, a detail that certainly hadn't escaped Remus's notice.
Rather than press the matter, Remus simply gave them an approving nod. He hadn't seen Harry looking quite so comfortable with someone in a long time, and considering everything happening around them, it was a welcome sight.
Harry noticed something. "Where's Tonks, Remus? I haven't seen her anywhere. Didn't she come with you?"
"She's staying with her mother," Remus replied, his face brightening. "She gave birth recently, you see. To our son, Teddy."
Harry blinked. "You have a son?"
Remus nodded, unable to suppress a proud smile.
"That's wonderful! Congratulations!" Harry exclaimed. But his delight faltered as he glanced at the preparations taking place around them. "Wait, then what are you doing here, Remus? You should be with Tonks and your son. This isn't the time to—"
"I know, Harry," Remus interrupted gently, raising a hand. "Believe me, I know. But I made a promise to your father and Sirius. I promised them to protect you." His smile softened. "And don't worry. Tonks has already given me her blessing, on the strict condition that I return home alive." He gave a small chuckle. "I intend to keep that promise, just as I intend to honour the one I made to James and Sirius."
"But, Remus..." Harry hesitated. Remus had a wife and a newborn son waiting for him. The thought of Teddy growing up without his father, as Harry himself had, was more than he wanted to contemplate.
Remus seemed to understand. He rested a hand on Harry's shoulder, his expression growing more earnest.
"Actually, Harry, that's partly why I wanted to speak with you." He paused before continuing. "I'd like you to be Teddy's godfather."
Harry stared at him.
"His godfather? Me?" he asked, almost certain he must have misheard. "Are you sure?"
"Quite sure." Remus smiled. "I wouldn't want anyone else for my firstborn."
For a moment, Harry couldn't find the words to answer. He thought of Sirius, who had been his own godfather, and how much that bond had meant to him despite the little time they'd been given together. Now Remus was asking him to become that person for his son. Harry swallowed, struggling to find an answer worthy of the trust being placed in him.
He turned towards Draceana, who had been listening quietly beside him. She met his gaze, and a faint smile touched her lips. "Scared, Potter?" she murmured.
Harry almost laughed. Leave it to Draceana to tease him at a moment like this. Yet the small nod she gave him afterwards was all the encouragement he needed.
He looked back at Remus. "Then... I'd be honoured," Harry answered, a smile forming on his face. "But only if you promise me you'll survive this, too."
Remus's expression softened. Without another word, he stepped forward and pulled Harry into a warm embrace.
"Thank you, Harry," he murmured. "And don't worry. I'll do everything I can to make it home."
Harry returned the embrace, holding on for a moment longer before they finally parted.
"You be careful too," Remus added, giving Harry's shoulder an affectionate squeeze. Then he turned towards Draceana. "And you as well, Miss Malfoy."
"Don't worry. I'm more than capable of making sure Scarhead and I don't get hurt, Professor Lupin," she replied, lifting her chin.
Remus laughed. "I'm no longer your professor, Miss Malfoy. Please, just call me Remus." He glanced at Harry before returning his attention to her. "Then... I shall entrust Harry to you."
Draceana regarded him for a moment. There was something rather unexpected about hearing those words from a man who had once been her teacher, particularly after everything that had happened between her and Harry. Nevertheless, she gave a small nod. "Very well... Remus."
Before he could reply, a familiar voice called from farther down the corridor.
"Remus!"
Kingsley was standing with several members of the Order, beckoning Lupin towards him.
"Sorry to interrupt, but we could use you over here. We're sorting out the final defensive positions."
"Of course, Kingsley!" Remus called back. He turned towards Harry and Draceana with an apologetic smile. "Well, duty calls, I'm afraid." He gave Harry's shoulder one last reassuring squeeze. "Remember, Harry. I intend to keep my promises."
"You'd better," Harry replied, managing a small smile.
With a final nod, Remus joined Kingsley and the others, leaving Harry and Draceana alone once more.
No sooner had Remus departed than another familiar face approached them.
"Harry."
It was Ginny. She appeared to have finished arguing with her mother, though judging by the determined look on her face, Harry doubted she'd given in without a fight.
Draceana's expression immediately soured at the sight of her. "What do you want, Weasley?"
"I'm not here for you, Malfoy," Ginny retorted, barely sparing her a glance. "I'm here for Harry."
"Yeah, what is it, Ginny?" Harry asked. He glanced towards the Weasleys, where Ron and Hermione were still talking with the rest of the family. Perhaps Ginny had taken the opportunity to slip away while they were occupied. "Shouldn't you be evacuating?"
"Mum wanted me to, but I managed to reach an agreement with her and Dad." Ginny folded her arms. "I can stay in the Room of Requirement. That way, I'll still be nearby without taking part in the fighting."
"I see." Harry was relieved she'd agreed to remain somewhere safe, though the way she lingered suggested there was something else on her mind.
"All right, you've given us your update," Draceana said, apparently having reached the same conclusion. "So what did you really come here for, Weasley?"
Leave it to Draceana to ask precisely what Harry had been thinking, without the slightest attempt at tact.
"Harry..." Ginny began again, ignoring Draceana. Her voice was quieter this time. "Can you answer me properly? This time, I mean."
Draceana glanced between them. Answer her? About what? Was there something between Harry and Ginny that she knew nothing about?
Harry, however, understood. He remembered Ginny's confession at the Burrow and the answer he'd left unresolved. At the time, he hadn't known what to say. But now, standing beside Draceana, he knew exactly what he wanted to

text:
"By Merlin," Remus said, his brow furrowing as he considered the implications. "Is that how the Dark Lord managed to come back? All those years ago, when everyone believed he was dead?"
"Yes," Harry replied. "When his Killing Curse rebounded, his body was destroyed, but his Horcruxes kept him alive. That's why he was able to return. Nobody had found them, let alone destroyed them."
Remus fell silent. He remembered the night James and Lily had died, and the years that followed, when everyone believed Voldemort was gone for good. Only now did he understand why the destruction of his body had not been enough.
Harry glanced around the room before continuing. "But we've managed to destroy four of them. Professor Dumbledore destroyed one, and we've found the others since then. That leaves two."
"Two, Harry?" McGonagall repeated.
"One of them is Nagini. Voldemort's snake."
"The snake?" Arthur spoke up suddenly. "You mean the one that attacked me?"
Harry turned towards him and nodded. "Yes, Mr Weasley. That same snake. Voldemort made her into a Horcrux."
Arthur's hand strayed to the scar beneath his robes, where Nagini's fangs had nearly cost him his life at the Ministry. Molly noticed and took his arm. Neither spoke.
"And the last one?" Kingsley asked. His expression had remained stern throughout the explanation, but there was a new urgency in his voice. "Do you know what it is?"
"Yes," Harry answered. "It's something that belonged to Rowena Ravenclaw. Her lost diadem."
Professor Flitwick looked up sharply at the mention of his House's founder, but Harry continued before he could ask anything.
"Voldemort hid it somewhere here, in Hogwarts. I've seen it through his eyes. I know it's here, but I don't know where he's put it. That's why I came back. I need to find that diadem and destroy it. And Nagini, too. If even one of them survives, Voldemort can't be killed for good."
Harry paused, looking from McGonagall to Kingsley, then towards Remus and the Weasleys. The revelation had left its mark on the room. Some exchanged bewildered glances, still struggling to grasp what they had heard, while others looked towards the windows, beyond which the afternoon light continued to fade. Harry knew what he was about to ask of them, and judging by their faces, some of them were beginning to realise it too.
"Please," Harry began, but the word caught in his throat. He swallowed and tried again. "I need your help. Voldemort knows I'm hunting his Horcruxes, and I still haven't found the last one here at Hogwarts." He looked at the people gathered before him, forcing himself to meet their eyes. "I just need time. Please."
"And the Carrows have already summoned him," Draceana added from beside him. "He'll be here soon."
Kingsley turned towards her. "Miss Malfoy, is it? Are you certain of that?"
"Quite certain," Draceana replied. Without waiting to be asked, she pulled back her sleeve, exposing the Dark Mark branded upon her forearm. "I know how their Marks work. I've got one myself."
A collective gasp swept through the office. Several faces hardened in alarm, while others stared at the unmistakable skull and serpent on her skin. Whatever questions they had entertained about Draceana's presence beside Harry, none of them had expected quite this.
"A Death Eater?" Kingsley's expression grew serious as his eyes moved from the Mark to her face. "Well, I suppose, being Lucius Malfoy's daughter—"
"She's with me," Harry interrupted firmly.
He held Kingsley's gaze, leaving no room for misunderstanding. Whatever the others might think of the Mark, he wasn't going to let them mistake Draceana for an enemy. He knew how much she hated that mark, how she had spent months keeping it hidden beneath her sleeves. Yet she had just exposed it before a room full of people who had every reason to distrust her, simply because it might help him. Harry glanced at her, struck by how readily she had done something he knew must have cost her. He would have to thank her later.
For a moment, nobody spoke. Kingsley looked from Harry to the Dark Mark on Draceana's arm, then back again. There were clearly questions he wanted to ask, but Harry's expression gave him little encouragement to pursue them. At last, he gave a small nod, accepting Harry's assurance for the moment.
Draceana quietly lowered her sleeve.
"Oh, dear..."
McGonagall's troubled murmur broke the silence, drawing everyone's attention towards her. She had listened to the exchange without interruption, but Harry's warning of Voldemort's approaching arrival had clearly given her something to think about.
"Albus did warn me that something like this might happen," she said, almost to herself. "Though I confess, I never imagined it would come about quite so soon."
Harry turned towards her. "Professor?"
McGonagall adjusted her spectacles. "You see Harry, Albus left me a letter containing his final wishes. Most of it was personal, but there was one instruction I never quite understood." She paused, glancing towards the empty chair behind Dumbledore's desk. "He told me that should you ever return to Hogwarts, Harry, I was to prepare the school for a fight and ensure that no evil presence remained within its walls."
Several professors exchanged startled looks. Harry stared at her.
"At the time, I could make little sense of it. I thought it another of his riddles. Merlin knows he was rather fond of those." A faint smile touched her lips, though it quickly faded. "But after Miss Lovegood informed me of your return, and everything that has happened with Severus and the Carrows..." She hesitated, her eyes returning to Harry. "Well, I believe I understand him now."
For a moment, McGonagall seemed to struggle with what she wished to say next. Then she straightened, recovering some of her usual firmness.
"Albus knew you would come back one day, Harry. And when you did, he expected Hogwarts to be ready."
Harry stood quietly, absorbing her words. His gaze drifted towards Dumbledore's portrait. Earlier, standing before the empty chair, he had silently sought the professor's guidance and received no answer. Yet now, through professor McGonagall, it seemed Dumbledore had left him one after all.
Molly Weasley looked from McGonagall to Harry, her fingers tightening around the edge of her cardigan. Dumbledore's final wishes had made one thing painfully clear: Hogwarts was about to become a battlefield, and Harry intended to be at the heart of it. While the others considered what they had heard, Molly approached him and took hold of his arm.
"Harry, dear..." Her voice faltered. "Must it be you?"
Harry opened his mouth, but before he could answer, she continued.
"Couldn't you leave this to us? You've already told us what we need to know. You could go somewhere safe with Ronald and Hermione. Ginny too, once we get her out of here." Molly tightened her grip on his arm, searching his face. "You're still so young, Harry. You've already done more than anyone could reasonably ask of you. Surely there's no need for you to keep putting yourself in danger. Let the adults take care of the matter."
Harry looked down at her hand on his arm. He knew what she was trying to do. Molly had always treated him as one of her own children, and even now, with Voldemort approaching Hogwarts, her first thought was to get him somewhere safe. For a moment, he wished he could give her the answer she wanted. But he had come too far to turn back now.
"I'm sorry, Mrs Weasley," he said quietly, meeting her eyes. "But I intend to finish this."
Molly's expression faltered, though Harry continued before she could protest.
"And it's not just because Professor Dumbledore entrusted me with the mission. This is something between Tom and me. It has been for a long time." He paused, watching her struggle to accept his answer. "I have to see it through. I'm sorry."
For a moment, Molly simply stared at him. Then a tear slipped down her cheek, and she lowered her head, unable to find anything else to say. She knew that once the boy made his decision, he would not back down. Arthur stepped forward and slipped an arm around his wife, drawing her gently against him. He held her close, his own face grave, but made no attempt to argue with Harry.
Harry's words seemed to have struck a chord with those gathered around him. They had known him since he was a boy, watched him grow through one hardship after another, and yet there was something about the determination with which he had answered Molly that gave even the more experienced members of the Order pause. Whatever reservations they still held, it was becoming clear that Harry would not be persuaded to abandon his mission.
Kingsley understood what needed to be done now. Harry had made his decision, and it was time for the adults to gave the boy what he needed. With that resolve, Kingsley stepped forward to speak on their behalf.
"Then, Harry Potter," he declared, his deep voice carrying through the office, "we shall do whatever we can to help you. If that means taking the fight to the Dark Lord himself, then so be it."
He turned towards the assembled professors and members of the Order, looking from one familiar face to another.
"Everyone?"
Remus was the first to nod, followed by Arthur, who still had an arm around Molly. Professor Flitwick gave a firm nod of his own, while Sprout straightened beside him. One by one, the others followed suit. A few exchanged uncertain glances before giving their agreement, but none voiced an objection. They knew what Kingsley was asking of them.
Satisfied, Kingsley turned back towards Harry and extended his hand.
Harry stared at the offered hand for a moment before taking it firmly. A tear slipped down his cheek, though he managed a small smile.
"Thank you," he said, his voice catching slightly.
He looked around the office at the familiar faces surrounding him. Even after learning the truth, they had chosen to stand with him. He could scarcely have asked for more.
Beside him, Draceana reached out almost instinctively and placed her hand over Harry's, which was still clasped in Kingsley's handshake.
"Thank you," she added quietly.
There was no sarcasm in her voice, no trace of her usual haughtiness. She meant every word. Unfortunately for Draceana, the unexpected display of gratitude had rather the opposite effect from what she might have hoped.
Kingsley's eyebrows rose. Remus turned towards her with mild astonishment, while Arthur blinked as though he wasn't quite certain he had heard correctly. Even McGonagall paused, her lips parting slightly before she thought better of whatever she had been about to say.
A Malfoy had just thanked them. Of her own accord.
Harry glanced at Draceana, struggling to keep a straight face. She, meanwhile, was becoming painfully aware of the attention. A faint pink crept into her cheeks, deepening when she realised that practically everyone was staring at her.
"What?" she demanded, folding her arms. "Is there something wrong with saying your gratitude?"
"No," Kingsley replied after a brief pause, recovering his composure. "Nothing wrong at all, Miss Malfoy."
His perfectly serious expression only made matters worse. Draceana's cheeks turned an even brighter shade of red, much to Harry's amusement.
Fortunately for her, Professor Sprout chose that moment to speak up, drawing everyone's attention away from the increasingly flustered Slytherin.
"T-Then we must inform the students," she said. "They need to know what's happening."
"We cannot have them wandering about the castle unaware of what's coming," Flitwick added, nodding towards the windows.
"Quite right, Pomona, Filius," McGonagall agreed. "And I'm already ahead of you. I've made arrangements for everyone to assemble in the Great Hall."
With that, most of the professors and members of the Order hurried off to make preparations, leaving only Harry, Draceana, Luna, and Mr and Mrs Weasley in the office.
Molly, however, still had one question on her mind. She had noticed the way Draceana placed her hand over Harry's during his handshake with Kingsley, and the gesture had left her rather curious. Now that the others had departed, she finally had an opportunity to ask.
"Harry, dear, pardon me for asking, but who exactly is Miss Malfoy to you?"
"His girlfriend," Luna answered cheerfully, without a moment's hesitation.
"Lovegood!" Draceana whipped around to face her. "I swear, one of these days…"
"Was it supposed to be a secret?" Luna asked innocently, seemingly unbothered by the threat.
Harry, meanwhile, had turned a rather impressive shade of red. He scratched his cheek awkwardly, avoiding Molly's questioning gaze.
"Something like that," he admitted under his breath, careful not to let Draceana hear him.
Molly and Arthur exchanged bewildered looks. Of all the things they might have expected to hear that evening, Harry Potter having a possible romantic attachment to Lucius Malfoy's daughter was certainly the most surprising of all. Arthur raised his eyebrows at his wife, who answered with a small, knowing smile. Whatever the precise nature of the relationship, they could hardly deny that something had happened between the two.
******
The Great Hall was already filled with students, assembled in neat rows according to their Houses, with the younger years standing at the back and the older students at the front. Among them were Neville, Seamus, Ginny, and the other members of Dumbledore's Army, who had left the Room of Requirement to join their fellow students. Luna, too, had returned from the headmaster's office and taken her place among the Ravenclaws.
Despite the orderly arrangement, the hall was anything but quiet. Conversations rippled through the rows, with each House seemingly occupied by a different rumour. The Gryffindors whispered excitedly about Harry Potter's supposed return, while the Ravenclaws exchanged accounts of the unconscious Carrows and the confrontation in their common room. Among the Slytherins, word had spread that Draceana Malfoy was back at Hogwarts, while the Hufflepuffs wondered what on earth had caused the disturbance in the headmaster's office. Everyone had heard something, but no one seemed to have the full story, leaving them equally puzzled as to why they had been summoned at such an unusual hour.
The murmurs died away as the great doors swung open, drawing every student's attention towards the entrance.
Professor McGonagall entered first, followed by the other professors, members of the Order of the Phoenix, the Weasleys, and several former students who had returned to Hogwarts. The professors made their way towards the front of the hall, while the others remained near the entrance. The unexpected arrival of so many adults only deepened the students' confusion, and whispers were already beginning to spread again when two more figures appeared in the doorway.
Harry Potter and Draceana Malfoy.
At the sight of Harry, excitement began to stir among the students, but before it could swell into cheers, they realized who the blonde girl walking beside him was.
"Harry Potter!"
"It's him! He's really back!"
"Wait, isn't that Malfoy?"
"Draceana Malfoy?"
The excitement quickly gave way to bewilderment. Harry Potter and Draceana Malfoy had been notorious for their bitter rivalry throughout their years at Hogwarts, and seeing them arrive together was peculiar enough. Several students half-expected an argument to break out before they even reached the front of the hall. Instead, the two simply walked side by side without exchanging a word, leaving their audience more perplexed than ever.
Among the Slytherins, Pansy Parkinson could scarcely believe what she was seeing.
"Dracy..." she whispered, her mouth falling slightly open.
Her friend had left Hogwarts near the beginning of the school year, and Pansy hadn't heard a word from her since. Now, after months of silence, Draceana had suddenly reappeared, looking more dishevelled than Pansy had ever seen in her lifetime. And somehow, of all the people in Hogwarts, she was walking beside Harry Potter.
Pansy had spent months wondering where her friend had gone and whether she was even safe. Now that Draceana was standing before her, she wanted nothing more than to call out, to demand where she'd been and why she hadn't sent so much as a letter. But the questions crowded together, and the sight of Potter beside her only made matters worse. For now, Pansy could do little more than watch, her eyes following Draceana as she passed.
Beside her, Goyle and Daphne looked equally bewildered, while Crabbe simply stared at the pair in silence.
At the front of the Great Hall, the professors took their places, with Professor McGonagall standing before them. Harry and Draceana remained a little to one side, still very much aware of the attention directed their way.
"That was awful," Draceana muttered under her breath.
"Are you all right?" Harry asked, glancing at her.
"Not really. Those stares... they're relentless. I thought I'd prepared myself for this."
"I thought you liked attention," Harry teased, hoping to lighten her mood.
"Not like this." Draceana hesitated, as though reconsidering her own answer. "Or perhaps not anymore. I don't know."
Harry studied her for a moment. There had been a time when Draceana Malfoy would have delighted in having an entire room turn to look at her, particularly if Potter himself had been forced to witness it. Now, standing beneath those same curious gazes, she seemed to wish she could disappear.
"Silence, please!" Professor McGonagall called from the front.
The students immediately straightened, and Harry and Draceana turned their attention towards the professor. Yet while Harry watched McGonagall, Draceana kept her eyes fixed firmly ahead, careful not to glance towards the Slytherins. She knew her friends were somewhere among them, and part of her longed to see their familiar faces again. But what could she possibly say to them? How could she explain everything that had happened since she left Hogwarts? She wasn't even certain how they would look at her now.
Pansy noticed, of course. She had been watching Draceana ever since she entered the hall, hoping her friend might look her way, if only once. But Draceana seemed determined to avoid the Slytherin rows altogether. Pansy pressed her lips together. Was Dracy avoiding her deliberately? Had something happened during those missing months that she was too ashamed to admit? For one bewildering moment, Pansy even wondered whether Potter had somehow bewitched her. It was a ridiculous thought, perhaps, but what other explanation was there for her friend standing so willingly beside the boy she had spent years despising? Unable to call out to her in the middle of the assembly, Pansy could only remain where she was, waiting for a glance that never came.
"Right," McGonagall began, surveying the assembled students. "I suppose I should begin with some important news. As of today, the Carrows have been relieved of their teaching duties."
The announcement was met with an immediate eruption of cheers from Gryffindor, Ravenclaw, and Hufflepuff. After everything the students had endured under the Carrows, the news was almost too good to believe.
"Silence!" McGonagall called again, raising her voice above the commotion. She waited until the cheering had subsided before continuing. "Furthermore, Severus Snape is no longer the headmaster of Hogwarts."
Another wave of excitement swept through the hall, louder than the first.
Harry couldn't help smiling as he looked towards his friends among the students. Neville, Ginny, Seamus, and the others were celebrating with an enthusiasm he hadn't seen in a long time. They had endured so much in his absence, and for once, they had something worth cheering about. Judging by their reactions, it was probably the best news they'd heard in months.
But as Harry watched them celebrate, their faces suddenly began to blur.
The Great Hall disappeared.
He found himself somewhere dark and unfamiliar, unable to move or make sense of what he was seeing. These sudden visions had become almost familiar to him by now, though they were usually accompanied by a sharp pain in his scar. Strangely, this time there was none. Then, before he could make sense of his surroundings, two figures came into view.
Ron? Hermione?
Harry could scarcely believe his eyes. He hadn't known what had become of them since they parted, and seeing them both alive and apparently unharmed brought a rush of relief. Then he noticed the basilisk fang in Hermione's hand.
They did it.
They had managed to retrieve at least one fang, from what he could see. Yet something about the vision was peculiar. Harry was accustomed to seeing through Voldemort's eyes, but this time he was looking up at Hermione from an unusually low angle. He was still trying to understand why when Ron spoke.
"Ready?"
Hermione nodded, though she looked nervous.
"Go ahead. I've got you," Ron reassured her, wrapping his arms around her to steady her.
Hermione raised the basilisk fang.
Wait. What are you—?
The fang came plunging towards him.
WAIT!
A searing sensation tore through Harry's entire being, as though something inside him were being ripped apart. He tried to scream, but before he could make a sound, darkness swallowed everything once more.
Was I... the cup?
There was no time to consider it. The vision shifted again, and Harry suddenly found himself standing on a stretch of open ground overlooking Hogwarts. The castle rose in the distance beneath the last fading light of the evening, its familiar towers looking strangely small from where he stood.
Then his gaze turned.
Rows upon rows of cloaked, masked figures stretched across the grounds behind him. Death Eaters. Hundreds of them, perhaps even thousands, standing in formation as they awaited their master's command. Harry's stomach lurched at the sight. Only moments ago, he had been watching his friends celebrate Snape's departure. Now he was looking at the army gathering beyond the castle walls.
The strange vision of the cup began to make sense. Voldemort must have been checking on his Horcruxes, and Harry had somehow witnessed the cup's destruction through their connection. If Voldemort had felt it too, he would know that another piece of his soul was gone.
His gaze shifted towards something beside him, and Harry caught sight of Nagini, enclosed within a shimmering magical barrier. Voldemort was keeping her close, taking every precaution to protect what remained of his soul. Harry could sense the fear beneath his determination to defend it.
At least Harry now knew exactly where Nagini was. That was something. But the discovery offered little comfort when an entire army was waiting outside Hogwarts, and everyone within its walls remained unaware.
Why hasn't he attacked yet? Harry wondered.
Before he could make sense of it, the vision abruptly released him.
"Harry? Harry?"
Draceana's voice was the first thing Harry heard as the Great Hall slowly came back into focus. He blinked, finding her standing beside him, watching him with a furrowed brow.
Draceana had noticed him grow strangely distant, his eyes fixed on something she couldn't see. "This is hardly the time to doze off, Potter," she whispered, though the concern in her expression rather spoiled the attempt at teasing.
"HE'S HERE!" Harry shouted.
Every head in the Great Hall turned towards him.
"Voldemort!" he exclaimed, his eyes wide with alarm. "He's here!"
A startled murmur swept through the students. Some looked towards the doors, others towards the windows, while several exchanged bewildered glances, wondering whether Harry Potter had finally lost his mind. The professors and members of the Order, however, understood his warning perfectly. McGonagall stiffened, and Kingsley immediately turned towards the entrance.
Then, almost as though it had been waiting for Harry to announce its owner's arrival, a voice spoke inside every head in the Great Hall.
"Greetings... esteemed professors... and students of Hogwarts."
The voice was cold and condescending, its strange, hissing pauses making even the greeting sound like a threat. It seemed to come from everywhere at once, leaving the students looking helplessly around for its source. The cheering had vanished entirely, replaced by an uneasy silence as several younger students huddled closer together.
"I understand... that some of you may be considering resistance. How very foolish." There was a pause, followed by something resembling a chuckle. "I have no desire to fight you. I hold the teachers of Hogwarts in the highest regard... and I would find it most regrettable if innocent magical blood were to be spilled."
Harry's stomach turned at the words. Voldemort spoke of innocent blood as though he hadn't spent years spilling it himself. Beside him,

While the Civil War was still raging, Southern land was being sold to Northern investors.

Under federal legislation passed in 1861 and 1862, land in rebellious states could be seized and auctioned when federal taxes went unpaid.

Northern businessmen, investors, and speculators purchased former plantations, sometimes acquiring thousands of acres. In South Carolina's Sea Islands, Boston businessman Edward S. Philbrick purchased approximately 8,000 acres in 1863.

Formerly enslaved people also participated in these auctions, although Northern investors acquired much of the acreage offered in the early sales.

The war was not merely destroying Southern wealth. It was also creating opportunities for others to acquire it.

An often-overlooked financial dimension of the American Civil War.

text:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

This week I’ve been thinking a lot about the human labor behind fancy AI models. 

The secret to making AI chatbots sound smart and spew less toxic nonsense is to use a technique called reinforcement learning from human feedback, which uses input from people to improve the model’s answers. 

It relies on a small army of human data annotators who evaluate whether a string of text makes sense and sounds fluent and natural. They decide whether a response should be kept in the AI model’s database or removed. 

Even the most impressive AI chatbots require thousands of human work hours to behave in a way their creators want them to, and even then they do it unreliably. The work can be brutal and upsetting, as we will hear this week when the ACM Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency (FAccT) gets underway. It’s a conference that brings together research on things I like to write about, such as how to make AI systems more accountable and ethical.

One panel I am looking forward to is with AI ethics pioneer Timnit Gebru, who used to co-lead Google’s AI ethics department before being fired. Gebru will be speaking about how data workers in Ethiopia, Eritrea, and Kenya are exploited to clean up online hate and misinformation. Data annotators in Kenya, for example, were paid less than $2 an hour to sift through reams of unsettling content on violence and sexual abuse in order to make ChatGPT less toxic. These workers are now unionizing to gain better working conditions. 

In an MIT Technology Review series last year, we explored how AI is creating a new colonial world order, and data workers are bearing the brunt of it. Shining a light on exploitative labor practices around AI has become even more urgent and important with the rise of popular AI chatbots such as ChatGPT, Bing, and Bard and image-generating AI such as DALL-E 2 and Stable Diffusion. 

Data annotators are involved in every stage of AI development, from training models to verifying their outputs to offering feedback that makes it possible to fine-tune a model after it has been launched. They are often forced to work at an incredibly rapid pace to meet high targets and tight deadlines, says Srravya Chandhiramowuli, a PhD researcher studying labor practices in data work at City, University of London.

“This notion that you can build these large-scale systems without human intervention is an absolute fallacy,” says Chandhiramowuli.

Data annotators give AI models important context that they need to make decisions at scale and seem sophisticated. 

Chandhiramowuli tells me of one case where a data annotator in India had to differentiate between images of soda bottles and pick out ones that looked like  Dr. Pepper. But Dr. Pepper is not a product that is sold in India, and the onus was on the data annotator to figure it out. 

The expectation is that annotators figure out the values that are important to the company, says Chandhiramowuli. “They’re not just learning these distant faraway things that are absolutely meaningless to them—they’re also figuring out not only what those other contexts are, but what the priorities of the system they’re building are,” she says.

In fact, we are all data laborers for big technology companies, whether we are aware of it or not, argue researchers at the University of California, Berkeley, the University of California, Davis, the University of Minnesota, and Northwestern University in a new paper presented at FAccT.

Text and image AI models are trained using huge data sets that have been scraped from the internet. This includes our personal data and copyrighted works by artists, and that data we have created is now forever part of an AI model that is built to make a company money. We unwittingly contribute our labor for free by uploading our photos on public sites, upvoting comments on Reddit, labeling images on reCAPTCHA, or performing online searches.  

At the moment, the power imbalance is heavily skewed in favor of some of the biggest technology companies in the world. 

To change that, we need nothing short of a data revolution and regulation. The researchers argue that one way people can take back control of their online existence is by advocating for transparency about how data is used and coming up with ways to give people the right to offer feedback and share revenues from the use of their data. 

Even though this data labor forms the backbone of modern AI, data work remains chronically underappreciated and invisible around the world, and wages remain low for annotators. 

“There is absolutely no recognition of what the contribution of data work is,” says Chandhiramowuli. 

Deeper Learning

The future of generative AI and business

What are you doing on Wednesday? Why not join me and MIT Technology Review’s senior editor for AI, Will Douglas Heaven, at EmTech Next, where we’ll be joined by a great panel of experts to analyze how the AI revolution will change business? 

My sessions will look at AI in cybersecurity, the importance of data, and the new rules we need for AI. Tickets are still available here.

To whet your appetite, my colleague David Rotman has a deep dive on generative AI and how it is going to change the economy. Read it here. 

Even Deeper Learning

DeepMind’s game-playing AI just found another way to make code faster

Using a new version of the game-playing AI AlphaZero called AlphaDev, the UK-based firm (recently renamed Google DeepMind after a merge with its sister company’s AI lab in April) has discovered a way to sort items in a list up to 70% faster than the best existing method. It has also found a way to speed up a key algorithm used in cryptography by 30%. 

Why this matters: As computer chips powering AI models are approaching their physical limits, computer scientists are having to find new and innovative ways of optimizing computing. These algorithms are among the most common building blocks in software. Small speed-ups can make a huge difference, cutting costs and saving energy. Read more from Will Douglas Heaven here.

Bits and Bytes

Ron DeSantis ad uses AI-generated photos of Donald Trump and Anthony Fauci
The US presidential election is going to get messy. Exhibit A: A campaign backing Ron DeSantis as the Republican presidential nominee in 2024 has used an AI-generated deepfake to attack rival Donald Trump. The image depicts Trump kissing Anthony Fauci, a former White House chief medical advisor loathed by many on the right. (AFP) 

Humans are biased, but generative AI is worse 
This visual investigation shows how the open-source text-to-image model Stable Diffusion amplifies stereotypes about race and gender. The piece is a great visualization of research showing that the AI model presents a more biased worldview than reality. For example, women made up just 3% of the images generated for the keyword “judge,” when in reality 34% of US judges are women. (Bloomberg)

Meta is throwing generative AI at everything
After a rocky year of layoffs, Meta’s CEO, Mark Zuckerberg, told staff that the company is intending to integrate generative AI into its flagship products, such as Facebook and Instagram. People will, for example, be able to use text prompts to edit photos and share them on Instagram Stories. The company is also developing AI assistants or coaches that people can interact with. (The New York Times)

A satisfying use of generative AI
Watch someone fixing things using generative AI in photo-editing software.

text:
The people of Koriukivka had already endured nearly eighteen months of German occupation when the killing began on March 1, 1943. Their town lay among the forests of northern Ukraine, in a region where Soviet partisans were fighting behind German lines and occupation forces were increasingly resorting to collective punishment. The countryside had become a dangerous place to live, not simply because armed men operated nearby, but because the German authorities treated civilian communities as legitimate targets whenever resistance challenged their control.

Two nights earlier, Soviet partisans belonging to a formation associated with Oleksii Fedorov had attacked the German-Hungarian garrison in Koriukivka, destroying military installations and releasing prisoners. Among those held by the occupation authorities were relatives of partisan fighters, including children. The raid was directed against an occupying military force, but German authorities decided that the civilian population would pay for it. Bruno Franz Bayer, an officer serving within the German rear-area command structure, ordered the town’s destruction, and a punitive detachment was assembled from German troops, Hungarian soldiers, auxiliary police and collaborators. Its purpose was not to recover territory or defeat an opposing army. It was to make an example of Koriukivka by destroying the town and killing its inhabitants.

On the morning of March 1, the detachment surrounded the settlement and began gathering residents under the pretence of checking their identity documents. People were assembled in groups of 50 to 100 and driven into buildings, where they were shot with automatic weapons. Elsewhere, armed men moved from house to house, killing those they encountered and setting fire to the structures. The violence spread through the town, leaving entire households dead and buildings burning, while those who managed to avoid the initial roundups attempted to hide or escape into the surrounding countryside.

One of the principal killing sites was a restaurant near the centre of Koriukivka, where as many as 500 people are believed to have been murdered. Among those taken there was Evhen Rymar, a father who later described carrying his young daughter Nina when the shooting began. A bullet struck him in the eye, and he lost consciousness, but somehow survived the attack. Three of his children were killed. In his testimony, preserved by the Ukrainian Institute of National Memory, he recalled that their bodies had been burned and that he had been unable even to bury them. The destruction had taken his children and denied him the ordinary consolation of a grave at which to mourn them.

Rymar’s account brings into focus something that can easily disappear when atrocities are described through enormous numbers. The people murdered at Koriukivka were not an anonymous population moving across a military map. They were parents, children, neighbours and relatives, people who had continued living their lives under occupation because they had nowhere else to go. Many had no connection to the partisan raid, and none had been given an opportunity to answer an accusation or defend themselves. Their deaths were not accidental consequences of combat. They were the intended result of an organised operation against civilians.

The killing continued throughout March 2, while fires consumed much of the town. Witnesses later described smoke and flames visible from surrounding communities many kilometres away. Some inhabitants survived by concealing themselves in cellars, industrial buildings or the nearby marshes, but even those who escaped the gunfire faced the destruction of their homes and the loss of relatives. The perpetrators returned on March 9 to burn remaining structures and kill survivors, demonstrating that the massacre was not a momentary outbreak of violence but a deliberate campaign of destruction carried out over several days.

When investigators examined the ruins later that year, they recorded approximately 6,700 people murdered and 1,290 buildings burned. Only ten brick buildings were reported to have survived. Subsequent research identified 1,893 victims by name, including 704 children and adolescents, but the majority of those believed to have died remain unnamed in the published accounting. Entire families had disappeared together, bodies had been burned, and the destruction made it extraordinarily difficult to reconstruct the lives that had ended there. The figures are necessarily estimates drawn from surviving evidence, but the scale of the crime is beyond serious dispute.

There is another part of Koriukivka’s history that deserves attention, precisely because it complicates the more familiar stories of Soviet resistance. A substantial partisan formation remained in the forests approximately 15 kilometres from the town while the massacre was taking place. Its commanders did not order an intervention, even though accounts indicate that some fighters wished to help the population. Historians have continued to examine what the partisan leadership knew, what military options were available, and why no attempt was made to stop the killing. Those questions matter, although they do not transfer responsibility for the massacre away from the German-directed occupation forces that planned and carried it out.

The partisans had attacked an enemy garrison, while the occupation authorities had chosen to murder thousands of civilians. These were fundamentally different actions, and the distinction must be preserved. Nevertheless, the failure to intervene challenges the comfortable assumption that armed resistance necessarily meant protection for the communities living nearby. Civilians in occupied territory could find themselves exposed to the demands of partisans and the reprisals of occupation forces, without possessing the means to protect themselves from either danger. Koriukivka reveals the terrible vulnerability of people whose lives depended upon decisions made by armed organisations over which they had little control.

The massacre also raises difficult questions about how the Second World War was remembered after the fighting ended. Other destroyed communities became internationally recognised symbols of Nazi brutality, including Lidice in the Czech lands, Khatyn in Belarus and Oradour-sur-Glane in France. Their remembrance was deserved, yet Koriukivka, where far more people were killed, remained comparatively obscure. The Soviet state celebrated partisan resistance as an essential part of its victory over Germany, but Koriukivka did not fit comfortably within that narrative. Public attention to the massacre would also have invited scrutiny of the nearby partisan formation and its failure to protect the inhabitants.

A memorial was eventually erected in Koriukivka in 1977, although its original emphasis was upon heroic resistance rather than the murdered civilian population. Local families and researchers preserved the history, but remembrance remained uneven, and the town never acquired the international recognition that its suffering warranted. The politics of memory had helped determine which communities became symbols of the war and which remained largely absent from the stories told beyond their own regions.

Today, the surviving testimony and investigative records allow historians to reconstruct much of what happened, although important questions remain about the decisions of individual commanders and the precise accounting of the dead. The German occupation system’s responsibility for the massacre, however, is clear. It was an act of organised terror intended to intimidate the countryside by demonstrating that an entire community could be destroyed in retaliation for an attack by armed resistance.

We often remember the Eastern Front through the names of cities that became battlefields, commanders who directed armies and soldiers who endured extraordinary hardship. Those histories are important, but they describe only part of the war. For millions of civilians under occupation, the defining experience was not an offensive or a retreat, but the constant possibility that armed men might arrive at their homes and decide that they no longer had the right to live.

Koriukivka was eventually rebuilt, and new generations grew up where the old town had been destroyed. But rebuilding streets and houses could not restore the children who never reached adulthood, the parents who never returned to their families, or the thousands whose names disappeared with the records of their lives. The people murdered there did not die in battle, and they did not choose to become part of a military operation. Their lives were taken because the occupiers decided that killing civilians was an acceptable instrument of war.

The history of the Eastern Front cannot be told through courage and victory alone. It must also make room for the atrocities that offer no reassuring conclusion, no last-minute rescue and no triumph capable of making the suffering meaningful.

Koriukivka is one of those histories. Approximately 6,700 people were murdered, most of their names remain absent from the published accounting, and the town’s destruction stands as evidence of what happens when a civilian population is treated as an instrument of military punishment.

We cannot give those people back their lives, but we can refuse to allow the story of their deaths to disappear behind the more familiar history of the war’s battles.

Nehemiah 4
 
New International Version
Opposition to the Rebuilding
4 [a]When Sanballat heard that we were rebuilding the wall, he became angry and was greatly incensed. He ridiculed the Jews, 2 and in the presence of his associates and the army of Samaria, he said, “What are those feeble Jews doing? Will they restore their wall? Will they offer sacrifices? Will they finish in a day? Can they bring the stones back to life from those heaps of rubble—burned as they are?”

3 Tobiah the Ammonite, who was at his side, said, “What they are building—even a fox climbing up on it would break down their wall of stones!”

4 Hear us, our God, for we are despised. Turn their insults back on their own heads. Give them over as plunder in a land of captivity. 5 Do not cover up their guilt or blot out their sins from your sight, for they have thrown insults in the face of[b] the builders.

6 So we rebuilt the wall till all of it reached half its height, for the people worked with all their heart.

7 But when Sanballat, Tobiah, the Arabs, the Ammonites and the people of Ashdod heard that the repairs to Jerusalem’s walls had gone ahead and that the gaps were being closed, they were very angry. 8 They all plotted together to come and fight against Jerusalem and stir up trouble against it. 9 But we prayed to our God and posted a guard day and night to meet this threat.

10 Meanwhile, the people in Judah said, “The strength of the laborers is giving out, and there is so much rubble that we cannot rebuild the wall.”

11 Also our enemies said, “Before they know it or see us, we will be right there among them and will kill them and put an end to the work.”

12 Then the Jews who lived near them came and told us ten times over, “Wherever you turn, they will attack us.”

معارضة إعادة البناء

🤔 Wild thought: SpaceX + Tesla + Nvidia, one AI ecosystem 🚀🚗🟩

(@elonmusk - IF anyone can construct an action plan to do a derivative approach to Acquiring/Merging NVDA to integrate SPCX TSLA NVDA and bring Jensen back - it would be you!!)

$SPCX runs its AI on $NVDA. Musk in August: "SpaceX has committed to using Nvidia GPUs exclusively because they are the best" 🔒

He said SpaceX expects "a very significant percent" of Nvidia's GPUs next year 📦

A buyout isn't realistic. A merger? Genius 🧠

Here's why 👇

🟩 WHAT NVIDIA HAS THAT OTHERS DON'T (YET)

💰 THE PROFIT (actual, Q2 FY27)
Revenue $96.2B, up 106% from a year ago
Gross margin 75.0%
Net income: GAAP $59.7B | Adjusted $54.0B
Q3 guide (forecast): $108B, plus or minus 2%

🏭 THE SUPPLY CHAIN
Nvidia holds the majority of TSMC's advanced packaging capacity (CoWoS), the step every top AI chip has to go through. UBS estimates about 60% in 2026 and about 49% in 2027 (estimates) 🇹🇼

💾 THE MEMORY
Supply and capacity commitments jumped from $119B to $279B in one quarter, mostly memory, with long-term HBM deals across SK hynix, Samsung and Micron

📈 THE SCALABILITY
That supply is already locked in for the next several years. The hyperscalers can't just buy that overnight 🔐

🛰️ SPACEX: THE COMPUTE
SpaceXSI's Colossus 1 runs 220,000+ Nvidia GPUs, with supercompute campuses planned in Texas and Arizona. Starmind AI satellites, basically Vera Rubin NVL72 computers in orbit, are targeted to start launching next year 🌌

🚗 TESLA: THE PHYSICAL AI
Tesla designs its own AI5 chip, now in trial production, headed into Optimus around April 2027 🤖

🏭 AND THE FAB
Terafab, the SpaceX + Tesla chip plant in Texas ($16.8B first phase), is targeting volume production around Q3 2028. Musk himself calls that timeline "very aggressive" ⚡

📈 WHY IT'S SO POWERFUL (my take)
This would be about as vertical as it gets 🏗️

Instead of paying Nvidia's margins, SpaceX would own them. The profit stays in-house and gets reinvested straight into more compute, more satellites and more robots 💸

Locked-in TSMC and memory capacity + SpaceX's speed of building = a huge profitability pipeline, and scaling no one else can match 🚀

⚖️ THE HYPERSCALERS
$META $GOOGL $MSFT $AMZN would be at a serious disadvantage. When one player controls the top chips, the TSMC capacity, the memory AND the compute buildout, everyone else is fighting for what's left 🏁

Yes, they have their own chips (TPU, Trainium and more), but in my view they'd struggle to keep pace 🐢

☁️ THE NEOCLOUDS (my take)
Different story. Neoclouds are built largely on Nvidia GPUs to compete with the hyperscalers, so they'd likely stay key customers and keep riding the same Nvidia roadmap 🤝

Compute → Intelligence → Productivity → Economic Value 💰

🗳️ COULD IT ACTUALLY HAPPEN?
A true merger needs both boards to say yes 🤝 Without that, it goes to shareholders: a tender offer, or a proxy fight to elect new directors. Every $NVDA director is up for election every year

📜 The hurdles, per Nvidia's charter, bylaws and Delaware law:
✅ No poison pill in place (but a board can adopt one quickly)
📣 Calling a special meeting takes 15% of the vote, held for 1+ year
🚫 No action by written consent
🔒 Delaware's Section 203: buy 15%+ and you're blocked from merging for 3 years, unless the board approves first or you reach 85% in the same deal

Plus massive antitrust hurdles ⚖️

Pure thought experiment, but think about it... 👀

Compute is the new capital. Own the assets 💰

Lead the Flock 🐏
