text:
🐓 HEN FEVER, A ROCKET MISFIRE, A CAPTURED CORRESPONDENT, A SHARPER IDEA & A SHUTTLE THAT LANDED ITSELF!

══════════════ ❧ ══════════════

THE WEIRDEST EVENTS IN HISTORY 🤯

══════════════ ❧ ══════════════

STRANGER THAN FICTION — NOVEMBER 15TH EDITION

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🕒 ESTIMATED READING TIME: 12 MINUTES

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🗺️ CONSPECTUS

📜 EPIGRAPH — A little truth to set the tone.

🎬 INTRO — Five stories. One very strange date.

❓ HISTORY QUIZ OF THE DAY — Test your instincts.

⭐️ MAIN EVENTS — Five moments when history got spectacularly weird.

🎙️ HARVEY’S CORNER — The rest of the story.

⚖️ CLOSING — The day, considered.

✅ QUIZ ANSWER — The answer revealed.

🍬 CANDY — One last sweet bite, with a look at tomorrow.

💋 SEND-OFF — Pass the madness along.

📣 THERE’S MORE HISTORY WAITING! — The daily lineup.

📚 SOURCES & FURTHER READING — Follow the evidence.

✒️ PUDD’NHEAD WILSON HAS THE LAST WORD — Mark Twain gets the final say.

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

📜 EPIGRAPH

“Truth is stranger than fiction, but it is because Fiction is obliged to stick to possibilities; Truth isn’t.” — Mark Twain, Following the Equator (1897). ☄️

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🎬 INTRO

November 15, having surveyed the available options and found “ordinary” insufficiently dramatic, has elected to throw a small parade of historical mischief instead.

A flock of feathered celebrities draws a crowd that treats them like visiting royalty, because apparently nothing says “modern spectacle” like birds with better PR than most politicians. A presidential demonstration ends not with a bang of triumph but with the sort of unexpected bang that rearranges the afternoon’s agenda. A young reporter boards a military train under the charming assumption that he is merely going to observe the war; the war, unimpressed by his press credentials, promptly reassigns him. An everyday grooming nuisance—the kind that normally ends in mild cursing and a trip to the drugstore—inspires an invention that upends an entire industry, while a spacecraft casually performs a maneuver that history had the bad manners to schedule several decades too early.

And somewhere in the middle of this unsolicited chaos, an artist decides the world has been looking at ordinary things all wrong and, with the sort of stubbornness that makes committees nervous, declines to let anyone else tell her what she is seeing.

Five strange events. One extraordinary artist. A modest helping of ingenuity, a larger serving of danger, an almost indecent amount of human ambition, and more than one occasion on which the plan, having been carefully explained to reality, was told to wait outside.

Cue the chaos. Let's roll. 💥

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

❓ HISTORY QUIZ OF THE DAY

On November 15, 1988, an uncrewed Soviet spacecraft completed two orbits of Earth before returning to a fully automated landing.

What made this flight particularly remarkable?

[A] It was the first spacecraft to orbit Earth without a rocket.

[B] It completed its orbital flight and landed without a human crew aboard.

[C] It was the first spacecraft to travel beyond the Moon.

[D] It launched from a moving aircraft carrier.

👇 (Answer at the end of the issue.)

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

⭐️ MAIN EVENTS

🐓 1849 — BOSTON’S GREAT CHICKEN MANIA

November 15, 1849 | Boston, Massachusetts, United States

Forget celebrity red carpets. In 1849, Boston had a poultry exhibition—and the birds were the stars.

Organized by poultry enthusiast Dr. J. C. Bennett, the exhibition was intended to bring together examples of recognized domestic breeds. At the time, buyers could be deceived by sellers passing off ordinary birds as purebred stock. Bennett wanted breeders and prospective buyers to compare genuine specimens side by side.

The response was extraordinary. The exhibition opened on November 15 at the Boston Public Garden, where a large tent had been erected to accommodate the feathered gathering. It attracted 219 participants displaying 1,423 birds. More than 10,000 people reportedly came to see the collection. The enthusiasm was so great that an event originally planned for one day continued into a second.

And these were not simply rows of ordinary barnyard chickens. The exhibition included an impressive variety of domestic fowl, alongside ducks, geese, pheasants, peafowl, pigeons, and other birds. The growing interest in breeding and improving poultry was becoming a serious pursuit—and a public attraction.

🧩 TRIVIA: Unlike modern poultry competitions, the 1849 exhibition had no established standard for judging the birds. It was primarily an opportunity for breeders and visitors to compare different breeds.

🐶 SPOT: Among the exhibitors was Daniel Webster, the prominent American statesman and senator. He entered seven domesticated wild geese and a pair of Java fowl. Apparently, even the political elite could catch a case of hen fever.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A desire to distinguish genuine breeds from impostors helped turn poultry breeding into a public spectacle. Boston discovered that a room full of birds could draw a crowd—and that chicken enthusiasm was no flight of fancy.

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

💥 1862 — LINCOLN, A ROCKET, AND A VERY BAD DEMONSTRATION

November 15, 1862 | Washington Navy Yard, Washington, D.C., United States

Abraham Lincoln had plenty on his mind in the middle of the Civil War. On this day, however, he made time for an experimental weapons demonstration at the Washington Navy Yard.

The President arrived with Secretary of State William H. Seward and Secretary of the Treasury Salmon P. Chase to watch inventor J. B. Hyde's experimental rocket being tested. Naval officer Captain John A. Dahlgren joined the party.

The demonstration did not go according to plan.

The rocket was defective and exploded during the trial. Lincoln escaped injury, but the incident was alarming enough to become a memorable entry in the historical record. The President had gone to observe a potential military innovation; instead, he witnessed a demonstration of just how unpredictable experimental weapons could be.

The episode is documented in Dahlgren's diary, which helps preserve the details of the visit and the mishap.

🧩 TRIVIA: The incident is recorded in The Lincoln Log, which draws on the Dahlgren diary preserved among the John G. Nicolay Papers at the Library of Congress.

⚠️ IRONY: A weapon intended to demonstrate the promise of military technology ended up demonstrating the hazards of testing it. The Civil War demanded innovation—but innovation did not always arrive with a reliable safety record.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Progress often begins with experimentation. The trick is making sure the experiment does not become the most dangerous part of the demonstration.

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🚂 1899 — WINSTON CHURCHILL: THE REPORTER WHO BECAME A PRISONER

November 15, 1899 | Near Chieveley, Natal, South Africa

At twenty-four, Winston Churchill was in South Africa working as a war correspondent for The Morning Post, covering the Second Boer War. He had come to report on the conflict. He was about to become part of it.

Churchill joined a British reconnaissance expedition aboard an armored train—a railway convoy fitted with protective armor and weapons. The train was commanded by Captain Aylmer Haldane and carried soldiers, a naval gun, and a telegraphist.

The railway was essential to British operations, but it also created a serious vulnerability. Trains could not maneuver freely, and a damaged track could turn a mobile military unit into a sitting target.

On November 15, the train travelled beyond its intended limits toward Chieveley. Boer forces had obstructed the railway. The train was ambushed, partially derailed, and came under fire.

Churchill helped clear the track and get the locomotive moving again. The engine and part of the train escaped with wounded men aboard. But Churchill returned toward the defenders and was captured by Boer forces.

He was taken to a prisoner-of-war camp in Pretoria. His reporting assignment had become a personal ordeal.

Churchill eventually escaped from captivity in December and made his way through hostile territory toward Portuguese East Africa. His escape made him famous in Britain, helping propel him toward a political career.

🧩 TRIVIA: Churchill's escape took place on December 12, 1899. He got over the prison enclosure while the other men involved in the escape plan failed to follow him at that moment. He was left to make his own way to freedom.

🌀 OBSCURE: Churchill's role in the train's journey beyond its authorized limit has been debated. Historian John Hussey's detailed reconstruction argues that Churchill was instrumental in persuading Haldane to go farther than ordered—a complication that makes the familiar heroic version considerably less tidy.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A war correspondent went looking for a story and became part of one. But history is rarely improved by polishing away the uncomfortable details.

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🪒 1904 — KING CAMP GILLETTE AND THE BLADE THAT CHANGED SHAVING

November 15, 1904 | United States Patent Office, Washington, D.C., United States

Before disposable razor blades, shaving could be a tedious business. Blades needed regular stropping and honing, and keeping a razor sharp was not something every user could manage easily.

King Camp Gillette believed there was a better way.

He had developed the idea of a thin, replaceable blade years earlier, but turning that idea into a practical product was a formidable engineering challenge. The blade had to be thin, sharp, durable, and inexpensive enough to manufacture in large quantities.

Gillette found an essential partner in engineer William Emery Nickerson, who helped develop the manufacturing process needed to produce the blades.

The American Safety Razor Company had been formed in 1901, and production began in 1903. On November 15, 1904, Gillette received U.S. Patent No. 775,134 for his safety-razor design.

The invention offered a new arrangement: buy a durable handle, then replace the blade when it became dull. The customer no longer needed to repeatedly sharpen and maintain the same blade. It was a practical improvement—and a business model built around repeat purchases.

The idea caught on. The company sold just 51 razor sets and 168 blades in 1903, its first year of production. By 1904, sales had risen dramatically to 90,000 razors and two million blades.

🧩 TRIVIA: Gillette's former employer, William Painter, had made his fortune through another disposable invention: the crown bottle cap. Painter encouraged Gillette to think about a product that customers would use up and need to buy again. The razor blade became a remarkably successful answer.

🧬 HUMAN: Despite building a hugely successful business, Gillette became an outspoken anti-capitalist utopian. He wrote and supported books proposing sweeping social and economic changes. The man whose name became synonymous with a consumer empire did not necessarily admire the economic system that made it possible.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: A great invention can solve an everyday problem—and create an entirely new way of doing business. Gillette's lasting achievement was not just a sharper blade; it was a new relationship between the product and the customer.

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🛰️ 1988 — BURAN: THE SHUTTLE THAT LANDED ITSELF

November 15, 1988 | Baikonur Cosmodrome, Soviet Union

The Soviet Union had spent years developing a reusable spacecraft called Buran, meaning “snowstorm” or “blizzard.” On November 15, 1988, it finally launched aboard the powerful Energia rocket.

There was no crew aboard.

Buran completed two orbits of Earth, returned through the atmosphere, and landed automatically on a runway at the Baikonur Cosmodrome. The entire flight—from launch to landing—was conducted without a human pilot.

The mission lasted approximately 205 minutes. Its success demonstrated something extraordinary: an orbital shuttle could carry out its flight and return to Earth under computer control.

The achievement was especially striking because the American Space Shuttle, although capable of sophisticated automated operations, landed with human pilots aboard and at the controls. Buran's uncrewed flight demonstrated a fully automated orbital mission and landing.

The Soviet spacecraft had completed its test mission successfully. But a successful flight did not guarantee a successful future. Buran never flew again. The program was ultimately abandoned amid the political and economic upheaval surrounding the collapse of the Soviet Union.

🧩 TRIVIA: The United Nations Office for Outer Space Affairs records Buran's November 15 mission as a two-orbit test flight with automatic landing at Baikonur. The spacecraft reached orbit and returned to the runway without a cosmonaut aboard.

⚠️ IRONY: Buran achieved the extraordinary technical feat it had been designed to demonstrate—and then never made another flight. Its first successful mission became its only one.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: Technology can be decades ahead of its time, but even a brilliant machine cannot escape the political and economic realities surrounding it.

────────────── ❧ ────────────────

🎙️ HARVEY’S CORNER

🎨 GEORGIA O’KEEFFE — THE ARTIST WHO REFUSED TO SEE THE WORLD ORDINARY

Good day, everybody.

Some artists paint what they see. Others paint what they want us to see. Georgia O’Keeffe did something rather different: she made the familiar look unfamiliar, the overlooked impossible to ignore, and the ordinary suddenly worth a second look.

Born November 15, 1887, near Sun Prairie, Wisconsin, Georgia Totto O’Keeffe grew up on a dairy farm as the second of seven children. Her artistic ability was recognized early, and she received art lessons while growing up.

She studied at the Art Institute of Chicago and the Art Students League in New York, where she learned traditional techniques. But she became dissatisfied with academic realism and the expectation that art should simply reproduce what the eye could see.

A turning point came in 1912, when she took a summer course at the University of Virginia. Her instructor, Alon Bement, introduced her to the ideas of art educator Arthur Wesley Dow. His approach emphasized composition, line, and design—and offered O’Keeffe a way to express feeling through form rather than merely copy appearances.

She began experimenting with abstraction, producing a remarkable series of charcoal drawings. In 1916, photographer and art dealer Alfred Stieglitz exhibited ten of these works at his avant-garde gallery, 291, in New York. He recognized an original voice. O’Keeffe's work soon attracted attention, and Stieglitz became an important promoter of her art.

In 1918, she accepted his offer of financial support to leave teaching and devote herself to painting in New York. Their personal and professional relationship developed, and they married in 1924.

By the 1920s, O’Keeffe had become known for her large-scale flower paintings and her images of New York skyscrapers. Her flowers were not dainty decorations. She enlarged and cropped them until their shapes, curves, and colors filled the canvas. Viewers were forced to look closely at forms they might otherwise have passed without noticing.

But there was a problem: many critics insisted on interpreting her flower paintings through sexual symbolism. O’Keeffe rejected those readings. She wanted people to look at the paintings themselves, not simply impose meanings on them because the artist was a woman.

Her response was not to abandon the subjects she loved. It was to continue painting them on her own terms.

In 1929, O’Keeffe travelled to northern New Mexico for the first time. The landscape made a profound impression. The vast skies, rugged mountains, adobe architecture, churches, and bleached animal bones offered new subjects and new possibilities.

She returned regularly, spending much of each year in the Southwest. After Stieglitz died in 1946, she moved permanently to New Mexico in 1949. She divided her time between Ghost Ranch and her home in Abiquiú, where the landscape became inseparable from her artistic identity.

Her paintings of desert bones and sweeping landscapes were not simply postcards of the Southwest. They were her way of expressing what a place made her feel.

She continued creating into old age, although failing eyesight increasingly limited her work. She completed her last unassisted oil painting in 1972 and, with the help of assistants, continued exploring her creativity until her retirement in 1984.

O’Keeffe died in Santa Fe on March 6, 1986, aged ninety-eight.

Her legacy is much larger than the famous flowers, skulls, and desert landscapes. She helped shape American modernism, built an artistic language that was unmistakably her own, and refused to let critics dictate how her work should be understood.

She once explained that she had to create an equivalent for what she felt when looking at something—not merely copy it.

That may be the most revealing way to understand her art. She was not asking us simply to look at a flower, a mountain, or a bone. She was asking us to see it differently.

And she spent a lifetime showing us how.

And now, you know the rest of the story.

—— ❧ ——

🧩 TRIVIA: O’Keeffe's breakthrough exhibition in 1916 featured abstract charcoal drawings—not the flower paintings for which she later became famous. Alfred Stieglitz exhibited ten of those drawings at his 291 gallery, introducing her work to the New York art world.

🧬 HUMAN: O’Keeffe resisted being defined primarily as a woman artist. She wanted to be regarded as an artist, full stop. Yet the repeated attempts to interpret her paintings through gendered assumptions reveal how difficult it was for a woman of her generation to control the way her work was discussed.

🎯 TAKEAWAY: O’Keeffe's greatest achievement may have been her refusal to let other people determine what she should see, paint, or become. She created her own artistic language—and left the world looking at familiar things in a new way.

⚖️ CLOSING

A flock of exhibition poultry brought Boston's curiosity to a boil—exactly the civic triumph one hopes for when the history books are written. Lincoln’s rocket demonstration helpfully established that presidential enthusiasm is not, in fact, a recognized substitute for sound engineering. And Winston Churchill set out to cover a war only to spend his afternoon as a Boer prisoner, his reporting career briefly interrupted by the minor inconvenience of having been captured by the very people he was covering.

King C. Gillette noticed that millions of men already resented shaving and decided the solution was a blade designed to be thrown away; the industry that followed has never looked back, though it has certainly found new ways to keep selling us the same basic necessity.

Decades later, the Soviet Buran circled the Earth and landed itself without a crew—a remarkable technical achievement that was never repeated.

Georgia O’Keeffe spent a lifetime reminding us that looking and truly seeing are different things; judging by the way we rush through the world, her lesson still has some catching up to do.

From a traffic jam of chickens to a single unused spaceplane, from a captured correspondent to a disposable blade, November 15 offered a reminder of how ambition can produce spectacular results, unexpected consequences, and unfinished business. Some people changed the way the world worked; others showed us just how quickly a promising venture can become a historical footnote.

Not much to celebrate, then, for a date that never promised to amount to much and, in that limited sense, delivered. 🤭

When Gov. Maura Healey signed an emergency preamble Nov. 6 putting a new full-term abortion law into immediate effect, she said the emergency was supposedly 9 disabled babies who needed to be killed in late-term abortions.

The Compassionate Care Coalition partnered with Wicker & Reed, a private adoption agency based at His Providence Church in Swansea, in response. All are ready and willing to welcome the babies, including those with serious medical needs whose lives may be short.

"We believe the most compassionate path is one where every mother is supported and every baby, however short their life, knows only love, warmth and comfort," said Sam Miele, chairman of the Compassionate Care Coalition.

Wicker & Reed is working with local churches and donors to cover birth-related and adoption expenses and to walk alongside any mother through pregnancy and delivery.

The mother's health and her doctors' care remain first in every case, the groups said. All 11 families are prepared to love and care for the babies for as long as they live.

text:
November 13 Saint Frances Xavier Cabrini: the first United States citizen to be canonized.
1850-1917
Patronage:
against malaria
emigrants (given on 8 September 1950 by Pope Pius XII)
hospital administrators
immigrants
orphans
.
“We must pray without tiring, for the salvation of mankind does not depend on material success; nor on sciences that cloud the intellect. Neither does it depend on arms and human industries, but on Jesus alone.”
.
She founded the Missionary Sisters of the Sacred Heart to care for poor children in schools and hospitals, and at the urging of Pope Leo XIII, moved to the United States to work among immigrants. Through her care for those who were struggling, hard work, and obedience, Saint Frances is regarded today as the Patron Saint of all immigrants.
.
Frances Cabrini was born in Sant’Angelo Lodigiano (Lombardy, Italy). Born two months prematurely, Frances was small and weak, and struggled for survival. Frequently ill as a child, she would remain physically frail and susceptible to illness her entire life. 
Frances’ parents were farmers, and her mother stayed at home each day with the children. In total, her parents produced eleven children, with Frances being the tenth. Sadly, only four of the Cabrini children survived their childhood. Despite numerous losses and tragedies in the family, both Frances’ mother and father were strong in the Catholic faith, and through their teaching and example, Frances came to love God. One of her favorite activities was listening to her father read the stories of missionaries from the Annals of the Propagation of the faith. More than anything, from and early age and throughout her life, Frances desired to travel to China as a missionary. 
.
Frances was especially devoted to the Sacred Heart of Jesus, which inspired her growing faith. With her parents’ support, she applied for admission to several religious orders, but was turned away by each due to her frequent illnesses and frail health. Disappointed, but not discouraged, Frances cared for her parents until their death, as well as raised her brothers and sisters. Throughout all of this, despite her frailties, she worked on the family farm—physical activity that both taxed her body, but also prepared her for the physical work that she would encounter throughout her life. Upon the death of her parents, Frances began studying to her teaching degree at a boarding school administered by the Daughters of the Sacred Heart. While her classmates complained, she was delighted that the students of the school were required to live in the convent with the religious sisters. Adding to her joy was the devotion of the sisters to the Sacred Heart. Upon graduation, she again petitioned to join the order, but was again refused, with her health cited. The Superior of the Order encouraged her, saying, “You are called to establish another Institute that will bring new glory to the Heart of Jesus.” 
.
Again disappointed, but not discouraged, Frances returned to her home town, and began teaching in a private school, spending her non-work hours devoted to charitable works and serving the poor. She was immediately recognized for her gentle spirit, teaching ability, faith, and obedience, and over the next several years, was requested to move from school to school by the diocese, filling vacant positions and invigorating educational facilities. Eventually, she was requested to move to the town of Codogno, and assume direction of the girls’ orphanage there, known as the House of Providence. The diocese wished to restructure the facility into a religious institute, and realized that despite her frail health, Frances possessed the faith and spirit to accomplish the task. Without hesitation, Frances accepted, and within the year, the five young women who taught at the House, entered their novitiate with Frances as their novice mistress.
.
In 1877, at the age of 27, Frances’ wish to take the veil was granted, and along with her five sisters, made her profession. In honor of Jesuit father Frances Xavier, Frances took the name Xavier, becoming Mother Frances Xavier Cabrini—as she would be known for the remainder of her life. Named superior of the community by her local bishop, she was encouraged to form a new religious institute. Along with the five sisters who took their vows with her, she founded the Institute of Missionaries of the Sacred Heart of Jesus in 1880. While some objected to the inclusion of the word “Missionaries” in the order’s name (as it implied overseas work, and the bishop intended that the sisters serve locally), Mother Cabrini was already thinking on a larger, grander scale. She had plans for her sisters to spread the Gospel beyond the borders of Lombardy.
Mother Cabrini left Lombardy to travel to Rome, as was the custom at the time, seeking approval from the pope for her fledgling order. She also wished to establish a mission house in Rome, from which she could then use as a base for international missions. 
.
Surprisingly, despite the youth of the foundress and the relative newness of the order, she received papal approval and permission to open two missions in Rome. Mother Cabrini also met the founder of the Missionary Institute of Saint Charles, who was looking for a religious woman to assist him with ministering to Italian immigrants overseas—specifically in New York. He requested that she assist, but Mother Cabrini was reluctant. Her plans were to send her missionaries to China, as she had always dreamed. However, when presented with a letter from New York Archbishop Corrigan, formally inviting the Missionaries of the Sacred Heart to establish a house in New York, she was moved to request an audience with the pope.
.
Ever obedient, and certain in the plan of the Lord, Mother Cabrini decided that she would do whatever Pope Leo XIII asked her to. She presented her dilemma to him, and following deliberation and conversation, he responded: “Not to the East, but to the West.” Disappointed, but not discouraged, Mother Cabrini and six of her sisters set out immediately for New York. Upon arrival, she was surprised to find that Archbishop Corrigan had not expected her so soon, and even more surprised when he suggested they return to Italy until he could prepare for her arrival. But Mother Cabrini answered, "Your excellency, the Pope sent me here and here I must stay." The archbishop admired her pioneer spirit, and so she and her sisters were permitted to begin their work. She and her companions spent the first night in a dingy tenement in the heart of the Italian ghetto. They could not sleep and stayed awake, tired, yet peacefully engaged in prayer. 
.
Soon afterwards, a local order, the Sisters of Charity, extended Mother Cabrini and her sisters hospitality and guided their first steps through the city. At once, the new sisters were faced with a language difference. Not speaking English, and being unfamiliar with the new countries customs, Mother Cabrini worked to establish her mission. She slowly gained the support of the Archbishop, eventually becoming dear friends. She secured the donation of a house for the Order, and soon thereafter, instituted an orphanage on the same property. A free school soon followed, all through donations and alms-gathering that the sisters undertook on a daily basis. Soon, based upon their good work—and the personal attention and spiritual direction they gave to each family in the Italian district—young women were requesting to join the order.
.
Mother Cabrini returned to Italy, accompanied by her first North American postulants, who began their novitiate in Codogno. After an audience with her friend, Pope Leo XIII, she returned to New York, and embarked upon the institution of a larger orphanage. This site eventually included the North American novitiate of the order. Purchased at a low price, due to the lack of fresh water on the site, Mother Cabrini soon discovered a underground spring (some called it a miracle!), which still provides water to this day.
.
From New York, the Missionary Sisters branched out throughout America, starting in New Orleans (school and orphanage), and continuing west. It became clear—both in New York and other areas—that the immigrants were not receiving the medical care that they needed in public hospitals. However, Mother Cabrini was not particularly inclined to undertake this ministry. It was not until she had a dream of Our Blessed Mother that she changed her mind. 
.
In her dream, Mother Cabrini saw Mary, the Mother of God, tending to a hospital patient. Asking Our Blessed Mother what she was doing, Mother Cabrini was surprised by her response: “I am doing the work you refuse to do.” Upon waking, Mother Cabrini moved quickly to establish a hospital for the Italian sick poor in New York City, and to her surprise, found herself to be a capable (even outstanding) healthcare provider and administrator. Hospitals were eventually established by the Missionary Sisters in Chicago and Seattle.
.
The Missionary Sisters recount how the great faith of Mother Cabrini allowed this fast and miraculous growth of the order to occur. In Seattle, for example, as she was looking for a site to institute an orphanage, Mother Cabrini had a dream in which she saw a beautiful house on a hilltop. The next day she and some sisters were walking when she waved down a chauffeur-driven limo and asked for a ride. The lady in the limo was happy to help the sisters, and on the way, Mother Cabrini spoke of the house she had dreamed of. When they arrived at the convent and were saying goodbye, the lady told her: "Mother Cabrini, that house you dreamed of is mine, I own it. I never thought of parting with it, but if I may be allowed to enter your Holy House for a moment and receive a glass of water in the name of Our Lord, your little orphans shall have their home with my blessing." When asked later how she had obtained such a beautiful property, Mother Cabrini would say "I paid for it with three treasures: my love, a dream, and a glass of water in His Name."
.
The Order had successfully established bases in three American cities, but Mother Cabrini was thinking bigger. She extended the Missionary Sisters work into Latin America, establishing schools in Nicaragua and Argentina. She established schools in Europe, including Paris, London, and Madrid. And she continued to work throughout the United States, including schools in Chicago, Scranton, and Newark. Based upon the needs of the Italian miners working in and around the Rocky Mountains, Mother Cabrini traveled to Denver and established schools, orphanages, and a mission center.
.
While until that point her focus had been solely on Italian immigrants, the Missionary Sisters began to see the needs of other immigrant groups, extending their work to Mexican immigrants in California. Despite her failing health, Mother Cabrini traveled across the country (and the world!), visiting each house, and personally establishing new locations. Her travels included: New York, Pennsylvania, Illinois, Louisiana, Colorado, California, Washington State, Central and South America and Europe.
.
During this time, she fulfilled another personal goal, and became a citizen of the United States. Mother Cabrini began contemplating missions in Alaska, and still felt pulled toward Asia. However, the impact of her travels began to take its toll, and at the age of 67, she died in Chicago, in a private room at Columbus Hospital, as she was preparing Christmas candy for the local children. Less than 30 years later, she was canonized as a Saint—the first United States citizen to be canonized—by Pope Pius XII. 
.
From the homily at the Canonization of Saint Frances Xavier Cabrini by Pope Pius XII: “Inspired by the grace of god, we join the saints in honoring the holy virgin Frances Xavier Cabrini. She was a humble woman who became outstanding not because she was famous or rich or powerful, but because she lived a virtuous life. From the tender years of her youth, she kept her innocence as white as a lily and preserved it carefully with the thorns of penitence; as the years progressed, she was moved by a certain instinct and supernatural zeal to dedicate her whole life to the service and greater glory of God. She welcomed delinquent youths into safe homes, and taught them to live upright and holy lives. She consoled those who were in prison, and recalled to them the hope of eternal life. She encouraged prisoners to reform themselves, and to live honest lives. She comforted the sick and the infirm in the hospitals, and diligently cared for them. She extended a friendly and helping hand especially to immigrants, and offered them necessary shelter and relief, for having left their homeland behind, they were wandering about in a foreign land with no place to turn for help. Because of their condition, she saw that they were in danger of deserting the practice of Christian virtues and their Catholic faith. Undoubtedly she accomplished all this through the faith which was always so vibrant and alive in her heart; through the divine love which burned within her; and finally, through constant prayer by which she was so closely united with God from whom she humbly asked and obtained whatever her human weakness could not obtain. Although her constitution was very frail, her spirit was endowed with such singular strength that, knowing the will of God in her regard, she permitted nothing to impede her from accomplishing what seemed beyond her strength.” 
.
Saint Frances Xavier Cabrini’s life was filled with disappointments… but she was never discouraged. Despite setbacks, weak health, and constant difficulty, the accomplishments of Mother Cabrini are remarkable. Ever humble, she took no credit, instead directing those who might compliment her work back to the Lord—to Jesus Christ—though which all things were (and are) accomplished. Throughout her life, Mother Cabrini found her strength in the Lord, and used every ounce given to her to serve others. We look to her today as a model of obedience, hope, service and strength. Mother Cabrini, pray for us!
.
Eternal Father, I wish to honor St. Frances Xavier Cabrini, and I give Thee thanks for all the  graces Thou hast bestowed upon her. I ask Thee to please increase grace in  my soul through the merits of this saint, and I commit the end of my life to her by this special prayer, so that by virtue of Thy goodness and promise, St.  Frances Xavier Cabrini might be my advocate and provide whatever is needed at that hour. Amen.

Safety protocols are critical and include:

Surfing only at familiar breaks with predictable, gentle waves (e.g., beach breaks).
Never surfing alone; always use a buddy system and inform shore contacts of plans.
Wearing high-visibility gear (red LED lights preserve night vision better than white) and thicker wetsuits.
Avoiding areas with known shark activity, river mouths, or complex reef structures.

text:
AI discovers a hidden heart signal that could predict sudden death | University of California - Berkeley, ScienceDaily

More than 300,000 people in the United States die from sudden cardiac arrest each year. This deadly emergency occurs when the heart's electrical system suddenly fails, causing the heart to stop pumping blood. It can strike older adults with known heart conditions as well as seemingly healthy young athletes. Although implanted defibrillators can prevent some of these deaths, doctors have long struggled to determine which patients need them most.

Now, researchers at UC Berkeley have identified a previously overlooked warning signal in routine heart scans that could make it easier to recognize people at risk before a fatal event occurs.

The discovery was made using artificial intelligence trained on more than 440,000 electrocardiograms, or EKGs, collected in Sweden. By comparing the electrical patterns recorded in these scans with information from death certificates, the researchers taught an AI system to recognize subtle differences between healthy individuals, patients with known heart risks, and people who eventually died from sudden cardiac causes.

The team then evaluated the technology using thousands of additional patient records from the United States and Taiwan, testing whether the patterns could reliably identify people at heightened risk in different populations.

AI Detects Hidden Heart Risks That Standard Tests Miss

The results suggest that AI can identify vulnerable patients more effectively than the conventional tests doctors typically rely on. Current screening methods largely focus on how much blood the heart pumps with each contraction, a measurement used to assess whether someone might benefit from an implanted defibrillator.

Using these traditional measurements, doctors can identify a group of patients with an annual sudden cardiac death rate of 4.6%. The AI system, however, identified a group with an annual death rate of 7%, demonstrating a greater ability to distinguish patients facing serious danger.

Importantly, the algorithm also recognized a broader population of people at elevated risk, including thousands who would not normally raise concerns under existing medical guidelines. Most of these individuals would have been classified as relatively low risk using conventional methods.

Another major advantage is that the AI system works with ordinary EKG images, which are already routinely collected in hospitals and medical centers around the world. This means the technology could potentially improve screening without requiring an entirely new type of medical test.

The findings, published in Nature, could eventually help physicians make more informed decisions about who should receive an implanted defibrillator. They also raise an intriguing scientific question about what changes inside the heart produce the electrical patterns that AI has learned to recognize.

"Medical decisions are really hard, and I think that's why AI is so exciting for me," said Ziad Obermeyer, an associate professor at UC Berkeley's School of Public Health and the study's lead author. "We can not only make better decisions, but also start to understand what's actually going on with these patients before their heart stops."

Why Sudden Cardiac Death Is So Difficult to Predict

Sudden cardiac arrest is different from a heart attack. A heart attack happens when blood flow to part of the heart becomes blocked or severely restricted. Cardiac arrest, by contrast, results from a failure of the electrical signals that coordinate the heartbeat.

Immediate CPR and an electrical shock from an automated external defibrillator can sometimes restore the heart's rhythm. However, roughly 90% of people who experience sudden cardiac arrest outside a hospital die within minutes, making early recognition of those at risk especially important.

For Obermeyer, an emergency physician whose research combines artificial intelligence, medicine, and health policy, sudden cardiac death remains one of medicine's most frustrating unsolved problems.

Because victims often die without warning, researchers have limited opportunities to observe what happens inside the heart immediately before it stops. An autopsy may uncover blocked blood vessels, hardened tissue, or other structural abnormalities, but it cannot fully reveal how the heart was functioning in the moments leading up to death.

"One thing that makes the problem very tragic, but also very well suited for AI, is that we have the cure for this problem," Obermeyer said. "If you knew you were one of the people who was going to drop dead, you would go to a cardiologist and you'd get a defibrillator implanted. The problem is that doctors can't figure out who needs one before it's too late."

The Problem With Current Heart Risk Screening

Doctors currently rely heavily on a measurement of how effectively the heart pushes blood out with each beat. Patients whose hearts pump below a specified threshold may be considered candidates for an implantable cardioverter defibrillator, a device that can deliver an electrical shock when a dangerous heart rhythm develops.

But obtaining this measurement generally requires a more extensive medical evaluation. Many people who eventually experience sudden cardiac arrest never receive such testing because they have no obvious reason to suspect they are in danger.

The approach also has limitations for patients who are identified as high risk. About two-thirds of implanted defibrillators in these patients never need to deliver a shock. As a result, many individuals undergo expensive, invasive procedures for potentially fatal emergencies that may never occur.

At the same time, thousands of people who are not recognized as being at risk die unexpectedly each year.

"In some fraction of those people, we could have prevented those deaths if we had just known it in time," Obermeyer said. "There are a lot of lives being lost from people who are dropping dead of sudden cardiac death that are preventable if we just had better AI tools to find these things."

The researchers hope that identifying more accurate warning signs could help doctors direct preventive treatments toward the patients most likely to benefit.

How Researchers Trained AI to Recognize Deadly Heart Patterns

Developing the algorithm required three independent collections of medical data gathered from different parts of the world.

The researchers began with six years of EKG recordings from Sweden's unified healthcare system. By linking these scans to death certificates, they could examine the electrical patterns of patients who later experienced sudden cardiac death and compare them with those of other patients.

The AI learned to identify combinations of spikes, waves, and other characteristics in the recordings that appeared to be associated with increased risk. Once the system had been trained, the team tested it against two additional datasets: two years of anonymized EKG records from a San Diego hospital system and a separate collection of patient data from Taipei.

This international testing helped researchers evaluate whether the algorithm's predictive abilities extended beyond the Swedish population used to develop it.

"Good AI starts with good data," said Obermeyer, who is also part of the joint UCSF-UC Berkeley Computational Precision Health program. "Unfortunately, data like the ones we used for this study are incredibly hard to access. It's a big part of why there's so little clinical AI in use today."

Obtaining and organizing the information was itself a massive undertaking. According to Obermeyer, assembling the datasets took approximately 10 years and involved contributions from two organizations he helped establish, Dandelion Health and Nightingale Open Science. Both organizations work to advance medical research through better access to data and artificial intelligence.

"It's one of the tremendous luxuries of being at Berkeley," Obermeyer said. "You can pursue these projects that just are a slow burn and then have -- hopefully -- a big return when they get over the finish line."

From Hidden Heart Signals to Lifesaving Treatments

The researchers have already begun exploring how the system might be used in actual healthcare settings.

Obermeyer is collaborating with medical systems in Sweden, Taiwan, and the United States to introduce the algorithm into hospital EKG databases. The goal is to examine existing heart scans for signs of elevated risk and identify patients who may benefit from additional monitoring.

Under the proposed approach, physicians would contact patients whose EKGs receive a high-risk assessment and offer them the opportunity to wear a patch that continuously records their heart's electrical activity.

These longer recordings could provide valuable clues about the biological processes responsible for the warning signals detected by the AI. Understanding those processes could help researchers explain why certain hearts are more vulnerable to suddenly developing fatal electrical disturbances.

For some patients, the additional information might ultimately support a recommendation to receive an implanted defibrillator, potentially preventing a sudden and otherwise unexpected death.

Obermeyer has also created a website where people interested in learning about their own risk can provide basic personal information and an email address. The research team can then contact them about EKG analysis when the technology becomes more widely available.

Could AI Reveal New Secrets About the Human Heart?

Beyond its potential to improve the prevention of sudden cardiac death, the discovery highlights how artificial intelligence could help scientists investigate medical mysteries that have resisted conventional approaches.

Rather than simply identifying patients who might need treatment, the algorithm has uncovered patterns in heart activity that researchers do not yet fully understand. Studying those signals could lead to new insights into the electrical disturbances responsible for sudden cardiac death and potentially reveal additional opportunities for prevention.

Obermeyer believes this ability to uncover previously unrecognized biological patterns could become one of AI's most important contributions to medicine, opening new directions for research while helping physicians make better decisions.

"There is also going to be a new way of doing science that comes out of these tools," Obermeyer said, "and it's fun to think about how that starts happening."

Mullin described his son Jim (then 15) suffering a severe traumatic brain injury during a high school wrestling match on January 17, 2020. Jim woke up roughly 26 hours later a “different kid”: short-term memory loss, inability to recognize his parents at first, loss of motor skills (couldn’t touch his nose, shuffled when walking, couldn’t do basic math), and regression from high-school level to roughly third-grade function. •  Later at Mar-a-Lago, Trump told Jim something to the effect of “Do you know why I love your dad? Because he loves you.”
Mullin became visibly emotional while telling the story, saying Trump “did it just because he cared” and not for publicity. text:
Margaret Mitchell had been working at Google for two years before she realized she needed a break.

“I started having regular breakdowns,” says Mitchell, who founded and co-led the company’s Ethical AI team. “That was not something that I had ever experienced before.”

Only after she spoke with a therapist did she understand the problem: she was burnt out. She ended up taking medical leave because of stress. 

Mitchell, who now works as an AI researcher and chief ethics scientist at the AI startup Hugging Face, is far from alone in her experience. Burnout is becoming increasingly common in responsible-AI teams, says Abhishek Gupta, the founder of the Montreal AI Ethics Institute and a responsible-AI consultant at Boston Consulting Group. 

Companies are under increasing pressure from regulators and activists to ensure that their AI products are developed in a way that mitigates any potential harms before they are released. In response, they have invested in teams that evaluate how our lives, societies, and political systems are affected by the way these systems are designed, developed, and deployed. 

Tech companies such as Meta have been forced by courts to offer compensation and extra mental-health support for employees such as content moderators, who often have to sift through graphic and violent content that can be traumatizing. 

But teams who work on responsible AI are often left to fend for themselves, employees told MIT Technology Review, even though the work can be just as psychologically draining as content moderation. Ultimately, this can leave people in these teams feeling undervalued, which can affect their mental health and lead to burnout.

Rumman Chowdhury, who leads Twitter’s Machine Learning Ethics, Transparency, and Accountability team and is another pioneer in applied AI ethics, faced that problem in a previous role. 

“I burned out really hard at one point. And [the situation] just kind of felt hopeless,” she says. 

All the practitioners MIT Technology Review interviewed spoke enthusiastically about their work: it is fueled by passion, a sense of urgency, and the satisfaction of building solutions for real problems. But that sense of mission can be overwhelming without the right support.

“It almost feels like you can’t take a break,” Chowdhury says. “There is a swath of people who work in tech companies whose job it is to protect people on the platform. And there is this feeling like if I take a vacation, or if I am not paying attention 24/7, something really bad is going to happen.”  

Mitchell continues to work in AI ethics, she says, “because there’s such a need for it, and it’s so clear, and so few people see it who are actually in machine learning.” 

But there are plenty of challenges. Organizations place huge pressure on individuals to fix big, systemic problems without proper support, while they often face a near-constant barrage of aggressive criticism online. 

Cognitive dissonance

The role of an AI ethicist or someone in a responsible-AI team varies widely, ranging from analyzing the societal effects of AI systems to developing responsible strategies and policies to fixing technical issues. Typically, these workers are also tasked with coming up with ways to mitigate AI harms, from algorithms that spread hate speech to systems that allocate things like housing and benefits in a discriminatory way to the spread of graphic and violent images and language. 

Trying to fix deeply ingrained issues such as racism, sexism, and discrimination in AI systems might, for example, involve analyzing large data sets that include extremely toxic content, such as rape scenes and racial slurs.

AI systems often reflect and exacerbate the worst problems in our societies, such as racism and sexism. The problematic technologies range from facial recognition systems that classify Black people as gorillas to deepfake software used to make porn videos appearing to feature women who have not consented. Dealing with these issues can be especially taxing to women, people of color, and other marginalized groups, who tend to gravitate toward AI ethics jobs. 

And while burnout is not unique to people working in responsible AI, all the experts MIT Technology Review spoke to said they face particularly tricky challenges in that area. 

“You are working on a thing that you’re very personally harmed by day to day,” Mitchell says. “It makes the reality of discrimination even worse because you can’t ignore it.” 

But despite growing mainstream awareness about the risks AI poses, ethicists still find themselves fighting to be recognized by colleagues in the AI field. 

Some even disparage the work of AI ethicists. Stability AI’s CEO, Emad Mostaque, whose startup built the open-source text-to-image AI Stable Diffusion, said in a tweet that ethics debates around his technology are “paternalistic.” Neither Mostaque nor Stability AI replied to MIT Technology Review’s request for comment by the time of publishing.

“People working in the AI field are mostly engineers. They’re not really open to humanities,” says Emmanuel Goffi, an AI ethicist and founder of the Global AI Ethics Institute, a think tank. 

Companies want a quick technical fix, Goffi says; they want someone to “explain to them how to be ethical through a PowerPoint with three slides and four bullet points.” Ethical thinking needs to go deeper, and it should be applied to how the whole organization functions, Goffi adds.  

“Psychologically, the most difficult part is that you have to make compromises every day—every minute—between what you believe in and what you have to do,” he says. 

The attitude of tech companies generally, and machine-learning teams in particular, compounds the problem, Mitchell says. “Not only do you have to work on these hard problems; you have to prove that they’re worth working on. So it’s completely the opposite of support. It’s pushback.” 

Chowdhury adds, “There are people who think ethics is a worthless field and that we’re negative about the progress [of AI].” 

Social media also makes it easy for critics to pile on researchers. Chowdhury says there’s no point in engaging with people who don’t value what they do, “but it’s hard not to if you’re getting tagged or specifically attacked, or your work is being brought up.” 

Breakneck speed

The rapid pace of artificial-intelligence research doesn’t help either. New breakthroughs come thick and fast. In the past year alone, tech companies have unveiled AI systems that generate images from text, only to announce—just weeks later—even more impressive AI software that can create videos from text alone too. That’s impressive progress, but the harms potentially associated with each new breakthrough can pose a relentless challenge. Text-to-image AI could violate copyrights, and it might be trained on data sets full of toxic material, leading to unsafe outcomes. 

“Chasing whatever’s really trendy, the hot-button issue on Twitter, is exhausting,” Chowdhury says. Ethicists can’t be experts on the myriad different problems that every single new breakthrough poses, she says, yet she still feels she has to keep up with every twist and turn of the AI information cycle for fear of missing something important. 

Chowdhury says that working as part of a well-resourced team at Twitter has helped, reassuring her that she does not have to bear the burden alone. “I know that I can go away for a week and things won’t fall apart, because I’m not the only person doing it,” she says. 

But Chowdhury works at a big tech company with the funds and desire to hire an entire team to work on responsible AI. Not everyone is as lucky. 

People at smaller AI startups face a lot of pressure from venture capital investors to grow the business, and the checks that you’re written from contracts with investors often don’t reflect the extra work that is required to build responsible tech, says Vivek Katial, a data scientist at Multitudes, an Australian startup working on ethical data analytics.

The tech sector should demand more from venture capitalists to “recognize the fact that they need to pay more for technology that’s going to be more responsible,” Katial says. 

The trouble is, many companies can’t even see that they have a problem to begin with, according to a report released by MIT Sloan Management Review and Boston Consulting Group this year. AI was a top strategic priority for 42% of the report’s respondents, but only 19% said their organization had implemented a responsible-AI program. 

Some may believe they’re giving thought to mitigating AI’s risks, but they simply aren’t hiring the right people into the right roles and then giving them the resources they need to put responsible AI into practice, says Gupta.

“That’s where people start to experience frustration and experience burnout,” he adds. 

Growing demand

Before long, companies may not have much choice about whether they back up their words on ethical AI with action, because regulators are starting to introduce AI-specific laws. 

The EU’s upcoming AI Act and AI liability law will require companies to document how they are mitigating harms. In the US, lawmakers in New York, California, and elsewhere are working on regulation for the use of AI in high-risk sectors such as employment. In early October, the White House unveiled the AI Bill of Rights, which lays out five rights Americans should have when it comes to automated systems. The bill is likely to spur federal agencies to increase their scrutiny of AI systems and companies. 

And while the volatile global economy has led many tech companies to freeze hiring and threaten major layoffs, responsible-AI teams have arguably never been more important, because rolling out unsafe or illegal AI systems could expose the company to huge fines or requirements to delete their algorithms. For example, last spring the US Federal Trade Commission forced Weight Watchers to delete its algorithms after the company was found to have illegally collected data on children. Developing AI models and collecting databases are significant investments for companies, and being forced by a regulator to completely delete them is a big blow. 

Burnout and a persistent sense of being undervalued could lead people to leave the field entirely, which could harm the field of AI governance and ethics research as a whole. It’s especially risky given that those with the most experience in solving and addressing harms caused by an organization’s AI may be the most exhausted. 

“The loss of just one person has massive ramifications across entire organizations,” Mitchell says, because the expertise someone has accumulated is extremely hard to replace. In late 2020, Google sacked its ethical AI co-lead Timnit Gebru, and it fired Mitchell a few months later. Several other members of its responsible-AI team left in the space of just a few months.

Gupta says this kind of brain drain poses a “severe risk” to progress in AI ethics and makes it harder for companies to adhere to their programs. 

Last year, Google announced it was doubling its research staff devoted to AI ethics, but it has not commented on its progress since. The company told MIT Technology Review it offers training on mental-health resilience, has a peer-to-peer mental-health support initiative, and gives employees access to digital tools to help with mindfulness. It can also connect them with mental-health providers virtually. It did not respond to questions about Mitchell’s time at the company. 

Meta said it has invested in benefits like a program that gives employees and their families access to 25 free therapy sessions each year. And Twitter said it offers employee counseling and coaching sessions and burnout prevention training. The company also has a peer-support program focused on mental health. None of the companies said they offered support tailored specifically for AI ethics.

As the demand for AI compliance and risk management grows, tech executives need to ensure that they’re investing enough in responsible-AI programs, says Gupta. 

Change starts from the very top. “Executives need to speak with their dollars, their time, their resources, that they’re allocating to this,” he says. Otherwise, people working on ethical AI “are set up for failure.” 

Successful responsible-AI teams need enough tools, resources, and people to work on problems, but they also need agency, connections across the organization, and the power to enact the changes they’re being asked to make, Gupta adds.

A lot of mental-health resources at tech companies center on time management and work-life balance, but more support is needed for people who work on emotionally and psychologically jarring topics, Chowdhury says. Mental-health resources specifically for people working on responsible tech would also help, she adds. 

“There hasn’t been a recognition of the effects of working on this kind of thing, and definitely no support or encouragement for detaching yourself from it,” Mitchell says.

“The only mechanism that big tech companies have to handle the reality of this is to ignore the reality of it.”

text:
There is something rather absurd about a nation which cannot quite decide whether it was born in 927, yet seems perfectly content to leave its public monuments in a state of perpetual artistic adolescence.

Æthelstan deserves a permanent statue, and not merely because he makes a considerably better historical proposition than a succession of fashionable installations which appear to have been selected by a committee suffering from an excess of imagination and a shortage of historical memory.

A statue of Æthelstan would offer something rather more substantial than another temporary exercise in contemporary artistic self-expression. Here are my reasons.

1. He deserves permanence. The man who helped bring England into political existence ought not to be less permanently represented in its capital than a succession of artistic commissions whose principal historical achievement may be to survive their own unveiling ceremonies.

2. He represents a beginning, not an interruption. In 927, Æthelstan established a united English kingdom. William the Conqueror, for all his military accomplishments, arrived in 1066 to conquer an already existing country. There is a rather important distinction between founding a house and breaking into it.

3. He was more than a warrior. Æthelstan was a lawgiver, patron of learning, Christian monarch and statesman. His reign helped establish the political, legal and cultural foundations of England. One might reasonably argue that these are rather better qualifications for a national monument than proficiency in rearranging the furniture of another man's kingdom.

4. He deserves recognition beyond the history books. A nation that cannot identify its own founding king should perhaps reconsider the manner in which it teaches its history. A statue would be a splendid place to begin.

5. The Fourth Plinth needs a sense of historical proportion. I have nothing against modern art, provided it does not demand that history permanently vacate the premises. There is room for experimentation in a great capital, but there ought also to be room for remembrance.

And now, a word about William the Conqueror.

I confess to finding the enthusiasm for a statue of William rather entertaining. Apparently, some people believe that England's greatest historical contribution was to be conquered by a French-speaking duke who arrived with an army, redistributed the property and installed a new management. One might as well commemorate a hostile takeover by erecting a statue of the acquiring company's chairman.

William was undoubtedly a formidable historical figure. But he did not found England. He conquered it. There is no shortage of monuments to conquest, and certainly no shortage of people willing to celebrate the victor. Perhaps, for once, we might honour the man who built the kingdom before somebody else decided to acquire it.

My preference is therefore quite unambiguous: Æthelstan, in bronze, permanently upon the Fourth Plinth. Let the revolving exhibitions revolve elsewhere. England's 1,100th birthday deserves something that will still be standing when the next fashionable artistic revelation has been packed into a removal van.

And if anyone considers this insufficiently progressive, I can only suggest that they try being historically literate. It is an old-fashioned accomplishment, but one with a surprisingly long shelf life.
